Qleisli Programming Language

Qleisli Programming Language

Qleisli is an experimental language for structured quantum algorithms. A Qleisli program prepares qubits, applies gates to them and measures them to obtain ordinary bits. The checker reads the whole program before any of that happens. It rejects a program that uses a qubit twice, loses one, or measures where its signature promised not to.

Three ideas

You will meet three ideas again and again in this book.

  • A quantum value has one owner, and the program uses that owner once. A gate takes an owner and returns one. A measurement takes an owner and returns a bit. The checker follows every owner to the place where the program gives it up.
  • A function declares its effect. The word before fn says whether the function computes on ordinary data, applies gates, prepares qubits or measures. The checker compares that word with the body.
  • A separate verifier decides acceptance. The compiler translates your source and proposes a result. An independent native program, built from Lean, checks the proposal before anything runs. A program you write and a program a tool generates pass through the same checks.

How to use this book

Read the first two parts in order. Each chapter builds on the projects and the vocabulary of the chapters before it.

Learning Qleisli is a course of nine lessons. If you can read a function and use a terminal, start with Measuring your first qubit. You’ll meet the quantum operations as you use them. Each lesson tells you which file to open, asks you to predict a result, and lets you run the program to check.

About Qleisli

Qleisli and its tools are independent projects. They are not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the Rust Project or the Rust Foundation.

Qleisli is pronounced exactly like Kleisli. Its initial Q marks the classical-to-quantum ecosystem lift without changing the pronunciation. See the canonical project name and pronunciation.

The Qleisli Constitution establishes the Qleisli Soundness Theorem, the Physical Realizability Theorem, and the Resource Safety Theorem as its three fundamental proof obligations.

Measuring your first qubit

A qubit is a quantum system with two basis states, called zero and one. What bit do you expect to see when you prepare the zero state and measure in that basis? Write a program to find out, then change its preparation.

Set up the tools

Open a shell at the root of the Qleisli repository. Keep this shell open for the lessons. Save the checkout path so you can find the tools and compare your programs with the bundled examples.

export QLEISLI_REPO="$PWD"

If you have a matching qleisli command and native verifier configured, go straight to the project below. To build them from this checkout you need Rust 1.85 or later and Lean 4.30.0 with Lake and its native build tools. Run both build commands from the repository root.

cargo build --locked --bin qleisli
(cd lean-kernel && lake build && lake env lean -DwarningAsError=true Audit.lean)
export PATH="$QLEISLI_REPO/target/debug:$PATH"
export QLEISLI_KERNEL="$QLEISLI_REPO/lean-kernel/.lake/build/bin/qleisli-kernel"

The first command builds the CLI. The second builds and audits the native verifier, a separate program that decides whether each of your programs is accepted. QLEISLI_KERNEL tells the CLI which executable to use for checking.

Prepare and measure

Create a practice directory. In the following lessons, run the commands from qleisli-lessons, the parent of your projects.

mkdir -p "$HOME/qleisli-lessons/bit-lab"
cd "$HOME/qleisli-lessons"

Save this manifest as bit-lab/Qargo.toml. It tells Qleisli which edition to use when reading this directory.

schema-version = 2

[qrate]
edition = "2026"

In bit-lab/main.qli, write a function that prepares a qubit and measures it.

observe fn main() -> Bit {
    let q = init0();
    measure_z(q)
}

Read the first line as a promise to the caller. The function is named main, the empty parentheses mean it takes no arguments, and -> Bit says it returns one ordinary bit. The word observe allows this function to measure a qubit. Choosing an effect covers the other words that can stand there.

Execution starts inside the braces. init0() prepares a qubit in the zero state. The let binding names its owner q. The final expression, measure_z(q), measures in the computational basis and returns the measured bit. Let’s see what that looks like in the terminal.

qleisli check bit-lab
qleisli run bit-lab

The checker accepts the project. The simulator prints one line.

0: 1.000000000000e0

Read the bit on the left and its probability on the right. Here the only outcome is 0, and its probability is one.

Change the preparation

Replace let q = init0(); with let q = h(init0());. The Hadamard gate h takes the zero state to an equal superposition of zero and one. Run qleisli run bit-lab again. The distribution gives each outcome probability one half. Use sample to see eight individual measurements, called shots.

qleisli sample bit-lab --shots=8 --seed=0

Each shot starts with a fresh preparation. Eight shots can give unequal counts even when the probabilities are equal. Try h(h(init0())) and predict what run will show. Applying Hadamard twice returns the qubit to its starting state, so zero has probability one again.

Next, follow the owner through a measurement.

Following a quantum owner

Suppose you want to return the same random bit twice. Your caller should get either (0, 0) or (1, 1). You already know how to produce one bit. What happens if you write the measurement expression twice?

This lesson uses four rejected programs. Each one shows a different part of the rule that shapes every Qleisli program.

Read the diagnostic

In the bit-lab project from the first lesson, replace main.qli with this deliberately invalid attempt.

observe fn main() -> (Bit, Bit) {
    let q = h(init0());
    (measure_z(q), measure_z(q))
}

Run qleisli check bit-lab. The checker points to the second use of q.

ownership: quantum ownership `q` has already been consumed

q has type Q<Bit>. It is an owner, a value that gives this program the use of a particular quantum system. The first call to measure_z consumes that owner and returns an ordinary Bit. By the time the checker reaches the second call, the function has already used q.

Keep the measurement result

Try repairing the program before reading on. You can introduce one let binding. Which expression should you evaluate once, and which value can you use in both positions of the pair?

Here is one repair for bit-lab/main.qli.

observe fn main() -> (Bit, Bit) {
    let q = h(init0());
    let b = measure_z(q);
    (b, b)
}

Run qleisli check bit-lab and qleisli run bit-lab. The checker accepts both uses of the ordinary bit. The outcomes are 00 and 11, each with probability one half. There was one measurement, and both positions in the returned pair contain its result.

An ordinary value such as b can be read as often as you like. An owner can be used once. The type tells you which of the two a name holds.

Pass an owner through a gate

Measurement is not the only operation that consumes an owner. Replace main.qli with this program and predict which line the checker rejects.

observe fn main() -> Bit {
    let q = init0();
    let r = h(q);
    measure_z(q)
}

Run qleisli check bit-lab. The diagnostic is the one you saw before, and it points to q in the last line.

ownership: quantum ownership `q` has already been consumed

A gate is a function from owners to owners. The call h(q) consumes q and returns the owner of the transformed qubit, which this program names r. After that line the qubit is reachable through r alone.

Change the last line to measure_z(r) and check again. The checker accepts the program. You can also keep one name for the qubit all the way through. Change the middle line to let q = h(q); and the last line back to measure_z(q). The second let binds the name q to the owner that h returned. You will see this shape wherever a gate acts on a named qubit.

Give up an owner you do not need

What if a function prepares a qubit and never uses it? Replace main.qli with a program that has one qubit too many.

observe fn main() -> Bit {
    let q = h(init0());
    let spare = h(init0());
    measure_z(q)
}

Run qleisli check bit-lab. The checker points to spare. Its diagnostic begins with this sentence.

ownership: local quantum ownership `spare` escapes neither through the result nor an explicit discard.

Every owner must leave the function in a way you wrote down. The function can return it, pass it to an operation, or measure it. Reaching the closing brace is not one of those ways. The rest of the diagnostic compares this rule with Rust, where an unused value may simply go out of scope.

Qleisli asks for more because losing a qubit is a physical event. If the qubit is entangled with others, they stay correlated with something the program can no longer reach. Interference that a later gate would have produced from them is lost. The language makes you say so. Add this line after the binding of spare.

    discard(spare);

Check and run the project. The checker accepts the program, and the outcomes 0 and 1 each have probability one half. discard consumes the owner and returns nothing.

Keep both branches even

An if chooses between two blocks at run time. What should the checker do when one block uses an owner and the other does not? Replace main.qli with this program.

observe fn main() -> Bit {
    let coin = measure_z(h(init0()));
    let q = h(init0());
    if coin { measure_z(q) } else { 0 }
}

Run qleisli check bit-lab. The checker points to the if.

ownership: branches must consume the same owners and preserve outer binding types

When coin is one, the first block measures q. When it is zero, the second block leaves q unused. After the if, the checker could not say whether q has an owner. So both blocks must consume the same owners.

Try the repair yourself. The second block has to give up q and produce the bit zero. Then predict the distribution before you run the program.

One repair changes the last line of main to this.

    if coin { measure_z(q) } else { discard(q); 0 }

The simulator reports 0 with probability three quarters and 1 with probability one quarter. Half of the runs take the second block and return zero. The other half measure q, which gives zero half of the time.

What you have seen

An owner leaves a function in one of four ways.

The programWhat happens to the owner
Passes it to a gate or another functionThe call consumes it. The result may contain an owner to use next.
Measures itmeasure_z consumes it and returns an ordinary bit.
Discards itdiscard consumes it and returns nothing.
Returns itThe caller receives it and takes on the same obligation.

Can two different qubits give the same distribution as one bit used twice? In the Bell-pair project you will measure two distinct owners. For the formal rules behind these diagnostics, see Quantum owners.

Building a Bell pair

In the previous lesson both output bits came from a single measurement. Here you will measure two qubits, one time each. First predict whether their results can disagree.

Entangle two qubits

From the practice directory, make another project using the same edition.

mkdir -p bell-lab
cp bit-lab/Qargo.toml bell-lab/Qargo.toml

Save the following function as bell-lab/main.qli.

observe fn main() -> (Bit, Bit) {
    let (left, right) = cnot(h(init0()), init0());
    (measure_z(left), measure_z(right))
}

Read the arguments to cnot from left to right. The first qubit is in an equal superposition and the second starts at zero. A controlled-NOT flips the second qubit on the component where the first is one. It takes the two input owners and returns two output owners, which the pattern binds to left and right.

qleisli check bell-lab
qleisli run bell-lab

The checker accepts the program. The simulator assigns probability one half to 00 and one half to 11. Before measurement the two qubits form an entangled Bell pair. The two names tell you which qubit each operation uses. The joint state determines how their measurements are correlated.

Try two independent preparations

Replace the first line inside main with let (left, right) = (h(init0()), h(init0()));. Keep the two measurement calls and run the project again. Each individual bit has equal chances of being zero or one. This time all four pairs, including 01 and 10, have probability one quarter. Look at pairs when you want to distinguish independence from perfect correlation.

Next, give the Bell circuit its own function and module so you can try different inputs.

Writing functions and modules

Suppose you want to use the circuit from the Bell-pair project with different inputs. Which lines belong to the circuit, and which lines choose what to prepare and measure? Let’s give the circuit a name, then move it into a file that other functions can use.

Give the circuit a name

Replace the contents of bell-lab/main.qli with these two functions.

unitary fn entangle(control: Q<Bit>, target: Q<Bit>) -> (Q<Bit>, Q<Bit>) {
    cnot(h(control), target)
}

observe fn main() -> (Bit, Bit) {
    let (left, right) = entangle(init0(), init0());
    (measure_z(left), measure_z(right))
}

Read the call in main first. Each init0() supplies one argument. Inside entangle, the parameters control and target name those two owners. The type after each parameter name tells you what the caller must pass. The type after -> tells you what comes back. Here that’s a pair of owners. The let pattern gives each returned owner a name in main.

Why does the last line of entangle have no semicolon? The call to cnot is the function’s final expression. Its value becomes the result of the function. The caller can pass those qubits on to another gate or, as main does here, measure them. The unitary function applies gates to its inputs. The measurements belong to the observe function. Choosing an effect explains those two words.

From the practice directory, check the project and run it.

qleisli check bell-lab
qleisli run bell-lab

You should see 00 and 11 with equal probability, just as in the original Bell circuit. Use that distribution to check your next edit.

Move the function into a module

Cut the whole entangle definition from main.qli and paste it into bell-lab/pair.qli. The file name gives the module its name, pair. At the top of main.qli, above observe fn main, add this import.

use pair::entangle;

Run qleisli check bell-lab. The checker points to the import on the first line. Look at the last part of the diagnostic.

project: `pair::entangle` is not public

The checker found the function. Moving it put the caller in a different module, and functions are private to their module by default. In pair.qli, change unitary fn entangle to pub unitary fn entangle. pub makes the function available to other modules. The use in main.qli lets the caller write its short name. Check and run again. The checker accepts the import, and the circuit gives the same two outcomes.

Try a different input

Leave pair.qli as it is. How could you make the measured bits disagree on every shot? The x gate flips a basis bit. Try giving the second parameter x(init0()) and predict which pairs you will see.

Run qleisli run bell-lab. The two outcomes are 01 and 10, each with probability one half. The target starts at one. On the component where the control is one, cnot flips the target back to zero.

Keep your pair.qli file. Next, choose an effect for two more functions in it. In Teleporting a qubit, you’ll use entangle to supply Alice and Bob with a shared Bell pair. For the rules that apply to imports, see Prelude, imports and qualified names.

Choosing an effect

You have written observe fn main and unitary fn entangle. The word before fn is the function’s effect. It is a promise to every caller about what the body can do to qubits. What happens when the body does more than the word allows? Break two promises in the Bell project and find out.

Prepare inside a unitary function

Every caller of entangle has to supply two qubits. Add a function to bell-lab/pair.qli, below entangle, that supplies them itself.

pub unitary fn fresh_pair() -> (Q<Bit>, Q<Bit>) {
    entangle(init0(), init0())
}

Replace bell-lab/main.qli with a program that calls it.

use pair::fresh_pair;

observe fn main() -> (Bit, Bit) {
    let (left, right) = fresh_pair();
    (measure_z(left), measure_z(right))
}

Run qleisli check bell-lab. The checker points to fresh_pair in pair.qli. Its diagnostic begins with this sentence.

effect: body effect `Isometry` exceeds asserted `Unitary` effect of `fresh_pair`.

A unitary function transforms the qubits it receives and returns the same number of qubits. entangle fits: two owners go in and two come out. fresh_pair receives no qubits and returns two. A function that also prepares qubits is an isometry. The checker worked that out from the calls to init0 and compared it with the word you wrote.

In pair.qli, change pub unitary fn fresh_pair to pub isometry fn fresh_pair. Check and run the project. The checker accepts it, and the simulator reports 00 and 11 with probability one half each.

Measure inside an isometry

Move the measurements out of main in the same way. Add a third function to pair.qli.

pub isometry fn read_pair() -> (Bit, Bit) {
    let (left, right) = fresh_pair();
    (measure_z(left), measure_z(right))
}

Replace main.qli with a program that only calls it.

use pair::read_pair;

observe fn main() -> (Bit, Bit) {
    read_pair()
}

Predict the diagnostic before you run qleisli check bell-lab.

effect: body effect `Observe` exceeds asserted `Isometry` effect of `read_pair`.

Measurement turns a qubit into an ordinary bit, and no gate can take that step back. A function that measures has the effect observe. Change pub isometry fn read_pair to pub observe fn read_pair, then check and run. You get the Bell distribution again.

Read the four words

The three quantum effects are ordered from the least to the most a body can do. Each word allows everything the words above it allow.

WordThe body canIn this book
unitaryApply gates to the owners it receivesentangle
isometryAlso prepare qubitsfresh_pair
observeAlso measure and discardread_pair, main

A function can call functions at its own level or below. read_pair can call fresh_pair, and fresh_pair can call entangle. The other direction fails. In main.qli, change observe fn main to unitary fn main and check the project.

effect: body effect `Observe` exceeds asserted `Unitary` effect of `main`.

The body of main contains no measurement of its own. The effect comes from its call to read_pair. An effect covers the whole body, including every function it calls. Change main back to observe fn.

Write the lowest word that the body fits. A caller that sees unitary knows the function neither prepares nor measures anything.

The fourth word, classical, marks a function on ordinary values. It receives no owners and returns none. Add one above main in main.qli.

classical fn agree(a: Bit, b: Bit) -> Bit { not (a xor b) }

Change the result type of main to Bit and its body to these two lines.

    let (left, right) = read_pair();
    agree(left, right)

What will qleisli run bell-lab print? The two bits of a Bell pair always match, so agree returns one every time.

1: 1.000000000000e0

In Searching four inputs a classical function does a second job. It describes a condition that a quantum operation then applies to all candidates at once.

Next, teleport a qubit with the entangle function you kept in pair.qli. For the rules, see Effects and effect assertions on declarations.

Teleporting a qubit

Alice has a qubit. Bob has half of a Bell pair, and Alice has the other half. How can Bob recover the state of Alice’s input if all she sends him is two ordinary bits? You’ll write a function that teleports its input, then try two inputs to find out why Bob needs both bits.

Use the shared Bell pair

From the practice directory, copy the manifest and the pair module from the functions and modules project. This lesson uses its public entangle function.

mkdir -p teleport-lab
cp bell-lab/Qargo.toml bell-lab/pair.qli teleport-lab/

Save the protocol in teleport-lab/transfer.qli. Its argument is a qubit chosen by the caller. Its result keeps Alice’s message alongside Bob’s corrected qubit so you can inspect each outcome.

use pair::entangle;

pub observe fn teleport(input: Q<Bit>) -> ((Bit, Bit), Q<Bit>) {
    let (alice, bob) = entangle(init0(), init0());
    let (input, alice) = cnot(input, alice);
    let phase_bit = measure_z(h(input));
    let parity_bit = measure_z(alice);

    let bob = if parity_bit { x(bob) } else { bob };
    let bob = if phase_bit { z(bob) } else { bob };
    ((phase_bit, parity_bit), bob)
}

Follow the three owners, as you did in Following a quantum owner. The caller supplies input. The first line of the function supplies alice and bob, one for each half of the Bell pair. Alice applies a CNOT to her two qubits and a Hadamard to the first, then measures both. Together those operations make a Bell-basis measurement. The measurements consume both of Alice’s owners.

Alice sends the two results to Bob. Read his two if expressions in order. A parity bit of one tells him to flip his qubit with x. A phase bit of one tells him to apply z, which reverses the sign of the amplitude for 1. Each branch returns the owner that Bob uses next.

Read all four messages

In teleport-lab/main.qli, start with an input whose measurement you can predict. The x gate prepares one from zero. What should the last output bit be if Bob has recovered that state?

use transfer::teleport;

observe fn main() -> ((Bit, Bit), Bit) {
    let input = x(init0());
    let (message, bob) = teleport(input);
    (message, measure_z(bob))
}

qleisli check teleport-lab
qleisli run teleport-lab

The checker accepts the project. The simulator gives these four outcomes.

001: 2.500000000000e-1
011: 2.500000000000e-1
101: 2.500000000000e-1
111: 2.500000000000e-1

Take 101 as an example. Alice obtained phase bit 1 and parity bit 0, so Bob applied only z. His readout is the final 1. All four messages are equally likely, and Bob reads one for every message.

Find a missing correction

Try removing just the let bob = if phase_bit { z(bob) } else { bob }; line from transfer.qli. Check and run the project again. The checker accepts the edit and you get the same four lines. On the state one, a sign change leaves the probability of measuring one unchanged. What input would let you see that the phase correction is missing?

Keep that line out for one more run. In main.qli, change the preparation to let input = h(x(init0())); and the readout to (message, measure_z(h(bob))). The preparation makes the minus state, a superposition in which the zero and one components have opposite signs. The Hadamard before readout measures Bob’s qubit in the X basis. If he recovers the minus state, that Hadamard takes it back to one.

Run the project and look first at the messages whose phase bit is one.

001: 2.500000000000e-1
011: 2.500000000000e-1
100: 2.500000000000e-1
110: 2.500000000000e-1

For messages 10 and 11, Bob reads zero. On those branches the two components have the same sign, and the final Hadamard takes that state to zero. Restore the phase correction and run again. Bob reads one for all four messages. You used the same protocol on two inputs and chose a measurement that makes a relative sign observable.

For one last experiment, return to the first main, which prepares one. Keep the phase correction and remove the parity correction. Which messages should give Bob zero? Run the project and check the middle bit of the two outcomes that end in zero. Restore the parity correction when you’re done.

The bundled protocol example puts Alice’s measurement and Bob’s corrections in reusable functions. Bennett and colleagues derive the protocol for an unknown input in the original teleportation paper.

Next, search four inputs with an algorithm that uses a relative sign to pick out a marked candidate.

Searching four inputs

Imagine a two-bit combination lock. You can write a function that recognizes the right pair of bits. How can a quantum program use that function to find the pair? We’ll build a small Grover search. You’ll be able to run it at three points and see exactly when the marked input becomes more likely.

Prepare the four candidates

From the practice directory, create a project with the same edition manifest you used in bit-lab.

mkdir -p search-lab
cp bit-lab/Qargo.toml search-lab/Qargo.toml

Write the following program in search-lab/main.qli.

use std::measurement::measure_z2;
use std::transform::hadamard2;

observe fn main() -> (Bit, Bit) {
    let prepared = hadamard2(join(init0(), init0()));
    measure_z2(prepared)
}

You’ve already prepared two qubits in the Bell project. Here, join groups their owners into a single owner of type Q<(Bit, Bit)>. hadamard2 applies a Hadamard to each qubit. With these two zero inputs, that gives each candidate an equal chance. measure_z2 measures both and returns their bits in order.

qleisli check search-lab
qleisli run search-lab

The checker accepts the program. The simulator prints four lines.

00: 2.500000000000e-1
01: 2.500000000000e-1
10: 2.500000000000e-1
11: 2.500000000000e-1

Mark one candidate

The rule for our lock fits in one line. A pair matches when both bits are one. Save this module as search-lab/oracle.qli.

use std::gate::z;

classical fn marked((a, b): (Bit, Bit)) -> Bit { a and b }

pub unitary fn mark(q: Q<(Bit, Bit)>) -> Q<(Bit, Bit)> {
    with_computed(q, marked) { |ancilla| z(ancilla) }
}

Start with marked. It takes an ordinary pair apart, gives its bits the names a and b, and returns one only for 11. The public function mark uses this rule on the quantum input. with_computed computes the predicate into a temporary qubit called ancilla. The z gate changes the sign of the component where that qubit is one. The computation is then undone to return the temporary qubit to zero.

In main.qli, add use oracle::mark; to the imports and change the final expression to measure_z2(mark(prepared)). Predict what will happen to the line for 11. Check and run the project again.

All four lines have the same probabilities as before. Each candidate started with an amplitude of +½. Marking takes the amplitude of 11 to −½. Measurement gives the squared magnitude of each amplitude, and both +½ and −½ give ¼. How can the program make use of that sign?

Turn the sign into a measurable difference

Replace search-lab/main.qli with this version. It adds a reflection between marking and measurement.

use oracle::mark;
use std::measurement::measure_z2;
use std::reflection::reflect_uniform2;
use std::transform::hadamard2;

observe fn main() -> (Bit, Bit) {
    let prepared = hadamard2(join(init0(), init0()));
    let marked = mark(prepared);
    let amplified = reflect_uniform2(marked);
    measure_z2(amplified)
}

Run qleisli check search-lab and qleisli run search-lab again. This time the simulator prints one line.

11: 1.000000000000e0

To see where the other three candidates went, follow their amplitudes. After marking, the four signed amplitudes have mean ¼. The reflection takes each amplitude to twice that mean minus its old value.

CandidateAfter markingAfter reflectionProbability
11−½2 × ¼ − (−½) = 11
Each of 00, 01, 10+½2 × ¼ − ½ = 00

Choose a different answer

Try changing the combination to 10 by editing just the predicate in oracle.qli. The first printed bit is a, and not flips a classical bit. Write down your expression before you check and run it.

One solution is a and not b. It returns one when the first bit is one and the second is zero. With the same reflection, the simulator reports 10 with probability one. As a final exercise, choose a predicate for 01 and check which output your program produces.

You have built one Grover iteration for a search with one marked input among four. You can see how the bundled example packages that iteration as a reusable function in $QLEISLI_REPO/examples/grover/search.qli. The standard library reference describes the operations used here. The v1 algorithm goals describe the larger search problem.

Next, state what an operation means and let the checker compare an implementation with it.

Stating what an operation means

In the search project you used reflect_uniform2 without reading its body. You trusted its name. Can a function ask for more than a name? In this lesson a caller states the operation it needs. The checker then compares each implementation you supply with that statement.

Declare a meaning

From the practice directory, create a project with the same edition manifest.

mkdir -p meaning-lab
cp bit-lab/Qargo.toml meaning-lab/Qargo.toml

Save this program as meaning-lab/main.qli.

classical fn flipped(b: Bit) -> Bit { not b }
meaning Flip: Bit = permutation_by(flipped);

unitary fn direct(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { x(q) }

unitary fn client[const U: Op<Bit, Flip>](q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit>
requires Applicable(U) { U(q) }

observe fn main() -> Bit {
    let a = client[checked_op(direct, Flip)](init0());
    measure_z(a)
}

Read it from the top. flipped is an ordinary function on one bit. The meaning line turns it into a specification named Flip: the operation on one qubit that sends each basis state to the state flipped names. A meaning says what an operation does. It contains no gates.

direct is an implementation. It uses the x gate.

client has a parameter in square brackets. U is an operation on Q<Bit> whose meaning is Flip. The caller chooses it when the program is checked, before any qubit exists. The requires line says what client does with U: it applies it.

In main, checked_op(direct, Flip) offers direct as that operation. The checker compares the gates in direct with Flip before it accepts the call.

qleisli check meaning-lab
qleisli run meaning-lab

The checker accepts the program. The simulator reports 1 with probability one, because client flipped a qubit that started at zero.

Supply a second implementation

A Hadamard on each side of z also flips a basis bit. Add this function below direct.

unitary fn sandwich(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { h(z(h(q))) }

Change main to call client twice, once with each implementation.

observe fn main() -> (Bit, Bit) {
    let a = client[checked_op(direct, Flip)](init0());
    let b = client[checked_op(sandwich, Flip)](init0());
    (measure_z(a), measure_z(b))
}

Check and run the project. The checker accepts both calls, and the simulator reports 11 with probability one. client did not change. It names the meaning it needs, and any implementation the checker has compared with that meaning can take the place of U.

Try an implementation that is almost right

Change the body of sandwich to z(x(q)). On a qubit that starts at zero, x gives one, and z leaves the probability of measuring one unchanged. Would main print the same line? Predict what the checker says, then run qleisli check meaning-lab.

contract: exact equation U E_in = E_out u does not hold

The diagnostic points to the second checked_op. The simulator never ran. The measured bits would have been the same, and the checker rejected the program anyway.

z reverses the sign of the amplitude for one. So z(x(q)) sends zero to one with a minus sign and sends one to zero with a plus sign. Flip gives both a plus sign. You saw in the teleportation project that a relative sign changes what a later measurement shows. A meaning is exact. Equal probabilities on one input do not satisfy it.

Restore h(z(h(q))) and check that the project passes.

Ask for what you use

The line requires Applicable(U) names a capability, a use of U that the caller must make available. Applicable lets client apply U. Running U backwards and running U under the control of another qubit are separate capabilities with their own names. A meaning does not grant them. A function lists each capability it uses, and the checker asks every caller to supply it.

You have stated a meaning, supplied two implementations and seen the checker reject a third. The bundled contract example does the same for an operation defined by a phase. Checked operations gives the rules for checked_op and meaning, and Operation access describes the capabilities.

Next, tour the tools with the projects you have built.

Working with the tools

You have typed qleisli check and qleisli run in every lesson and read only the last lines of their output. This lesson goes through the commands one at a time on a single small program. At the end you will know what each command reports, and which questions the report leaves for the next part of the book.

A program to work on

Replace bit-lab/main.qli with a coin flip. The lines that begin with //! and /// are documentation comments.

//! A coin that the caller reads once.

/// Prepares an equal superposition and measures it.
observe fn main() -> Bit {
    let q = h(init0());
    measure_z(q)
}

Read the check report

Run qleisli check bit-lab and read every line this time.

checked source: bit-lab
native checks: IR structure, ownership, interface, classical scope and decoded execution view; 1 concrete local roots, 24 bundled roots
checker: /path/to/qleisli-kernel
checker identity: unpinned
native decisions: 76; native requests checked: 2
entry request checked: false
source preservation: not proved

The counts depend on your program and on the bundled standard library.

LineWhat it tells you
checked sourceThe project directory that the command read.
native checksThe checks that the native verifier ran, and the number of functions it checked. One is yours. The others belong to the standard library.
checkerThe path of the native verifier, the separate executable that made the decisions. It is the one you named in QLEISLI_KERNEL.
checker identityunpinned means the tool ran that file without comparing it to a known build.
native decisionsThe number of times the verifier accepted something during this check. Repeated decisions count each time.
entry request checkedfalse means the verifier checked main without a separate request. A request asks the verifier to check one more stated property of an artifact. Without one, the decision covers the checks on the native checks line.
source preservationnot proved means the checks cover the program that the compiler handed to the verifier. They do not prove that it matches your source.

The report is careful about what it claims. Two of its lines say what the check did not establish. The production boundary defines every field.

Notice the word checker in the report. The lessons have said “the checker” for whatever accepted or rejected your program. Two programs share that work. The qleisli command checks your source and prints the diagnostics you have repaired. The native verifier decides acceptance, and the report’s checker line names it.

Run and sample

qleisli run bit-lab prints the distribution of the result.

0: 5.000000000000e-1
1: 5.000000000000e-1

run computes these probabilities from a simulation of the whole program. sample draws individual results instead. It needs the number of shots and a seed, and the same seed gives the same shots.

qleisli sample bit-lab --shots=8 --seed=0

1
0
0
1
0
0
0
1

Give the result to another program

check, run and sample accept --format=json. A script can then read the result without parsing text.

qleisli run bit-lab --format=json

{"format":"qleisli.result","version":1,"command":"run","outcome":"ok","diagnostics":[],"result":{"distribution":[{"bits":[false],"probability":0.5000000000000001},{"bits":[true],"probability":0.5000000000000001}]}}

A rejected program gives the same envelope with its diagnostics in the diagnostics list. Put the ownership mistake from the second lesson back and run qleisli check bit-lab --format=json to see one. Restore the coin flip afterwards.

Render the documentation

qleisli doc takes one source file and prints its documentation comments as Markdown, with the signature of each function.

qleisli doc bit-lab/main.qli

The output begins with the module comment and continues with one section for each function. Below its title it prints this line.

Source documentation only; no type, ownership or contract verification is implied.

doc reads comments and signatures. It does not check the program, so it needs no verifier.

Keep the checked program

The compiler translates your source into an intermediate representation (IR), a lower-level form of the program that the verifier checks. emit-ir writes that form to a file.

qleisli emit-ir bit-lab --output=coin.qirf

emitted checked IR: coin.qirf
native checks: IR structure, ownership, interface, classical scope and decoded execution view
checker: /path/to/qleisli-kernel
checker identity: unpinned
artifact root request checked: false
source preservation: not proved

Open coin.qirf in an editor. It is a short JSON file that lists the preparation, the Hadamard and the measurement. verify-ir checks such a file on its own, without the source. A file has no manifest, so you name the edition on the command line.

qleisli verify-ir coin.qirf --edition=2026

The verifier accepts the file and prints the same checks. Try changing the gate name "h" in the file to "hh" and run verify-ir again.

invalid_ir: Lean native checker rejected the artifact/request; no fallback

The verifier decides from the bytes in front of it. It does not matter who wrote them.

Export a circuit

The interop commands exchange programs with other formats. They are experimental test features and are not suitable for real quantum hardware.

qleisli interop emit-qasm bit-lab --input=qli

The command prints a JSON result. Its text field holds an OpenQASM 3 program with a reset, an h gate and a measurement. qleisli --help lists every command and option.

What did the check establish?

You have seen the same few lines after every command.

  • A separate executable makes the decisions.
  • It checks a form of the program that is not your source.
  • The report says which statements about main the verifier compared, and which it did not.
  • Nothing proves that the checked form matches what you wrote.

Why is the system built this way? The next part of the book answers by following a project through it. Start with System architecture.

System architecture

In Working with the tools every report named a separate checker executable. This chapter explains that design. It names the parts of the system and follows one of your projects through them. The two chapters after it look inside the compiler and the verifier.

Two programs and one decision

Qleisli uses a Rust host and a separate native Lean verifier. The host is the qleisli command you have been running. It reads source programs or external artifacts and prepares an intermediate representation (IR) for checking. The verifier is the executable you named in QLEISLI_KERNEL. It decides whether the submitted artifact meets the checks for the requested mode. An execution decision from the verifier authorizes the host to use the checked representation for a supported run, sample or export.

Mermaid source

The host proposes and the verifier decides. The host has no path around a rejection. When the verifier is missing or incompatible, the host rejects every command that needs a decision. A command that only reads source, such as qleisli doc, runs without it.

The lessons said “the checker” for whatever accepted or rejected a program. From here on the two programs have their own names. The compiler inside the host checks source and reports the diagnostics you repaired. The verifier decides acceptance.

Components

ComponentResponsibility
Source projectGroups .qli modules and selects the language edition in Qargo.toml. The bundled standard library supplies reusable operations.
Rust hostProvides the qleisli CLI and Rust library. The Python client calls the CLI. The compiler lowers source, and input adapters prepare proposals for supported external formats.
Native verifierIndependently checks proposals in a separate process. The verifier chapter explains what an execution decision binds.
Simulation and exportThe Rust host uses the accepted representation to simulate or sample supported programs. Export additionally requires the checks for the selected format and target profile.

A project through the system

Take the bell-lab project from the Bell-pair lesson. Each command you ran there drives a part of the diagram.

CommandWhat the system does
qleisli check bell-labThe compiler reads the project and checks the source. It lowers each concrete function to IR and submits the IR to the verifier. The report lists the decisions.
qleisli run bell-labThe host also obtains an execution decision for main, then simulates the accepted representation. The result is a distribution over the measured bits.
qleisli sample bell-labThe host follows the same path and reports sampled outcomes from the simulated model.
qleisli emit-ir and verify-irThe first writes the checked IR to a file. The second sends such a file to the verifier without any source.

A rejection can come from either program. The ownership diagnostic in Following a quantum owner came from the compiler, which could name the source line. The invalid_ir rejection of the edited file in Working with the tools came from the verifier, which saw only the file.

Why the decision is separate

The compiler does many things. It parses, resolves names, specializes and lowers, and it grows with every convenience the language gains. A mistake in any of those steps could let a wrong program through. So the system does not rely on the compiler being right. The compiler’s output is a proposal, and an independent program checks it. That program is written in Lean, and it decodes its input itself.

The same rule covers every way a program can arrive. Source you write, source a tool generates and an IR file from elsewhere all reach the same verifier and receive the same checks. Who wrote a program gives it no authority.

Status and limits

The simulator implements a reference model. External formats such as OpenQASM 3 and QIR have bounded experimental profiles. Native acceptance covers the submitted artifact and its requested checks. Correspondence to the original source, the execution result, or emitted hardware operations requires its own evidence.

Going deeper

Continue with Compiler architecture. For the policy this chapter summarizes, read Policy, constitutional harness and execution. The production boundary lists what each check covers, and target realization covers export.

Compiler architecture

Every diagnostic you repaired in the lessons had a code before its message: project, ownership, effect, contract. This chapter walks through the stages of the Rust compiler in order and shows where each of those diagnostics arose.

The compiler loads and checks Qleisli source, then lowers supported programs into IR and evidence proposals. Source checks explain errors in source terms. The independent native verifier decides acceptance of the resulting artifacts.

Mermaid source

Loading and parsing

Project loading fixes the source modules, imports and edition. This stage read your Qargo.toml and every .qli file of the project. It reads and checks a module whether or not another module imports it. The project diagnostic about a function that is not public comes from here.

The parser builds syntax trees with source locations. Those locations are the line and column at the start of every diagnostic. A parse diagnostic means the parser could not read the text as a program. Source text specifies both steps.

Source checking

The common source checker resolves names and checks types, effects, ownership and the requirements of operation calls. It checks both arms of a branch and the body of a zero-iteration fold.

DiagnosticWhat the source checker did
ownership in Following a quantum ownerThe parser read both calls to measure_z. The checker recorded that the first call consumed q, so it could point to the second use.
ownership on an ifThe checker compared the owners that each block consumed and found a difference.
effect in Choosing an effectThe checker computed the effect of the body from its calls and compared it with the word before fn.

All of this happens before lowering, which is why these messages can use the names from your source. The type model describes the checks.

Specialization and lowering

Specialization resolves static arguments to concrete types, sizes and operation providers. In Stating what an operation means, checked_op(direct, Flip) is a static argument of client. Specialization resolved U to direct in the first call and to sandwich in the second.

Elaboration expands supported surface forms into operations in a selected intermediate representation. For example, the source checker checks both arms of if static, then elaboration selects the arm determined by the concrete condition.

The compiler has three lowering routes. Each produces a different proposal.

RouteProposal
Finite projectFinite Raw operations and a serialized QIRF artifact.
Selected RawA Raw operation program for the selected source entry.
Selected hierarchyA composition of operations and proposals for the finite leaves on which it depends.

The coin.qirf file you wrote with emit-ir is a QIRF artifact from the first route. The elaboration contracts specify which forms each route supports.

Handing over

Concrete artifacts and any applicable requests go to the native verifier. The host can map failures back to source locations when it has the corresponding source information.

The contract diagnostic is an example. The compiler lowered the gates of sandwich and proposed them together with the meaning Flip. The verifier compared the two and rejected the equation. The host then reported that rejection at the checked_op in your source.

Status and limits

A generic declaration may pass source checks before a concrete instantiation has a native decision. Support for a source form depends on the chosen lowering route. An IR check establishes the properties of the submitted artifact in its checked scope. A source-preservation claim also needs evidence connecting the original source and dependencies to that artifact. That gap is the line source preservation: not proved in every check report.

Going deeper

Continue with Verifier architecture. Diagnostics and recovery lists the diagnostic codes. Surface-to-core elaboration and Static values, constraints and bounded specialization give the rules for the two lowering steps, and the production boundary states the scope of each check.

Verifier architecture

The compiler ends by handing over a proposal. This chapter follows the proposal into the native verifier. It explains three lines of the check report from Working with the tools: the checker identity, the entry request and source preservation.

The native verifier is the qleisli-kernel executable built from the Mathlib-free Lean package in lean-kernel/. You built it in the first lesson and selected it with QLEISLI_KERNEL. The Rust host submits a proposal to this process. The verifier decodes the input independently and checks the artifact, request and evidence required by the selected mode.

Mermaid source

Request and independent checks

The host sends a versioned QLV3 envelope containing the edition, requested scope, original payload and any required views. The invocation selects a mode and product version. The verifier checks this context and applies the mode’s checks to the decoded data.

The verifier does not reuse the compiler’s conclusions. It decodes the bytes it receives and checks them itself. Two modes are familiar from the lessons.

ModeWhat the verifier checksWhere you saw it
Ordinary QIRF checkOwnership and classical scope of the decoded programThe line native checks of every report, and verify-ir on coin.qirf
Finite contractThe requested equation against the decoded artifactThe rejected checked_op in Stating what an operation means

The compiler had already checked ownership in your source. The verifier checks ownership again in the IR, because the IR is what runs.

Execution binding

Passing the checks is not yet permission to run. The host could, by mistake, simulate something other than the program the verifier checked. The execution binding closes that gap.

An execution view describes the data the Rust host retains for execution. The host encodes the view in the canonical QDV1 format. The verifier derives its own view from the data it decodes and checks, then compares the encoded bytes. The requested scope determines which views it compares. An inspection result covers inspection. The host constructs its private accepted execution handle only from a matching execution decision.

You can see the two scopes in the Bell-pair project. qleisli check bell-lab checks the project’s concrete functions. When you run qleisli run bell-lab, the CLI requests an execution decision for main before it simulates the two measurements.

Rejection

A malformed input, a failed check or a view mismatch rejects the request. The host also rejects when the selected verifier is missing or incompatible. There is no fallback checker and no automatic download. The execution-view reference specifies the envelope, scope, comparison and reply formats.

What a decision does not cover

The report states three limits of a decision.

Report lineThe limit
checker identity: unpinnedThe host ran the executable you selected. It did not compare that file with a known build.
entry request checked: falseThe verifier checked main without a separate request. The decision covers the checks on the native checks line. It establishes no independently requested property of main.
source preservation: not provedThe decision covers the IR. No proof connects that IR to the source text.

Status and limits

The separate lean/ package contains mathematical models and proofs about the executable checks. The two admitted guarantees concern ownership and classical scope of the decoded ordinary root. Source and runtime correspondence, target realization and full quantitative resource bounds have separate proof obligations.

Going deeper

The production boundary gives the scope of each check and every field of the report. The execution-view reference defines the binding, and the primitive boundary defines the operations the verifier admits. The authority hierarchy and the initial guarantees record what the project claims on the strength of these checks.

Rust core crate map closes this part with a proposed layout for the host’s code.

Rust core crate map

The root Cargo manifest defines one production package, qleisli, with a library and a CLI target. Its compiler, native-checker client, simulator, and interchange code are modules of that library. The diagram proposes a future Cargo workspace for those responsibilities. Package names and splits are design candidates.

A solid arrow goes from a Cargo package to a package it depends on. The dashed arrow is a native process call to the Lean verifier. Mermaid source

Proposed crate responsibilities

PackageResponsibility
qleisliPublic library API and CLI composition. Selects the source, check, execution, or export route.
qleisli-compilerLoads and checks source, specializes it, and produces Core IR, Circuit IR, and lowering evidence.
qleisli-core-irThe canonical typed, first-order program representation, including ownership, effects, and exact contracts.
qleisli-circuit-irA structured circuit representation with ordered wires, reusable composition, and explicit measurements.
qleisli-ir-typesShared representation types such as ordered ports and exact coefficients for the two IRs.
qleisli-kernel-clientEncodes native requests, validates replies, and constructs private execution handles from matching Lean decisions.
qleisli-runtimeSimulates and samples supported programs using accepted execution handles.
qleisli-interopAdapts supported external inputs into proposals and exports supported target formats under their applicable checks.

Boundaries

The compiler and IR crates produce or represent proposals. Core IR carries the canonical program meaning. Circuit IR represents a lower-level structure whose correspondence to Core needs checked evidence. Source-to-Core correspondence and target realization have their own evidence obligations.

The native verifier is built from a separate Lean package. It decides whether each submitted artifact and its evidence satisfy the requested checks. The Rust client binds the decision to the exact retained data before the runtime or exporter uses it. Qleisli source projects select their own qrate and edition through Qargo.toml. Cargo packages organize the Rust implementation.

Status and limits

The map is a packaging proposal informed by the planned Core and Circuit IR boundary. Workspace membership, public package names, and re-exports need review alongside compatibility and the compiler design.

History

The Core and Circuit IR design records the intended IR and preservation boundaries. The v1 compiler design describes the requirements for the eventual implementation boundary.

Source text and lexical boundary

The source text of a Qleisli program is the UTF-8 bytes of its modules. This chapter specifies how the scanner and the parser read source text in constitutional edition 2026. It also specifies the source forms and the source obligations that the frontend checks on every program.

Every program goes through one mandatory check, the common judgment. It checks each complete original AST. It runs before any concrete profile decides eligibility.

Two loaders read source text, one for each route of the CLI. The project loader reads a source root for the project route. The selected loader reads explicitly supplied modules for the selected-entry route. The chapter also uses these terms:

TermMeaningDefined in
Project route, selected-entry routeThe two routes of the qleisli CLIDiagnostics and recovery
Finite project, Selected Raw, Selected hierarchyThe three lowering profilesElaboration
Native checkerThe checker executable that lean-kernel/ buildsElaboration

Each rule names the class of diagnostic that the common judgment reports for a program that breaks the rule. Codes maps each class to the code of each route. A syntax error has the code parse on both routes, except for the limit refusals that Status and limits lists.

Two other chapters cover neighboring subjects. The qrate and artifact Reference keeps two things apart. One is the canonical identity of a module or a declaration. The other is the storage of source files and the resolved configuration. The gaps that it records in edition binding are separate from the scanner and parser checks.

The elaboration whitelist specifies the permitted expansion from surface forms to core forms. It also specifies evaluation order, owners, phase, original locations and the independent checking obligations that stay open. It grants no unsupported projection.

Source loading and the common judgment

Loading turns the bytes of the modules into a form that the checker can read. Whichever loader reads a program, the result is one source representation, and the common judgment checks it.

Rules:

  • Both loaders must use one scanner, one token stream, one parser and one source Module/Span representation.
  • The common judgment must check each complete original AST first. Finite or selected concrete eligibility is decided after it.
  • The common judgment supplies these facts about a program: declaration and lexical identities, types, static premises, owner and access rules, body dependencies and principal effects.
  • The common judgment checks every declaration. This includes private and unused siblings, both arms of a branch and the body of a fold with zero iterations.
  • A program that only parses has no source approval and no native verification evidence. Neither parsing nor source checking adds emitter support or an Op<A,B> form.
  • A source-semantic error takes precedence over an unsupported concrete form. This holds even when the error is in an unused declaration.
  • When a profile does not support the projection of a declaration and that definition is requested, the result is an eligibility failure with a location. The original body is not skipped, and the failure is not a fallback source approval.
  • Both loaders add the eight ordinary source modules of the fixed registry and validate its edition-2026 manifest. The bundled modules undergo the same common judgment as caller source.
  • Each loader applies its byte policy to bundled bytes before copying or parsing. A module placed under std:: is exempt from no check.
  • The selected loader reserves all eight bundled module slots. It accepts 1 through 56 supplied modules. Status and limits gives its byte limits.

Implementation note. src/frontend/check.rs and the modules under src/frontend/check/ implement the common judgment. One private source collection retains the complete original bytes, the common AST and the provenance. A filesystem entry retains its selected path. An in-memory entry carries no invented file or manifest.

Implementation note. The project loader moves the collection into the mutable Project compatibility view. Three kinds of operation rebuild their facts from the original ASTs that the view holds at the time they run: finite checking, compilation and checked-effect operations. After a caller mutates the view, nothing reuses a stale parallel collection or a stale approval. Documentation and rendering that read source only gain no semantic checking from this. The selected loader retains its immutable originals. It records a concrete projection result for each declaration only after the common judgment is complete.

Native check modes

The implementation notes and the status section of this chapter refer to four modes of the native checker. Each mode has a short name:

Short nameMode of the native checkerRequestSpecified in
ordinary-v2 check--ordinary-root-checkqleisli.ordinary-root-request version 2, profile finite-ordinary-root-v2Ordinary input/result requests
runtime-v2 check--runtime-root-checkqleisli.runtime-root-request version 2, profile finite-runtime-root-v2Mixed runtime root requests
v5 source check--qmatch-source-v5-checkqleisli.qmatch-request version 5Version 5: source-body requests
encoded-contract check--qirf-contractA qleisli.native-contract encoded equationEntrypoints

QDV1 is the canonical encoding of an execution view. The execution-view chapter specifies the encoding and the comparison that the native checker makes with it. This chapter writes “QDV” for a record in that encoding.

Bytes, characters and positions

This section says which bytes and characters the scanner accepts, and how a diagnostic points into the source. Source is a sequence of UTF-8 bytes. A span is a half-open byte interval in the original input: it includes its first offset and excludes its last.

Rules:

  • Source must be UTF-8. Source loading, scanning and diagnostics must not normalize its bytes.
  • LF and CRLF are the accepted line endings. Ordinary whitespace is ASCII space or tab.
  • Bare CR, vertical tab, form feed and non-ASCII whitespace are rejected (parse).
  • Bidi controls and other control characters are rejected, including in comments (parse).
  • The scanner rejects every Unicode scalar value that has either of two properties in Unicode 17.0.0 (parse). The properties are Default_Ignorable_Code_Point and General_Category=Format (Cf). They cover Unicode tags, variation selectors, U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE and U+FEFF, including a leading U+FEFF.
  • The diagnostic of a rejected scalar prints the offending U+XXXX code point and its original byte span. The span covers the complete UTF-8 encoding of the scalar.
  • The scalar rule applies everywhere: inside all comments, to documentation input such as qleisli doc, and to bundled and project sources. The scanner does not repair the text. It preserves the original bytes and rejects the scalar, and the author removes the scalar from the source.
  • An identifier begins with an ASCII letter or an underscore. ASCII letters, digits and underscores follow.
  • A comment may contain ordinary Unicode prose that satisfies the same scalar rules.

The pinned properties come from the Unicode 17.0.0 derived core properties and general categories.

Comments and documentation

A comment holds prose for readers of the source. A documentation comment also belongs to an item. An outer documentation comment stands before its item, and an inner one stands at the start of the module or the body that it documents.

SpellingKind
//A line comment
/* ... */A nested block comment
//! and /*! ... */Inner documentation comments
/// and /** ... */Outer documentation comments
////, /*** and /**/The start of an ordinary comment

Rules:

  • An unclosed block comment is rejected (parse) with the common unterminated block comment diagnostic.
  • Character validation applies equally to code, ordinary comments and documentation comments. A comment cannot hide a forbidden control.
  • Documentation text may normalize CRLF to LF in its extracted metadata. Source offsets refer to the original bytes.
  • Outer documentation must precede a function, a type, a type member or a use item (parse).
  • Inner documentation must start a module, a type body or a function body (parse).
  • Both loaders classify comments and place documentation by the same rules. One common check attaches documentation to declarations. It rejects misplaced documentation before either profile checks source. No profile may silently ignore invalid placement.
  • Type and member documentation attaches to the original occurrences of the type and the member.
  • Documentation metadata only describes. Rendering from source alone makes no verification claim.

Implementation note. parse_documented_module returns the documentation metadata. Ordinary module loading may retain only the syntax and the original source.

Punctuation and tokens

The grammar reads tokens, and tokens are built in two steps. The physical scanner recognizes individual punctuation marks. The common lexer then forms the tokens of the grammar from them.

Rules:

  • The lexer forms a composite token only from immediately adjacent marks. Whitespace and comments never join marks. For example, :: is distinct from : /* comment */ :.
  • The token stream includes the arithmetic and comparison marks. ==> is == followed by >. It is not an alternative arrow.
  • The scanner and the parser never retry another grammar. They never choose a backend from the input.
  • The lexer scans the complete file before parsing. The diagnostic for a retired token later in the file can therefore come before a grammar error earlier in the file.
  • A file can exceed the token capacity at a token that also has a migration diagnostic. The capacity rejection keeps precedence over that migration diagnostic.
  • Empty parentheses in a type position are rejected (parse) with a diagnostic that directs the author to Unit. The value and the pattern are ().
  • The shared syntax can represent these forms: the empty pattern and block, the empty yield, empty specialization brackets and a trailing comma after a parameter.
  • The recursion budget of the parser counts the quantum wrapper and its basis parse together. Status and limits gives the scanner and parser limits.

Reserved words and contextual words

A reserved word has a fixed role in the grammar, so a program cannot use it as a name.

The common grammar reserves these words in every identifier position: use, meaning, static, Op, requires, Apply, Adjoint, Controlled, permutation_by, phase_by, checked_op, bind_op, inverse_op, then_op, tensor_op, controlled_op, repeat_op, conjugate_op, pub, classical, basis, isometry, iso, unitary, observe, fn, let, if, else, qfor, do, pure, with_computed, apply_contract, adjoint, repeat_static, qif, qmatch, enum, struct, match, true, false, not, xor, and, Unit, Bit, CBit and Q.

Rules:

  • A function, a binding or a module path must not use a reserved word as its name. For example, a declaration or a finite filesystem module name that uses checked_op, enum, struct, match or qmatch as an ordinary identifier must be renamed.
  • The rule does not reach a comment or a longer identifier that contains a reserved word. isotope and iso_value are ordinary identifiers.
  • One exception serves imports. It admits basis, observe and classical as module names immediately after std::.
  • A second exception serves static Nat positions. The static-Nat grammar permits Q, Op, Unit, Bit and CBit in three positions: as a const Nat formal, as a static fold index, or as the first name atom of a Nat expression. The exception is confined to those Nat positions. The reserved-word rules apply unchanged to ordinary runtime identifiers, to Basis and Op formal names and to the tails of qualified paths.
  • qfor starts an explicitly static quantum-owner fold. for static starts an ordinary-only fold.
  • checked_op is the exact-meaning constructor that Checked operations specifies. classical fn declares a total ordinary computation. The basis expression is a distinct form, and Coherent basis maps specifies it.
  • The selected route names its modules by explicit keys. Those keys keep their separate validation rules. They are not unified with finite filesystem module names.

Some words are reserved only so that the parser can reject a retired form with a located migration error. Such a word is never an accepted alias, and it is not an ordinary identifier.

Reserved wordRetired formReplacement
isoThe effect prefix iso fnisometry fn
do, pureThe coherent notation do p <- q; pure ebasis q as p { e }
bind_opThe exact-meaning constructorchecked_op
Apply, Adjoint, ControlledCapability requirementsApplicable, Adjointable, Controllable
inverse_op, controlled_opStatic operation descriptionsadjoint(U), controlled(U)
repeat_op, repeat_staticStatic repetitionpower(U, k), and power(U, k)(q) for an application
CBit, true, falseThe old type and literal usesBit, and 0/1

do and pure introduce no accepted expression, alias, monadic operation or state preparation. The lexer retains the tokens for CBit, true and false so that the parser can reject their old uses with a targeted diagnostic. Retaining the tokens does not keep those uses accepted. adjoint(U) is the static description and adjoint(U)(q) is its application. The two-argument form is retired.

A contextual word has a role in one position and is an ordinary identifier elsewhere:

WordRoleElsewhere
Applicable, Adjointable, ControllableA capability requirement in a requires clause, followed by an operation parameter in parenthesesAn ordinary identifier
Bits, CBits, NatA type name or a kind name. Type-position CBits<n> is rejected; the replacement is Bits<n>.A valid name in identifier positions
asSeparates the quantum input expression and the pattern in basis input as pattern { expression }An ordinary identifier
mutThe marker of let mut name = ..., which the common judgment rejectsAn ordinary identifier: let mut = 0; mut is an ordinary immutable binding and its use
for, in, carry, yieldfor in for static, the in and carry parts of either fold header, and yield at the start of a fold tailAn identifier
controlledcontrolled(op)(args) is the controlled-application constructOrdinary single-stage name resolution: controlled(q) is an ordinary call to an identifier
inverseThe two-stage form inverse(U)(q) is rejected (parse), and the diagnostic suggests adjoint(U)(q). Adjoint application gives the rules.Normal name resolution: inverse(q) is an ordinary call, and a function or a local named inverse is an ordinary name
qletNoneAn ordinary identifier

Neither spelling of controlled guesses the category of a resolved provider, and neither grants control access.

Numerals and natural expressions

A numeral is a run of decimal digits. A program writes numerals as Bit literals, as static Nat literals and inside natural expressions such as a repetition count.

Rules:

  • A numeral token retains its decimal spelling. The scanner does not convert it to a machine integer, infer a Bit or Nat category, or grant a static value.
  • The common parser for natural expressions rejects a numeral with leading zeroes, except 0 itself. It also rejects a literal that exceeds i128.
  • The parser retains addition, subtraction, multiplication and parentheses with their source spans. Multiplication binds more tightly than addition or subtraction.
  • Static checks require an expression to be nonnegative, bounded and supported.
  • A power repetition count has the 2^e form, with a compound exponent in parentheses. This is not general exponentiation in the natural-expression language.
  • Finite lowering evaluates each original power count under its complete static bindings. It computes with checked ordinary-u32 intermediates, and it bounds every nested count to 0 through 4096. An outer count of zero does not excuse an invalid inner count or the closed contract of a child.
  • Ordinary Bit expressions and basis Bit expressions recognize the literals 0/1 with one shared recognizer. Other numerals are not Bit values. This rule does not change static-Nat literals, and it infers no quantum owner from a numeral.

Bindings, patterns and evaluation order

A pattern names the parts of a value where a program binds it: in a parameter, a let or a fold carry. This section gives the rules for patterns, for the names they bind and for the order in which expressions evaluate before binding. One common traversal of patterns applies the runtime rules for wildcards, for duplicate names and for exact tuple and Unit shapes.

Rules:

  • Ordered static kinds and runtime parameter names retain the ordinals of their original declaration and their binder identities.
  • A static kind may refer only to static parameters that precede it. Registering the complete declaration does not make a forward static kind available.
  • Each quantum value has a fresh dynamic owner identity. These identities are distinct from the lexical keys.
  • Arguments and right-hand-side expressions evaluate completely, once and from left to right, before binding.
  • A parameter of an ordinary or a classical function uses the name, wildcard and tuple pattern syntax. The colon annotates the entire parameter pattern, and the source argument list keeps that parameter as one argument. For example, unitary fn first((a, _): (Bit, Bit)) -> Bit { a } takes one ordinary pair.
  • Pattern checking preserves exact arity and nesting. It rejects duplicate parameter names (class binding), and it checks quantum ownership even in unused declarations.
  • A tuple pattern does not implicitly split a quantum register.
  • Argument expressions keep their evaluation order and their effects, and they run before the callee binds its parameters. A wildcard or Unit pattern does not erase the computation that produced its argument.
  • A runtime parameter, a let binding or a fold-carry binding must not shadow an active static Nat, Basis, Op or fold-index binder (class shadow). Static formals may shadow global declarations.
  • Once a right-hand side is completely evaluated, a consumed quantum owner may be rebound. Hiding a live owner is rejected. This includes a zero-axis owner and an owner nested in a product.
  • A static name used as a runtime value is a located type error. Reuse of a consumed runtime owner is an ownership error.
  • A resolved local value used as a callee is a wrong-category error. The checker never retries through a global declaration of the same name.

Assignment and let mut

A checked program contains no assignment and no mutable binding. The raw AST retains bare lexical assignment and a let mut name = ... marker solely so that the checker can refuse them with a typed diagnostic. See the assignment and mutability boundary.

Rules:

  • Neither form can occur in a successfully checked program, and neither is lowered to replacement.
  • For an assignment, the checker inspects the type of the resolved destination before it checks the right-hand side. Even a consuming right-hand side does not authorize replacing a place that contains a quantum value.
  • For a mutable binding, the checker checks the type of the initializer. The type tells quantum ownership (class ownership) apart from unsupported ordinary mutability (class unsupported).
  • Both refusals retain the original byte locations.
  • General field and index assignment syntax and ordinary reassignment are unsupported. These diagnostic forms grant neither.

Declaration resolution

Resolution finds the declaration that a name refers to. An unqualified call resolves its name in this order:

  1. Lexical runtime and static bindings.
  2. Ordinary declarations of the same module, and explicit imports.
  3. The six derived names of the ordinary prelude.
  4. A language primitive, only when the spelling is otherwise unbound.

Rules:

  • The first place that binds the name selects the use. A fault in that use is the error that the checker reports, and no fallback exists. This holds for a moved binding, for a wrong callable category and for a failed ordinary type, effect or access check.
  • A local binding that has been moved shadows a declaration with the same name. When the local lookup fails, the checker does not fall back to that declaration.
  • Primitives require no import and no prelude, and their names are not reserved. Qualified foundation paths and hidden aliases are unavailable.
  • An ordinary standard-library import keeps its visibility, its public effects and its source and body obligations.
  • An imported declaration keeps its canonical module and declaration name. Imports add no runtime action and no verification privilege.
  • Visibility is checked before use. A private declaration cannot be imported from another module or selected as a host entry. Cross-module imports and host-selected entries require public visibility.
  • On the selected-entry route, the host can supply a provider. The checker checks such a provider from the context of the entry module, even when the provider is unused.
  • Both loaders resolve imports against the complete tables of registered declarations. A valid reference to a sibling resolves against the same tables, whether the sibling is declared before or after the reference. A call to a sibling in the same module may use a private declaration.
  • A cycle that consists only of unused imports is permitted, because imports have no runtime action.
  • Every self-import is a declaration-name collision. This includes a private or public declaration imported into its own module. Duplicate imports and clashes with local declarations are rejected.
  • The diagnostic for a missing member, a private member, a collision or a retired foundation entry points to the final path token. The diagnostic for a missing module points to the complete use span.
  • The checker builds one graph from every original body. Runtime calls, static providers, classical dependencies and Meaning dependencies all enter this checked graph. Mutual cycles are rejected.
  • Only one kind of recursion is permitted: a runtime self-call to the identical DefId with the checked Nat decrease. The directly transformed runtime form of such a call is permitted too. A recursive opaque provider, a classical or Meaning cycle or a failed decrease does not qualify.
  • Names, effect fixed points and zero-count repetition cannot stand for the required decrease proof.
  • Transparent pub use, root-qualified references and the explicit prelude opt-out follow the prelude and import contract.
  • The checker discovers no standard library from its surroundings, and a reserved std module cannot be replaced. as, glob and relative imports are unsupported.
  • Evidence retains the original source, dependencies, canonical names and static bindings.

The primitive boundary gives the canonical primitive identities and the complete migration of the 27 retired qualified entries.

Implementation note. src/frontend/resolve.rs and resolve/locals.rs retain the associations among canonical declarations, lexical uses and original spans. The common typed primitive catalog has 13 bare typed identities. The finite and selected concrete emitters keep their profile-specific adapters. Private Rust debug representations are not canonical names or evidence formats. Their printed fields change with the internal resolver.

Parsed finite type declarations

enum Name { A, B, ... }
struct Name { field: Type, ... }

A program declares its own finite ordinary types with these two forms. An enum declaration has fieldless variants. A struct declaration is a record with named fields. Either may follow pub, and each record field has its own pub marker.

The common judgment elaborates a declaration into an ordinary nominal type tree. The tree keeps the original module, declaration and source identity, the variant order and the complete ordered field types.

Four expression forms use these types:

FormMeaning
Type::VariantAn explicit fieldless variant
Type { field: expression, ... }A record literal
value.fieldAn ordinary field of a record
match value { Type::A => arm, ... }Ordinary selection on an enum value

The type model specifies these forms and their capacities.

Rules:

  • A declaration has at most 64 members, which is the source product limit.
  • Payload variants, discriminant assignments, tuple structs and generic type declarations are not parsed.
  • An empty record is a distinct declaration. The parser does not replace it with Unit.
  • Parsing does not make an empty enum, or invalid or duplicate type members, semantically valid. Three faults are rejected at the original offending name: a collision between a function and a type, an empty enum, and a duplicate variant or field name. These name checks come before finite field elaboration.
  • A field must have an ordinary finite type. Unknown, recursive, non-type and quantum-owned fields are rejected.
  • A closed field size reuses the arithmetic and the premise checks of the Nat helpers. It adds no general const<T>.
  • A signature keeps both T and Q<T>. Nominal identity is not reduced to physical width.
  • The common resolver for modules, imports and reexports also resolves nominal names. They form a distinct type category that is local to the collection. A transparent reexport keeps the original declaration and its visibility. Source-path traversal keeps each alias module.
  • Each module or import spelling must have an unambiguous binding.
  • A local ordered Basis binder cannot fall back to a global enum. A consumer that expects a callable or an operation rejects a type target.
  • The common judgment checks the variant, record and field forms. It checks them with their original type and member identity, their visibility and the written initializer order.
  • An ordinary match must use exact qualified enum labels, and its arms must be exhaustive and disjoint. It has at most 64 arms. A runtime block allows an expression or a block for each arm. A classical body allows an ordinary expression for each arm.
  • Each declaration keeps its whole original span, its body span and its ordered variants or fields. A named type path keeps all its qualified segments and their byte span.

The project route accepts this program, and main returns 1. The record literal writes its fields in an order other than the declared order:

struct Empty {}
struct Packet { bit: Bit, empty: Empty }
