Surface-to-core elaboration

An elaboration is the expansion of one surface form of a .qli program into operations of an existing core representation. A surface form is a construct as the program writes it, such as a call, a pattern or a fold.

This chapter specifies the convenience elaborations that edition 2026 permits. It gives a contract for each one. A contract names the surface form and the target of the expansion. It states the evaluation order, the owners, the exact phase and the source spans. It lists the refusals, and it lists the obligations that the expansion leaves open. The chapter is subordinate to the authority hierarchy.

The chapter introduces no syntax, no primitive, no implicit conversion, no evidence authority and no supported emitter.

Rules:

  • An elaboration may insert only the uniquely determined operations that its section describes.
  • An elaboration must preserve five things: the evaluation order, the complete type trees, the logical owners, the exact phase and the original source attribution.
  • An elaboration must not infer an arbitrary isomorphism, a permutation, cleanup, operator equality or an unavailable capability.

Source and acceptance boundary

This section names the check that comes before elaboration and the check that decides acceptance after it.

The common checker applies the common source judgment to the complete original AST of a program. Elaboration comes after this judgment.

A target is an existing representation that an expansion produces. Three targets exist, and they are distinct:

TargetProposals that it produces
Finite projectFinite Raw and QIRF proposals
Selected RawSelected-source Raw proposals
Selected hierarchySelected hierarchy and finite-leaf proposals

The Target field of a contract identifies an existing representation on one or more of these targets. It does not claim that one canonical typed Core or one converged emitter has replaced them. Each target supports a bounded profile of programs.

The native checker is the checker executable that lean-kernel/ builds. It decides whether a proposal is accepted. It decides this independently of the component that produced the proposal.

Rules:

  • The common checker checks every declaration, both arms of every branch and the body of a fold with zero iterations.
  • Static bindings and immutable facts are inputs to concrete elaboration. They are not accepted handles of the native checker.
  • A supported surface form may have an unsupported projection or target. A failure must not select a weaker checker.
  • Every resulting artifact, dependency and independent request must pass the production gate that applies to it.
  • Handwritten IR and generated IR have the same requirements for independent acceptance.
  • Four activities confer no acceptance: Rust normalization, source checking, source-step comparison and proposal generation.
  • Valid output alone does not prove source preservation.

Implementation note. The common checker is src/frontend/check.rs with the modules under src/frontend/check/. The Rust frontend parses, reports diagnostics and generates proposals. It issues no acceptance.

Whitelist

The whitelist names every surface form that has an elaboration contract in this chapter. Literal values, sealed operations and explicit structural maps keep their separate type and primitive contracts. An implementation detail or an Issue candidate does not enlarge the whitelist.

Surface formPermitted expansionSection
Runtime products, patterns and ordinary callsBinding of the exact value tree, and expansion of the checked body of the calleeRuntime products, patterns and calls
Whole-owner excl callsOne checked consuming call. The same lexical binders retain the returned values.Whole-owner exclusive calls
Static indexed access and slice accessAn ordered partition, one checked call, and reconstruction from the updated selected ownersStatic ordered-axis places
Ordinary Boolean expressions and classical fn callsEager operations on ordinary valuesOrdinary expressions and classical functions
Enum values, record values and value.fieldOrdinary values that keep their nominal typeNominal values
Runtime classical ifClassical branches, with complete joins of the result and the frameRuntime classical branches
Ordinary matchClassical branches on the enum tag, with complete joins of the result and the frameOrdinary match
Static naturals, aliases and bounded helpersExact checked substitution, with no runtime instructionStatic natural computation
Bracket specialization and if staticClosed checked instances and the selected armSpecialization and static selection
for static and qfor staticExplicit threading of the carry over a closed finite rangeFinite folds
Static operation descriptions and applicationOperations bound to their providers, and checked transformation proposalsOperation descriptions and application
controlled(U)(c,q) and two-arm qifThe exact controlled action, which retains the inactive identity actionCoherent control
qmatch(s,q) { label => arm, ... }The exact selected action on the target, with one arm for each selector labelExact-label coherent selection
basis q as p { e }The specified coherent lift with the coefficient +1Coherent basis maps
Existing with_computed formsThe checked construction of compute, use and uncomputeComputed workspace
apply_contract(F, S, q)One application of the implementation F, with a checked obligation of function equality against SFunction contracts

The whitelist is not a list of every accepted surface form. Status and limits names the accepted forms that this chapter does not specify.

Each entry has one section. The section gives a description, a contract table and examples. Every contract table has the same eight fields:

FieldContent
SourceThe surface form that the entry covers
TargetThe representation that the expansion produces
Evaluation orderWhen each part of the form evaluates
OwnersThe quantum owners that the form consumes and returns
Exact phaseThe action, with its phase, that the expansion must keep
Source spansThe original locations that the expansion retains
RefusalThe programs that the form rejects
Open obligationsThe requirements that the expansion leaves to independent checks

The last field states requirements. It discharges no guarantee and adds no ledger entry. The linked Reference sections specify the detailed grammar, the capabilities and the profile limits.

Each example says which check accepts or rejects the program. Diagnostics and recovery defines the project route, the selected-entry route and the codes of each. An example that names the common checker gives the class of the failure in that checker.

Runtime products, patterns and calls

A runtime product is an ordered tuple of runtime values. A let pattern or a parameter pattern binds the leaves of such a value. An ordinary call binds its arguments to the parameters of a resolved function and expands the checked body of that function.

FieldContract
SourceOrdered runtime products, let patterns and parameter patterns, and resolved calls of ordinary functions
TargetBindings of the exact value tree and the checked body of the callee, as Raw operations or as supported selected source steps
Evaluation orderEach right-hand side and each argument evaluates completely, once, from left to right, before binding. An argument list is not one automatically packed tuple.
OwnersEach quantum leaf moves once. Destructuring (Q<A>,Q<B>) never splits Q<(A,B)>. The expansion preserves pending arguments and the suspended owners of the caller. Ordinary leaves may be copied or ignored.
Exact phaseBinding, grouping and call expansion insert no gate and no phase. The expansion preserves the action of the callee and its ordered interface.
Source spansThe expansion keeps the original spans of the parameter, the right-hand side and the call. A failure of an argument identifies the argument or the call. Emitted operations of the callee retain their origins in its original body.
RefusalA mismatch of the exact arity or tree; duplicate names within one pattern or parameter list; a wildcard, an implicit drop or a reuse of a live quantum owner; an unresolved callee; an invalid body; an unsupported projection. Ordinary runtime shadowing keeps its lexical rules.
Open obligationsThe emitted ownership, scope and effect rules and the dependencies need an independent check. Call expansion needs correspondence with the original body. The validity of fresh IR alone does not supply it.

See exact trees and functional abstraction.

The project route rejects this function. split(q) returns (Q<(Bit,Bit)>,Q<Bit>), and the pattern (a,b) does not split the owner Q<(Bit,Bit)>:

unitary fn run(q:Q<((Bit,Bit),Bit)>)->Q<((Bit,Bit),Bit)>{ let ((a,b),c)=split(q); join(join(a,b),c) }

The project route accepts the function with a second explicit split:

unitary fn run(q:Q<((Bit,Bit),Bit)>)->Q<((Bit,Bit),Bit)>{ let (ab,c)=split(q); let (a,b)=split(ab); join(join(a,b),c) }

Evaluation and owner lifetime boundaries

This section states when the parts of an expression evaluate and where the lifetime of a quantum owner may end.

An access call is a call that marks at least one argument with excl or ctrl. A place is such a marked argument. It is a whole lexical owner, or a static selection of the axes of one.

Evaluation order

Statements, arguments and tuple fields evaluate in the order in which the source writes them.

Rules:

  • For every supported expression form, statements execute in source order.
  • A call evaluates its arguments completely, once, from left to right, before it enters the callee.
  • Tuple fields follow the same rule. A nested expression evaluates before the operation that encloses it.
  • An ordinary Unit result does not suppress the effects of an argument. (h(excl q), z(excl q)); finishes H before it starts Z, just as h(excl q); z(excl q); does.
  • Ignoring a product of ordinary Unit values inserts no quantum destruction.

Owner lifetime

The rules below say when a temporary owns a quantum value, and what the end of a scope does to a live owner.

Rules:

  • A temporary may own a quantum value while that value flows to an explicit consumer, a binding or a result. measure_z(h(init0())) is such a chain.
  • The end of an expression statement, a wildcard binding, a shadowed binding or a local block must not silently destroy a live quantum owner. The checker rejects an unreturned local owner at its binding. It rejects a discarded quantum expression at that expression. Both routes report the code ownership.
  • Ordinary Bit, Unit and product values may be ignored.
  • The language has no observable classical destructor and no quantum drop glue.
  • The exit from a scope cannot choose measurement, discard, reset or clean discharge for the programmer.

Places and access calls

The rules below say what a place is and when the caller can use its owners again after an access call.

Rules:

  • A place is formed by its call. It is not a reference value with an inferred lifetime.
  • An access call supplies its owners in argument order and executes the callee once.
  • The call restores the lexical operation rights only after it retains the returned values and completes any reassembly of a selected parent. This happens before the next argument, tuple field or statement starts.
  • A call inside the body of the callee completes before the enclosing call returns.
  • The end of a surrounding block preserves the updated outer owner. It does not restore an earlier state.
  • Four forms are unsupported: stored or escaping views, nested place projections, implicit method autoref and arbitrary reference lifetimes.
  • A static axis selector uses the original resolved static context and has no runtime effect.
  • A shorter lifetime grants no control capability, restores no dirty workspace and proves no clean release. The distinct obligations for effect, sector and exact workspace apply. These rules supply no workspace syntax and no evidence.

Order of operations

The rules below say what elaboration retains of the written order, and what a reordering needs.

Rules:

  • Elaboration retains the ordered source steps, the call boundaries, the original owners and the source locations. Raw instructions retain the ordered edges of their owner tokens.
  • Scheduling convenience does not permit a reorder of operations that do not commute. Neither do names that appear to be separate.
  • A proposed reordering needs a separately justified transformation that preserves exact phase, reference behavior and all applicable contracts.
  • Source evaluation follows the written order. A transformation of executable code requires its own evidence for the changed owner flow and for the other contracts.

Implementation note. Independent source replay rejects an altered gate chain even when the type, effect and ownership interface of that chain is native-valid.

Examples

The Finite project target and the Selected Raw target accept this program. Each target emits the same Raw program as it emits with h(excl q); z(excl q); in place of the tuple statement. main returns 1 with probability one:

use std::state::init0;
use std::gate::x; use std::gate::cnot; use std::gate::z;
fn done(a:Unit,b:Unit)->Unit{()}
unitary fn pair(q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{h(excl q);z(excl q);q}
pub observe fn main()->Bit{let q=init0();(h(excl q), z(excl q));h(excl q);measure_z(q)}

The project route rejects the next program with the code ownership. The binder q holds a live owner at the end of the block:

use std::state::init0;  use std::gate::x; use std::gate::z;
observe fn main() -> Unit { let q = init0(); () }

Whole-owner exclusive calls

A whole-owner exclusive call lets a program transform an owner and keep its name. A call such as h(excl q) supplies the live lexical owner q to one consuming call. The same binder then retains the returned quantum value.

FieldContract
SourceU(excl q), or a call whose arguments all mark distinct whole lexical Q<A> owners. A retained concrete ctrl call is admitted after a fresh native sector check, on the targets that Status and limits names.
TargetThe consuming call. After it, the value of each argument binder is replaced by its exact ordered returned owner. The access expression returns ordinary Unit.
Evaluation orderThe expansion resolves the original source occurrences. It supplies the owners once, in argument order, and the callee executes once. A copied AST occurrence acquires no second lexical identity.
OwnersThe same lexical owner identities hold the returned values. The form requires three things: a checked Unitary effect that the caller can see, an independent check of the body, and the exact original owner interface. A later consuming call makes its binder spent. A shadow cannot restore it.
Exact phaseThe expansion preserves the complete action of the callee, including entanglement, ordered axes and zero-width phase. It inserts no inverse and no cleanup.
Source spansThe expansion retains the original identifiers of the callee and of the arguments, their byte spans and the origins in the body of the callee. The span of a contextual marker does not replace the span of an owner identifier.
RefusalOverlap; a spent, hidden or nonquantum argument; a changed owner partition or tree; a nonunitary body; mixed arguments outside the checked profile; an escaping access; a failed native check of the control sectors; an unavailable concrete projection. Static selections follow their own rule. Checker-free ctrl, which is ctrl in a lowering that runs without the native checker, is unsupported. An original control obligation without a concrete interval in each retained specialization rejects.
Open obligationsEmitted artifacts and requests need independent checks. The lookup-level scope-update model has premises on finite maps, type embedding and update provenance. It is not a proof of source preservation and not a quantitative resource certificate. General footprints, lifetimes and access declarations are pending.

See whole-owner exclusive calls.

The effect of the callee follows the public-effect rule. The effect that counts depends on the module that contains the call.

Rules:

  • Outside the original module of the callee, the checked public contract counts. Inside that module, internal inference counts.
  • A body can have a sharper effect than its public contract. Specialization, inlining and cache reuse cannot turn that sharper effect into eligibility for external source.

Implementation note. Native-checked Selected Raw lowering also checks unused closed functions that lead to control obligations. It invents no static bindings.

The project route rejects this program with the code contract. h does not preserve the computational-basis sectors of q, and the check covers bad although no function calls it:

use std::state::init0;
use std::gate::x; use std::gate::cnot;
unitary fn bad(q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{h(ctrl q);q} pub observe fn main()->Bit{0}

Ordinary Unit arguments in access calls

An access call can take ordinary arguments beside its marked places. A checked mixed call passes () or a lexical Unit value beside its marked places.

Rules:

  • The call evaluates the original arguments once, in their written order. It reserves a marked owner when it reaches that argument.
  • A later argument must not use a reserved owner as an ordinary value.
  • A quantum owner such as Q<Unit> needs an access marker and an ownership check, like every other owner.
  • The named callee receives the complete ordered value list, including each Unit at its source position.
  • The independently checked Raw interface carries only the marked quantum ports.
  • The callee returns those owner types in their original relative order. The call restores them to their original places and returns ordinary Unit.
  • The checked operation retains its exact phase and the same interface to untouched owners.
  • An exclusive named call may also take ordinary Bit arguments when the selected callee lowers to a single checked ordinary branch.

The selected-entry route with the native checker accepts update:

unitary fn turn(tag: Unit, data: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { h(data) }

pub unitary fn update(data: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> {
    turn((), excl data);
    data
}

Implementation note. The native source-body check validates the named call, the returned owners, the Raw interval and any extraction and reinsertion. For an access body without selection, basis or Meaning evidence, it requires an original access receipt and complete coverage of the selected invocation; see the native scope. For ordinary Bit arguments, it uses the original condition and both Raw arms. It verifies each parked owner in both arms and at the checked branch return, and it preserves port order and zero-width owners. The dormant checker admits a mixed ctrl call from a closed nongeneric body after the native source check covers that exact original occurrence. It checks the marked quantum sectors of the callee again.

Declared access parameters

A function can write the access marker in its own signature. A finite function with a closed selected specialization may declare a marked owner slot, as in target: excl Q<Bit>, and write a Unit result.

Rules:

  • The call must supply the exact marker at that argument position.
  • The body must check as Unitary and must leave each marked owner live on its original binder.
  • The ordinary result is Unit at the written call. The body may return () or a value of type Unit, including a parameter.
  • The returned quantum owners carry the updated state, including its exact phase.
  • A declared access requires the finite check of the original body. For every ctrl slot it also requires the applicable exact sector check.

The selected-entry route with the native checker accepts update:

pub unitary fn flip(target: excl Q<Bit>) -> Unit {
    h(excl target);
    ()
}

pub unitary fn update(target: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> {
    flip(excl target);
    target
}

Implementation note. The native call boundary reads the marked owners in parameter order and verifies the returned Raw ports. The production source check retains the declaration and the marked call as original occurrences. When it checks a specialization, it also retains explicit static arguments such as type(Bit).

Static ordered-axis places

A static ordered-axis place lets an access call act on selected axes of a register. It selects axes of a live Q<Bits<N>> owner as an argument of the call. That owner is the parent. excl q[i] and ctrl q[i] select one axis. excl q[a..b] and ctrl q[a..b] select the explicit half-open range q[a..b].

FieldContract
Sourceexcl q[i], ctrl q[i], excl q[a..b] and ctrl q[a..b] as arguments of an access call, where q is a live lexical Q<Bits<N>> parent. An index selects Q<Bit>. A range selects Q<Bits<b-a>>. The two interfaces are distinct even at width one.
TargetThree steps. The expansion partitions the parent, in order, into selected owners and remainder owners. It calls the callee once with all selected arguments. It reconstructs the parent from the updated returned values, in the reverse of the extraction order. Existing Split/Join instructions perform the partition on the Finite project and Selected Raw targets. The Selected hierarchy target uses its operations for bit extraction, reinsertion and empty owners.
Evaluation orderA selector uses the original resolved static context and has no runtime effect. The callee executes once. The parent is reassembled before the next argument, tuple field or statement starts.
OwnersThe parent is live after the call, and the access expression has ordinary Unit type. The callee has a Unitary effect and returns the exact ordered selected interface. Empty selected owners and empty remainder owners retain their logical identities. An empty range selects no axes. A whole-owner access overlaps every other access on that parent, including an empty range.
Exact phaseThe partition inserts no physical SWAP, preparation, measurement or cleanup. Empty owners retain their scalar phase. The expansion preserves the action of the callee on the ordered selected interface.
Source spansEach selection retains its parent-owner occurrence, its static selector, its access role and the original byte spans.
RefusalA parent that is not a live lexical Q<Bits<N>>; a bound that the common checker cannot prove, 0 <= a <= b <= N for a range or 0 <= i < N for an index, under the original static context; two selections on the same parent that are not provably disjoint; a runtime index; arithmetic overflow; budget exhaustion; a callee without a Unitary effect; a callee that does not return the exact ordered selected interface; bare indexing as a value or as an ownership-extraction operation; a ctrl selection without its sector check; checker-free control emission. Each failure occurs at compile time. No runtime bounds panic exists.
Open obligationsThe emitted program needs native Raw checking. A ctrl selection needs a fresh native sector check of the concrete callee on its ordered selected ports. General source preservation and quantitative resource correspondence are proof obligations.

Rules:

  • Different parent names alone are not evidence of different axes. The checks use resolved binding identities.
  • ctrl keeps its separate original sector obligation. The annotation grants no permission.
  • The common checker checks every original declaration, both branch bodies and the body of every fold.
  • The premises of static branches and of loops take part in the arithmetic proof. This includes impossible contexts, as for other static obligations.
  • The checks of names, types, effects and ownership cover unexecuted code as well.

Implementation note. The common AST represents each selection as a parent-owner occurrence and a static selector. The project compiler submits its emitted program to native Raw checking. The selected path also replays source steps against the partitions and the reassembly. A dormant action with closed ports can be checked without evaluating the register extraction of an inactive branch. On the Selected hierarchy target, source replay checks the original ordered ports of each partition and the phase-free graph interval. For supported pure ctrl calls, replay binds the original ordered call interval in that same graph. Lean checks the sectors of the exact action during the invocation that checks the executable hierarchy.

The bounded resource correspondence counts the live wires of the indexed Raw access and its reassembly. The selected operation and any emitted physical implementation have their own resource checks.

The common checker accepts this function:

use std::gate::cnot;pub unitary fn f(q:Q<Bits<2>>)->Q<Bits<2>>{cnot(ctrl q[0],excl q[1]);q}

The selected-entry route rejects the next program with the code size. Index 2 is outside Q<Bits<2>>, and the check covers unused although no function calls it:

unitary fn unused(q:Q<Bits<2>>)->Q<Bits<2>>{h(excl q[2]);q}pub unitary fn f(q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{q}

Ordinary expressions and classical functions

This section covers the classical computation of a program. An ordinary expression computes a Unit, Bit or product value. A classical fn is a total function on ordinary values.

FieldContract
SourceOrdinary expressions of Unit, Bit or product type, the eager operators not, and and xor, and supported calls of a classical fn
TargetOrdinary evaluation and Raw classical operations, including selected Raw register transport where the target supports it. No truth table is substituted at runtime.
Evaluation orderOperands and complete arguments evaluate once, in source order. and is eager, including its right operand.
OwnersAn ordinary result has no quantum owner. Input expressions keep their effects and their quantum consumption. Ignoring a result cannot omit its measurement.
Exact phaseOrdinary Boolean evaluation inserts no quantum action. Input expressions keep their complete action or instrument.
Source spansThe expansion keeps the original byte spans of the operand, the call, the parameter and the definition.
RefusalWrong exact types or arity; a forbidden capture; an invalid classical body or dependency; unavailable transport. A live Q<A> is not an ordinary A argument.
Open obligationsLexical use, complete phi inputs and value operations need a check. The original computation and the surrounding instrument must be preserved. Coherent use needs the separate lift obligation in addition.

See classical declarations and ordinary Bits transport.

The Finite project target and the Selected Raw target accept this program. Both measurements run in source order, although left ignores b:

use std::state::init0; use std::gate::x;
classical fn left(a: Bit, b: Bit) -> Bit { a }
pub observe fn main() -> Bit { left(measure_z(x(init0())),measure_z(init0())) }

Nominal values

A nominal value is an ordinary value of a declared enum or struct type. Type::Variant names a fieldless enum variant. Type { field: expression, ... } constructs a record. value.field projects one field of an ordinary record.

FieldContract
SourceFieldless Type::Variant, explicit Type { field: expression, ... } and ordinary value.field, in runtime blocks and in classical bodies
TargetOrdinary values that keep their nominal type. A variant becomes one Raw classical constant for each tag coordinate. A record keeps its field values in declaration order. A projection selects the stored field.
Evaluation orderRecord initializers evaluate in written order. The record type keeps declaration order. A projection evaluates its receiver once.
OwnersEvery field has an ordinary finite type. Q<Record> is one owner, with no implicit decomposition or observation. Initializer calls keep their ownership transitions.
Exact phaseConstruction and projection are ordinary computation and insert no quantum action. Initializer calls keep their effects and dependencies, so observation cannot hide behind a Unitary or Isometry annotation.
Source spansType references use the original occurrence table, including public reexports and local shadowing. Member names and diagnostics retain their original source spans.
RefusalA missing or repeated field; a field value of another type; a private field outside its declaring module; a projection from a value that is not an ordinary record; a local Basis name or runtime name in place of a global type with the same spelling; a payload variant; an imported bare variant; shorthand, record update and method forms.
Open obligationsCommon preparation supplies no accepted handle. Execution requires a typed native route. That gate does not prove original AST lowering, the decoder and native compiler, or numerical runtime preservation.

The type model specifies these forms and their routes.

The project route accepts this program. The initializers of Result are written in an order other than the declaration order:

enum Tri { Zero, One, Other }
struct Empty {}
struct Result { choice: Tri, flag: Bit, empty: Empty }

pub observe fn main() -> Result {
    let q = basis unit(()) as _ { 0 };
    let bit = measure_z(h(q));
    let tag = if bit { Tri::One } else { Tri::Zero };
    let flag = match tag { Tri::Zero => 0, Tri::One => 1, Tri::Other => 0 };
    Result { empty: Empty {}, flag: flag, choice: tag }
}

With pub unitary fn main in place of pub observe fn main, the project route rejects that program with the code effect.

Runtime classical branches

A runtime classical branch selects one of two arms by an ordinary Bit, such as a measurement result. Runtime selection is distinct from coherent control and from static selection.

FieldContract
Sourceif condition { ... } else { ... } with an ordinary Bit condition
TargetRaw ClassicalBranch with both operation lists and simultaneous classical and quantum phis, or the supported selected branch representation
Evaluation orderThe condition evaluates once. Runtime executes the selected arm. Source checking visits both arms.
OwnersBoth arms agree on the exact returned trees and on outer consumption. The join merges the returned leaves and the complete surviving frame of the caller and of pending arguments. IDs are globally fresh across arms. Phi renaming prepares no state and loses no reference correlation.
Exact phaseThe expansion preserves the action and the unnormalized outcome weight of each arm. It inserts no coherent superposition and no branch normalization.
Source spansThe operations of an arm retain their original spans and their nested branch-index paths. An inserted join uses the span of the branch.
RefusalA quantum condition; different types or owner frames; lost branch-local owners; invalid phis or an invalid body; an unsupported target.
Open obligationsBoth arms, the scope, the ownership and the simultaneous phis need a native check. The complete source instrument must be preserved, with external references and the correlations of the caller frame.

The Finite project target accepts this program, and main returns 1. The selected-entry route rejects it with the code unsupported: the form is valid, and its selected projection is outside the profile.

use std::state::init0;
use std::gate::x; use std::gate::cnot;
pub observe fn main()->Bit{
let q=init0();let u=if 1{x(excl q);()}else{()};measure_z(q)}

The project route rejects the next program with the code type_mismatch. The condition is a quantum owner:

use std::state::init0;  use std::gate::x; use std::gate::z;
observe fn main() -> Unit { let q = init0(); if q { () } else { () } }

Ordinary match

An ordinary match selects one arm by the variant of an ordinary enum value.

FieldContract
Sourcematch value { Type::A => expression, ... } on an ordinary enum value. Every declared variant occurs exactly once, as an exact qualified label. A runtime arm is an expression or a block. A classical arm is an ordinary expression.
TargetOrdinary comparisons of the tag coordinates, and nested Raw ClassicalBranch operations with their joins
Evaluation orderThe scrutinee evaluates once. Runtime executes the arm of its variant. The common checker checks every arm, including the arms of a constant constructor in an unused function.
OwnersThe scrutinee is an ordinary enum value. All arms return the same complete type tree and preserve the same outer owner frame, including zero-width owners.
Exact phaseThe tag comparison is ordinary computation and inserts no quantum action. Each arm keeps its dependencies and effects. A constant scrutinee cannot hide an observing arm behind a pure public label.
Source spansLabels resolve through their original type declarations and visibility. Member names and diagnostics retain their original source spans.
RefusalA scrutinee that is not an ordinary enum, including a live Q<T>; a missing or repeated variant; a label of a foreign enum, even with equal spelling, width or cardinality; a wildcard, payload or complement pattern; more than 64 arms; arms with different type trees or owner frames; an unsupported target.
Open obligationsThe source judgment provides no accepted handle. Execution requires a typed native route. Neither route provides implicit measurement or a source-preservation theorem.

The type model specifies the form. Parenthesize a record literal in a scrutinee, so that its braces differ from the arm list.

The project route accepts this program, and main returns 1:

enum Tri { A, B, C }
classical fn flag() -> Bit {
    match Tri::C { Tri::A => 0, Tri::B => 0, Tri::C => 1 }
}
fn main() -> Bit { flag() }

The project route rejects the next program with the code type_mismatch. The match omits two variants, and the check covers unused although no function calls it:

enum Tri { A, B, C } classical fn unused() -> Bit { match Tri::A { Tri::A => 0 } } fn main() -> Bit { 0 }

Static natural computation

Static natural computation evaluates natural expressions during checking. A program uses it for values such as a width or a repetition count. A static binding is not a runtime value.

FieldContract
SourceSupported natural expressions, static let, and Nat helpers that are provisional, bounded and acyclic
TargetExact affine templates, substitution and closed checked naturals. A checked unused alias inserts no runtime instruction.
Evaluation orderOrdered static binders and helper arguments resolve in their static context. Substitution is simultaneous. The names of a callee cannot rewrite the binders of its caller.
OwnersNone. The static environment contains no live quantum owner and no runtime input.
Exact phaseNormalization inserts no phase. A result that an explicit phase operation uses is the exact specified parameter of that operation.
Source spansThe expansion keeps the original spans of the arithmetic, the argument, the premise and the binder. It never keeps spans of generated replacement text.
RefusalA value that depends on a runtime value; a forward kind dependency; a duplicate or shadowing binding; nonlinear arithmetic; an unproved subtraction or premise; a cycle; overflow; work exhaustion. Acyclic forward references to helpers keep normal declaration resolution.

See static arithmetic and helpers.

The Finite project target accepts this program. The alias width is checked and erased, and main returns 0:

pub observe fn main()->Bit{static let width=2+1;0}

Both routes reject the next program. The static alias n depends on the runtime value a:

pub observe fn main()->Bit{let a=1;static let n=a+1;0}

Specialization and static selection

Bracket specialization closes a declaration by supplying its complete static arguments, as in run[2]. if static selects one arm by a static comparison.

FieldContract
SourceOrdered const parameters, complete bracket arguments and if static comparison
TargetA supported closed instance and the selected static arm, after the complete check of the original source
Evaluation orderExplicit static bindings and provider identities resolve before runtime application. Static selection evaluates no runtime condition.
OwnersThe expansion preserves the exact interface and the owners of the runtime instance. A dead source arm is checked.
Exact phaseThe substitution of parameters does not quotient phase and does not change axis order. The expansion retains the selected action.
Source spansThe expansion keeps the spans of the definition, the argument, the comparison and the arm.
RefusalIncomplete or wrong bindings; unproved constraints or access; an invalid dead arm; non-decreasing dependencies; an unsupported instance. No inference from width and no fallback exists.
Open obligationsThe closed artifact and the provider evidence need a native check. General preservation under specialization and resource bounds for a family are separate obligations.

The static rules specify termination and capacities. Helper spellings are provisional where those rules say so.

The project route accepts this program. run[0] selects the else arm and run[2] selects the first arm, so main returns (0,1):

use std::state::init0; use std::gate::x;
unitary fn flip[const n:Nat](q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{qfor static i in 0..n carry q=q{yield x(q);}}
unitary fn apply[const V:Op<Bit>](q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit> requires Applicable(V){V(q)}
unitary fn run[const n:Nat](q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{
  if static n>=1 {apply[flip[n-1]](q)} else {q}
}
pub observe fn main()->(Bit,Bit){(measure_z(run[0](init0())),measure_z(run[2](init0())))}

The selected-entry route rejects the next function with the code name. The dead arm calls an unknown function:

pub unitary fn f(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { if static 0 == 0 { q } else { missing(q) } }

Finite folds

A finite fold repeats its body over a closed static range and threads a carry from each iteration to the next. for static carries ordinary values. qfor static carries quantum owners.

FieldContract
Sourcefor static for ordinary values or qfor static for quantum owners, with an explicit range, carry pattern, initializer and yield
TargetClosed finite iteration of existing fold and source steps, then a supported Raw or hierarchy proposal
Evaluation orderThe initializer evaluates once. The carry threads in increasing index order over [start,end). Zero iterations return the evaluated initial value.
OwnersThe expansion preserves the exact carry tree. qfor carries a quantum owner, including empty-width owners. An owner outside the carry cannot be a hidden capture. The expansion inserts no discard at exit and no reassembly.
Exact phaseSerial composition retains the phase of every iteration. An empty iteration sequence is the identity on the retained carry.
Source spansThe expansion keeps the spans of the bound, the carry, the body and the yield in every instance.
RefusalAn invalid range or a runtime bound; the wrong fold category; a carry-tree mismatch; a missing yield; a hidden capture; an invalid zero-count body. A limit failure keeps its category.
Open obligationsThe complete composition, the owners and the dependencies need a check. Finite unrolling proves neither a general family theorem nor a quantitative bound.

See fold rules.

The selected-entry route accepts this function for n from 0 to 3. At n = 0 the function acts as the identity:

use std::gate::x; pub unitary fn f[const n:Nat](q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{qfor static i in 0..n carry a=q{yield x(a);}}

The selected-entry route rejects the next function with the code type. An ordinary fold cannot carry a quantum owner:

pub unitary fn f(q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{for static i in 0..0 carry a=q{yield a;}}

Operation descriptions and application

A static operation description names an operation that is bound to its provider. A constructor builds a description from other descriptions, such as the adjoint of an operation or a power of it. An application applies a description to runtime owners.

FieldContract
Sourceadjoint, power, then_op, tensor_op, conjugate_op, controlled and checked_op, in the specified positions of a static description and of an application
TargetDescriptions bound to their providers, and existing untrusted transformation proposals for a circuit, a finite contract or a hierarchy. No runtime closure exists.
Evaluation orderThe complete description is checked before application. Runtime arguments evaluate once in source order, including at power zero. Adjoint reverses the operation order and conjugates the action.
OwnersThe exact basis tree and the runtime group are retained. A tensor description uses its packed basis. It does not implicitly join separate owners.
Exact phaseAdjoint conjugates phase. Power repeats the complete action. Serial, tensor and conjugate descriptions retain the ordered action. Meaning is a separate obligation, never an access grant.
Source spansThe expansion keeps the original spans of the constructor, the operand, the count, the Meaning and the input through nested descriptions.
RefusalMissing access; a wrong basis, interface or Meaning; an unsupported provider, transform or count; an unresolved obligation; a capacity failure. These reject in unused and zero-count contexts as well. Constructing adjoint(U) itself requires Adjointable(U).
Open obligationsProviders, retained bodies, exact transformations and requested Meanings need an independent binding to the emitted artifacts. A valid unbound circuit is insufficient.

See access derivations, repetition and checked operations.

The same eight fields apply to each constructor below. The constructors are the existing endomorphic description actions. They do not admit the adjoint of an isometry in general. An arrow gives the order of execution at runtime. A matrix product acts right to left.

DescriptionExact expansion/action
Resolved provider/specializationRetain the closed body, the bindings and the dependency evidence. No operation-name substitution occurs.
adjoint(U)The justified adjoint action of U. On the supported circuit path, reverse and conjugate the retained steps.
power(U,n)n serial copies of U, with the identity at zero. All original provider and access obligations are retained.
then_op(U,V)Execute U, then V, on the same exact basis. The matrix action is V U.
tensor_op(U,V)Apply U to the first basis block and V to the second ordered block. Retain one shared outer control when controlled.
controlled(U)Retain the control, the identity on zero and the exact U on one, including the scalar phase of U.
conjugate_op(C,U)The ordering C† → U → C, with matrix action C U C†. Do not silently substitute C† U C.
checked_op(U,M)Retain the implementation of U and attach the independent exact M obligation. This inserts no runtime gate and no capability.

Composing descriptions does not automatically transport an attached Op<A,M> refinement. Functional abstraction specifies the refinement rules and the obligation rules of the common judgment, and the concrete independent checks.

The project route accepts this program. power(eighth_phase,4) is four serial copies of T, and both checked_op descriptions carry the same exact Meaning:

//! Two implementations of one phase-fixed meaning share an unchanged client.
use std::state::init0;

use std::gate::z;
use std::gate::t;

classical fn z_phase(b: Bit) -> (Bit,(Bit,Bit)) { (0,(0,b)) }
meaning ZMeaning: Bit = phase_by(z_phase);

unitary fn direct(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { z(q) }
unitary fn eighth_phase(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { t(q) }
unitary fn decomposed(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { power(eighth_phase,4)(q) }

/// The caller supplies evidence for the same exact Z operator.
unitary fn client[const U: Op<Bit,ZMeaning>](q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit>
requires Applicable(U) { U(q) }

observe fn main() -> (Bit,Bit) {
    let a = client[checked_op(direct,ZMeaning)](h(init0()));
    let b = client[checked_op(decomposed,ZMeaning)](h(init0()));
    (measure_z(h(a)),measure_z(h(b)))
}

The selected-entry route rejects the next function with the code access. f applies controlled(power(U,0)) and declares no Controllable(U). The check covers the body although the fold has zero iterations:

pub unitary fn f[const n: Nat, const U: Op<Bits<n>>](c: Q<Bit>, q: Q<Bits<n>>) -> (Q<Bit>,Q<Bits<n>>) { qfor static k in 0..0 carry pair = (c,q) { let (c,q) = pair; yield controlled(power(U,0))(c,q); } }

Coherent control

Coherent control applies an operation to a target owner under a Q<Bit> control, without measuring the control. controlled(U)(c,q) applies U when the control is one. qif(c,q) { 0 => F, 1 => G } applies F when the control is zero and G when it is one.

FieldContract
Sourcecontrolled(U)(c,q), or qif(c,q) { 0 => F, 1 => G } with both arms in that order. A qif arm is a named operation or an inline block { ... }.
TargetFinite Join → ApplyUnitary → Split over the ordered (Bit,A), with the bound controlled circuit and its evidence; otherwise the supported hierarchy construction. Controlled U retains the inactive identity. qif retains its specified zero and one actions.
Evaluation orderThe control evaluates, then the target, each completely and once. The control is not measured and is not used as a classical condition.
OwnersThe form consumes two inputs, packages them temporarily for the finite controlled action and returns (Q<Bit>,Q<A>) in order, even for zero-width A. The complete target tree and the reference frame are retained. Packaging prepares no state. A block arm binds the written target name and returns one owner of the exact target type. Other runtime owners of the enclosing scope are unavailable in the block.
Exact phaseThe control is the first low axis. The inactive identity has coefficient +1. The active phase is retained, including scalar Unit phase and kickback.
Source spansThe expansion keeps the control argument, the target argument and the names of the provider or of the arms. Generated control structure retains the origin of the expression.
RefusalA missing Controllable capability; wrong owners or arity; aliases; an invalid arm; an omitted or reordered arm; a block arm whose target is not a name, whose body is not Unitary, or that does not return the target owner; an unsupported interface. Unitarity grants no control access.
Open obligationsThe provider or body identity, the exact action, the axes and the owners need an independent check. Probabilities, or tests on known inputs, do not discharge coherent correspondence or reference correspondence.

The inactive identity belongs to the specified controlled meaning. No rewrite of a qif with an omitted arm is admitted. Exact-label coherent selection specifies the block arms that qif shares with qmatch.

The selected-entry route with the native checker accepts this function. Its second arm is an inline block:

#![no_implicit_prelude]
pub unitary fn route(s:Q<Bit>,q:Q<Bit>)->(Q<Bit>,Q<Bit>){
    qif(s,q){0=>h,1=>{let r=h(q);phase[1,1](r)}}
}

The common checker rejects the next program with the class ownership. The block arm uses the control s, which is unavailable in the block:

unitary fn keep(q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{q} pub observe fn f(s:Q<Bit>,q:Q<Bit>)->(Q<Bit>,Q<Bit>){qif(s,q){0=>keep,1=>{ h(s) }}}

Exact-label coherent selection

qmatch(selector, target) { label => arm, ... } selects among its arms coherently. It applies one arm to the target for each basis label of the selector. It does not measure the selector. On a Bit selector it agrees exactly with qif.

FieldContract
Sourceqmatch(selector, target) { label => arm, ... }. An arm is a resolved static operation or an inline block. The labels cover the logical basis of the selector exactly once, in any order. A label is a canonical decimal ordinal for Unit, Bit and closed Bits<n> with 0 <= n <= 6, and a qualified variant name for a fieldless enum.
TargetA proposed circuit on the selector axes followed by the target axes, emitted in a Raw root. On the route that checks the original source, each selection binds one literal, contiguous Raw interval and its owner frame.
Evaluation orderThe selector evaluates, then the target, each once. The selector is not measured. The written arm order does not change the action.
OwnersThe form consumes one Q<A> selector and one distinct Q<B> target and returns (Q<A>, Q<B>) with both complete type trees unchanged. Zero physical width removes neither owner. A block arm binds the written target name and returns one owner of the exact target type. Other runtime owners of the enclosing scope are unavailable in the block.
Exact phaseWith arm s denoting the exact operator U_s, the action maps |s,y> to sum_z U_s[z,y] |s,z> and extends linearly, including to inputs entangled with an external reference. All arm phases are exact. Selector axes precede target axes, so (s,y) has the coordinate s + 2^selector_bits * y.
Source spansEach selection retains its own source position and its ordered arms. On the route that checks the original source, it also retains its literal Raw interval.
RefusalA wildcard, range, payload or guard label; a dynamic arm call; a missing, repeated or out-of-range label; more than 64 arms; a selector that is not one Q<A> owner of a supported basis; a target that is not one distinct Q<B> owner; an arm with another target interface, without a Unitary effect or without the Controllable capability; an unsupported target. Unitarity alone grants neither control nor inverse access.
Open obligationsThe proposed circuit needs a fresh native encoded equation against the independently obtained exact block meaning. The emitted Raw root needs ordinary native checking. Three things do not prove preservation of the original source: common enum checks, native acceptance of a proposed circuit, and conformance tests.

Source text specifies the form, its block arms and its routes.

The common checker accepts this program. The labels are written in an order other than the ordinal order:

unitary fn keep(q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{q} unitary fn f(s:Q<Bits<2>>,q:Q<Bit>)->(Q<Bits<2>>,Q<Bit>){qmatch(s,q){3=>keep,0=>keep,2=>keep,1=>keep}}

The common checker rejects the next program with the class type. The label 1 is missing:

enum E{A,B,C} unitary fn keep(q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{q} fn f(s:Q<Bit>,q:Q<Bit>)->(Q<Bit>,Q<Bit>){qmatch(s,q){0=>keep}}

Coherent basis maps

A coherent basis map applies an injective function on basis labels to one quantum owner. The program writes the function as an expression on a label pattern.

FieldContract
Sourcebasis q as pattern { expression }
TargetFinite or selected Raw LiftBasis with a complete supported label map
Evaluation orderq evaluates once, before the labels are bound. The restricted total expression evaluates in a separate basis scope.
OwnersThe form consumes one Q<A> and returns one Q<B>. Label patterns do not split runtime owners. Separate inputs are not implicitly joined.
Exact phaseEach transition has coefficient +1, linearly, with the identity on an arbitrary external reference. Amplitudes and ordered output labels are retained.
Source spansThe expansion keeps the original spans of the input, the label pattern and the body.
RefusalA wrong owner or tree; an outer capture; an unsupported body or callee; a noninjective complete map; reuse; an unavailable profile.
Open obligationsThe complete lift, its injectivity and its effects need an independent check. The correspondence of the source to the table is separate from the validity of the table.

See coherent basis maps, including Unit and the difference between label copying and state copying.

The project route accepts this program. main returns (1,0):

use std::state::init0;
classical fn flip(x: Bit) -> Bit { not x }
unitary fn lifted(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { basis q as b { flip(b) } }
pub observe fn main() -> (Bit,Bit) {
    let q = init0(); let reference = init0(); let q = lifted(q);
    (measure_z(q),measure_z(reference))
}

Selected elaboration rejects the next function with the code ownership. The constant map is not injective:

pub unitary fn f(q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{basis q as a {0}}

Computed workspace

with_computed gives a scoped body one temporary ancilla. It computes the ancilla from a source register by a classical predicate, runs the body, and uncomputes the ancilla.

FieldContract
SourceThe two-argument form with_computed(source,predicate), or the three-argument form with a logical contract
TargetRaw ComputeUseUncompute, or the certified retained-body construction with finite evidence, within each supported profile
Evaluation orderThe source evaluates once. The form computes the specified ancilla, executes the checked scoped body and then uncomputes.
OwnersThe predicate takes one ordinary parameter of the exact tree of the source. The two-argument body returns the ancilla. The three-argument body returns the data and the ancilla. Capture and protection rules are explicit. No standalone Release0 is inserted.
Exact phaseThe expansion preserves the specified use or logical action. An exact all-input clean return is required. A cleanliness check alone cannot certify the live action or its phase. Approximate cleanup cannot discharge this obligation.
Source spansThe expansion keeps the origins of the source, the predicate, the body, the returned owner and the logical contract.
RefusalA wrong predicate arity or tree; an unsupported body; an Observe effect; lost, aliased or protected owners; a failed equality or cleanup; capacity exhaustion. A one-Bit ancilla body outside the canonical empty/Z/T token chain must act as an exact eighth-root diagonal. Non-diagonal or unrepresentable actions reject. No exception that is based on a name supplies evidence.
Open obligationsThe retained compute, use and uncompute steps and the exact logical and cleanup contract, with references, need an independent check. Syntax and Unitary annotations supply no clean evidence.

See scoped bodies and predicate trees.

Implementation note. The two-argument path retains an already canonical empty/Z/T token chain through the protected gate. For the other supported one-Bit ancilla bodies, the native checker checks a whole-original equation and a canonical-witness equation for the same exact eighth-root diagonal, before scalar/Z/T normalization. Chunking supplies only an untrusted matrix proposal. The graph, dependency, source and shared-work capacities apply.

The project route accepts this program, which uses the two-argument form. main returns (1,1) with probability one:

use std::basis::and2;
use std::basis::xor2;
use std::state::init0;

use std::gate::x;
use std::gate::z;

classical fn predicate((a,b): (Bit,Bit)) -> Bit { xor2(and2(a, b), 0) }
observe fn main() -> (Bit, Bit) {
    let q = join(h(init0()), x(init0()));
    let q = with_computed(q, predicate) { |a| z(a) };
    let (a, b) = split(q);
    (measure_z(h(a)), measure_z(b))
}

The project route rejects the next program with the code unsupported. The body h(a) is not diagonal:

use std::state::init0;  use std::gate::x; use std::gate::z;
classical fn p(x: Bit) -> Bit { x } observe fn main() -> Bit { measure_z(with_computed(init0(), p) { |a| h(a) }) }

Function contracts

A function contract pairs an implementation with a specification. apply_contract(implementation, specification, input) applies implementation to one quantum owner. It records the obligation that implementation equals specification. The form has two overloads, a pure one and an observing one.

FieldContract
Sourceapply_contract(implementation, specification, input). In the pure overload, both names denote closed functions with the interface Q<A> -> Q<A> and a Unitary effect that the caller can see. A declared finite Meaning may supply the specification instead. In the observing overload, both names denote closed ordinary functions with an Observe effect that the caller can see, one Q<A> argument and the same complete finite result type.
TargetPure overload on Raw: a circuit Contract step that carries the checked receipt. Pure overload on the hierarchy: a checked finite leaf that embeds the complete receipt-bearing wrapper bytes. Observing overload: the emitted call interval of the implementation, with a private native instrument equation.
Evaluation orderThe input evaluates first, once. A declared Meaning supplies the request and is never projected as a runtime function. The observing overload executes only the implementation.
OwnersThe form consumes one exact quantum owner and returns the result of the implementation. In the observing overload, the complete result nesting, the ordered quantum and classical projections, zero-width owners, hidden histories and residual states are significant.
Exact phaseThe function-equality check is an exact equation between the implementation and the specification. A replacement with an equal matrix and different implementation or specification bytes cannot substitute for the original receipt, which is bound to the source.
Source spansThe obligation binds both original definitions, the interface, the category, the effect and the source span. Raw emission keeps the original pair, owner, direction and ordered axes for source replay.
RefusalA local value in place of a function name; a classical fn or a Meaning as the implementation; a function with static parameters; a function without exactly one Q<A> parameter of the input basis; different result types; a failed equation; an observing Meaning; lowering without the native checker.
Open obligationsThe function-equality obligation is pending until the independent native evidence gate discharges it. Binding the identity of a Meaning or a provider is not matrix equality, injectivity, all-input clean return, provider correspondence or source preservation. Both emitted artifacts need fresh native acceptance.

The type model specifies both overloads.

The project route accepts this program, which uses the observing overload. measure_z(h(h(q))) and measure_z(q) are the same instrument:

use std::state::init0;  use std::gate::x;
use std::gate::z; use std::gate::t; use std::gate::cnot;

classical fn predicate(value: Bit) -> Bit { value }
unitary fn identity(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { q }
unitary fn specified_phase(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { z(q) }

fn reference(q: Q<Bit>) -> Bit { measure_z(q) }
fn implementation(q: Q<Bit>) -> Bit { measure_z(h(h(q))) }
observe fn main() -> Bit { apply_contract(implementation,reference,x(init0())) }

The project route rejects the next program with the code contract. The implementation relabels the public outcome of the reference:

use std::state::init0;  use std::gate::x;
use std::gate::z; use std::gate::t; use std::gate::cnot;

classical fn predicate(value: Bit) -> Bit { value }
unitary fn identity(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { q }
unitary fn specified_phase(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { z(q) }

fn reference(q: Q<Bit>) -> Bit { measure_z(q) }
fn implementation(q: Q<Bit>) -> Bit { not(measure_z(q)) }
observe fn main() -> Bit { apply_contract(implementation,reference,init0()) }

Explicit maps and unsupported candidates

Some maps are explicit operations of the source program. The program writes them, and no elaboration inserts them. This section also names conveniences that the language does not admit.

Rules:

  • split/join, Unit insertion and removal, and the register primitives are explicit specified maps. They keep their original ordered interfaces and the coefficient +1.
  • An elaboration must not insert such a map to repair an argument tree.
  • Bit, Bits<1>, Unit and Bits<0> are distinct. Tuples of different arity or nesting are distinct. Packed owners are distinct from separate owners.
  • Canonical reassociation is not definitional equality. It is not an admitted implicit elaboration.
  • An ordinary literal does not prepare a quantum state.
  • init0 is not a primitive. It is the ordinary standard-library function std::state::init0, declared pub isometry fn init0() -> Q<Bit> and defined by basis unit(()) as _ { 0 }. It keeps its explicit Isometry contract.
  • basis is a coherent map. It is not sugar for arbitrary state preparation.
  • Beyond explicit selected-place access, no implicit view partition and no implicit reassembly is admitted.
  • No insertion of excl or ctrl, no arbitrary wire permutation and no cleanup is admitted.
  • A convenience may be added only after its complete contract and its checking evidence exist. The candidate list of an Issue is insufficient.

Register primitives on the Selected Raw target

On the Selected Raw target, the register primitives take_bit[N,K] and put_bit[N,K] expand into structural instructions.

Rules:

  • Each requires its statically established premise K < N.
  • Each expands to three existing Split/Join instructions.
  • take_bit preserves the ordered remainder. put_bit inserts the bit at its declared axis.
  • Empty prefixes, empty suffixes and the Bits<0> remainder are logical owners through the structural operations.
  • The expansion emits no physical SWAP, preparation, measurement or implicit discard.

These primitives and the lowering of selected places use the same structural instructions. Explicit indexed access and slice access connect common checking to ordered partition and reconstruction under the static-place rules. Such access does not insert a source take_bit/put_bit call, and it does not infer an access mode.

Implementation note. Independent source-step replay checks the original partition, the intermediate fresh owners and the returned wire order of each take_bit and put_bit. Native validity is a separate fresh decision.

Selected Raw lowering with the native checker accepts this function:

use std::gate::x; use std::gate::z;
pub unitary fn main(input:Q<(Bits<2>,Bit)>)->Q<(Bits<2>,Bit)>{
    let(q,r)=split(input);
    let(b,rest)=take_bit[2,1](q);
    join(put_bit[2,1](b,rest),r)
}

Original locations and failure

This section states the original location that each emitted operation retains, and how kinds of failure stay distinct.

Rules:

  • A span is a half-open UTF-8 byte interval in the unnormalized original source.
  • Emitted operations retain their origins in the original expression and body. Finite nested branches retain operation and arm-index paths.
  • An enclosing expression must not overwrite the origin of a child or of a callee.
  • An inserted operation without a more specific origin uses the span of its expression.
  • Unsupported profiles and work limits keep distinct diagnostics. Exhaustion is not mathematical invalidity.
  • A migration error names the original tokens.

Implementation note. After a finite native rejection, diagnostic mapping selects the longest retained operation-path prefix, and otherwise the original caller or declaration. This mapping is post-rejection metadata only. It cannot change acceptance, manufacture evidence or hide a failure.

Migration correspondence

Some earlier spellings of these forms are retired. The table below maps each retired form to its explicit form. A migration derivative is a separate source that uses the explicit form.

Rules:

  • Production rejects retired forms. It does not retry a legacy grammar, and it applies no compatibility rewrite that accepts them.
  • A migration derivative has its own bytes and provenance.
  • A migration must preserve the original source, its diagnostics and its artifacts, and must validate the complete derivative.
  • A migration must not weaken owners, access, effects or Meaning to make a rewrite succeed.
Preserved old formExplicit formPreserved contract
[static n: Nat, ...][const n: Nat, ...]Ordered explicit kinds and arguments; no inferred specialization
adjoint(U,q) / earlier inverse(U)(q)adjoint(U)(q)Adjoint action and its access premise
repeat_op(k,U) / repeat_static(k,U,q)power(U,k) / power(U,k)(q)The count, the exact provider and group, and evaluation of the input exactly once
inverse_op(U) / controlled_op(U)adjoint(U) / controlled(U)The identity and the access of the bound description
Apply / Adjoint / Controlled predicatesApplicable / Adjointable / ControllableProvider access; an annotation grants nothing
do p <- q; pure ebasis q as p { e }The same CoherentLift, coefficient +1 and injectivity
bind_op(U,M)checked_op(U,M)The exact interface and Meaning, and the original provider evidence

The table is not a general automatic rewriter. An unimplemented draft acquires no claim of historical equivalence. Types and stdlib keep their separate migration contracts.

An artifact that carries source can change its bytes after a source edit. This can happen even when the operator and the interface meaning are equal. A migration must never erase identity to force byte equality.

Status and limits

Further limits:

  • A mixed access call with a ctrl marker is admitted from a closed nongeneric body only.
  • An exclusive named call takes ordinary Bit arguments only when the selected callee lowers to a single checked ordinary branch.
  • A declared access parameter requires a finite function with a closed selected specialization.
  • Coherent basis maps gives the limits of each profile for basis.
  • Nominal values and ordinary match execute through a typed native route. They execute in eligible closed ordinary project roots and in nongeneric public selected roots. The legacy selected projection rejects them as unsupported. General selected integration is unfinished.
  • An ordinary match and a qmatch each have at most 64 arms.
  • A built-in qmatch selector is Unit, Bit or a closed Bits<n> with 0 <= n <= 6. The legacy hierarchy projection refuses qmatch. Source text gives the limits of each qmatch route.
  • The observing overload of apply_contract uses the finite Raw profile in selected compilation. Hierarchy lowering and checker-free emission reject that overload.
  • Raw lowering and hierarchy lowering without the native checker reject a program with outstanding function contracts.

Two preserved comparisons check the migration table:

  • The operation-application comparison checks a complete two-qubit source in its old spelling and in its explicit spelling, on separately identified binaries. Both sources receive fresh source checks. The proposed bytes agree, with SHA-256 32adb61c4a2b24c77dd89f83d0761b427d7509b85b0c4a3b4f93b313d50b9bd4. Emission is not acceptance, so those separate checks are necessary.
  • The capability-name comparison retains 34 equal checked artifacts and one measurement-adjoint refusal. Its selector verifies exact predecessors and derivatives without rewriting first sources or independent oracles.

The coherent-basis and checked-operation regressions do not compare bytes. They retain exact interfaces and independent small complex tests of action or instrument, phase, axis, provider and reference.

Proofs

The items below describe the theorems that concern the forms of this chapter, and what those theorems do not establish.

  • The compatible access theorem uses the ordered physical wires of each checked call as its footprint. Any wire that both calls use must be ctrl in both. The exact local reconstruction preserves every shared control bit, and the other modified coordinates are disjoint.
  • For a checked pair of adjacent calls with a structural return, the theorem states an equality of complex amplitudes. The original Raw root and the exchanged operator composition agree after the same output permutation, for every input and every external reference column. The equality retains conditional phase and entanglement.
  • A protected-phase theorem exchanges adjacent literal phases in their original physical action.
  • Qleisli.SharedControlCommutation proves exact matrix equality for common control sectors that act on disjoint ordered target factors. Its single-control bridge concerns the hierarchy definitions of tensor, control and sequence. The bridge includes unchanged surrounding operations and arbitrary amplitudes of an external reference. Zero-width factors retain their scalar phases.
  • Qleisli.RoutedControlCommutation extends that connection to two original hierarchy entry bodies with distinct intermediate routes. Its explicit premises bind the original definition records, same-artifact node typing, fresh wiring summaries, computed two-sided inverse permutations and provider evaluations. Literal coordinate decompositions identify a common control, disjoint ordered targets and untouched factors. The resulting exact matrix equality preserves arbitrary amplitudes of an external reference.
  • Typing alone establishes neither those coordinate decompositions nor matching provider meanings. The two commutation results derive no source footprint from ctrl or &mut. They prove no arbitrary routing of owners or axes, and they authorize no source reordering. Width premises do not discharge Q<Unit> ownership. Four obligations are open: source footprint, general lowering, acceptance and work preservation.
  • Neither commutation proof is a constitutional guarantee or a guarantee admission. Their bounded examples and proof records are in tests/fixtures/constitution_v030/shared-control-commutation/ and tests/fixtures/constitution_v030/routed-control-commutation/. The emitted-source examples of the second distinguish the conditional Lean theorem from runtime checks and bounded matrix observations. Their zero-axis sources use Q<Bits<0>>, not an identification with Q<Unit>.
  • The QPTL theorem QPTL.FiniteMatrix.scratchMarginal_eq_iff proves a partial-trace equivalence for finite Kraus families on positive semidefinite unit-trace inputs. It concerns a finite trace-preserving channel whose workspace starts in a fixed pure state.
  • The equivalence has two sides. One side is the exact return of the workspace marginal on every live input. The other side is factorization with the same workspace state for every joint input with an external reference.
  • In a scratch basis that contains the clean state, the unwanted diagonal populations are sums of squared Kraus coefficients. Their vanishing on all live basis inputs forces every unwanted coefficient to vanish.
  • The live output includes any declared classical outcome register with its original probabilities. The live factor is the joint output with scratch traced out, and it retains the reference coordinates.
  • The exact requested live action, the coherent phase, the dirty-workspace identity and the quantitative costs have their own contracts.

Preservation

  • Independent source replay is not a general source-preservation theorem and not a proof of an optimizer.
  • General source preservation and quantitative resource correspondence are proof obligations.
  • The bounded migration comparisons are migration evidence. They are not universal source preservation, complete QS/PR/RS, a generic QFT implementation or release approval.

Guarantees and specification review

  • Two scoped guarantees are admitted: QS-QLV1-OWNERSHIP-2026-01 for ownership and QS-QLV1-SCOPE-2026-01 for classical scope. Both keep their original decoded-root premises.
  • Four obligations are pending: the broader source and semantic QS obligation, the forward PR obligation, the quantitative RS obligation and the EXACT obligation. Their interpretations are QS-2026-01, PR-2026-01, RS-2026-01 and EXACT-2026-01.
  • The contracts of this chapter are adopted source contracts. A contract table discharges no guarantee and adds no ledger entry.

  • The capability-name comparison was made after the operation-application comparison.

Ordinary types, quantum owners and equality

An ordinary finite type is a type of finite classical values: Unit, Bit, Bits<n>, an ordered tuple, a fieldless enum or a record. A quantum owner is a value of type Q<A>. It is the linear ownership of one quantum system whose basis is the ordinary finite type A. Type equality is definitional: two types are equal only when their complete trees agree.

This chapter specifies these types for edition 2026. It covers their values, the linear rules of owners, type equality, patterns, static parameters, operation types, the transforms of operations, nominal types and the selected-entry commands. It is subordinate to the authority hierarchy. The frontend uses the canonical ordinary spellings Unit, Bit, Bits<n>, 0 and 1.

To see the linear rule in a running program, follow a quantum owner through measurement and try using its ordinary result twice.

Routes, profiles and checks

The CLI checks source through two routes: the project route, on a source root, and the selected-entry route, with --entry and --module bindings. The chapter uses these terms:

TermDefinition
Common judgmentThe one source check that both routes apply to every complete original declaration and body. The common frontend is the only source grammar and the only source judgment.
Native checkerThe checker executable that lean-kernel/ builds. It decides the acceptance of a proposal independently of the component that produced it.
Finite projectThe lowering profile of the project route. It lowers the closed instances of a project to finite Raw and QIRF proposals.
Selected projectionThe body projection that Instantiation::elaborate performs on the selected-entry route.
Selected RawThe lowering profile that lowers the selected projection to a Raw proposal.
Selected hierarchyThe lowering profile that lowers the selected projection to hierarchy and finite-leaf proposals.
Typed routeThe path that lowers the original source through the common emitter and submits a typed root request to the native checker: finite-ordinary-root-v2 or finite-runtime-root-v2. Both CLI routes use it. Typed routes gives the use of each request.
v5 source checkThe native check of a version-5 original-source request. Its report names the profile finite-source-basis-context-v5, finite-source-qmatch-context-v5, finite-source-meaning-context-v5 or finite-source-access-context-v5.

Rules:

  • The common judgment runs before every check of concrete eligibility. It retains exact type trees, owners, static premises, access and principal effects.
  • The common judgment covers every original declaration, owner rule, effect rule, capability, dependency and static branch. This includes private and unused declarations, both arms of a branch, the body of a loop with zero iterations and all eight ordinary bundled modules.
  • The checker reports a source-semantic error before it decides whether the program is eligible for a concrete profile.
  • An input that is a directory or a qrate and an input of explicit modules differ in three ways: the loader, the provenance and the concrete consumer. After the common judgment, the project route requires its concrete declarations to fit the Finite project profile. The selected-entry route seeks native acceptance only for the requested concrete specialization.
  • Native results distinguish those scopes. They do not certify every possible specialization, and they do not establish general source preservation.
  • Four things have their own checks after the common judgment: closed host bindings, concrete capacity, emitted evidence and native acceptance.
  • A generic check that succeeds does not imply that concrete lowering succeeds.
  • All frontend output is an untrusted proposal. The native gates are mandatory: the root, request, contract, hierarchy and finite-leaf gates.

After a rule, the chapter names in parentheses the common checker class of a program that breaks the rule, as in (ownership). The code parse marks a syntax error. Codes maps each class to the code that a route reports.

Implementation note. The selected projection consumes the original resolved identities of the common judgment, with its completed lexical facts and effect facts. It records a projection restriction per declaration. A restriction excuses no check: the checker checks an unused definition, both branches and an empty loop all the same.

Ordinary finite types

An ordinary finite type describes classical data. The same type also serves as the basis of a quantum owner Q<A>.

The ordinary finite types are Unit, Bit, Bits<n> and ordered tuples of finite types. Nonempty fieldless enums and records with finite ordinary fields are ordinary finite types too. n is a checked static natural. Basis is the static kind of these finite type trees.

TypeValue and ownership
UnitOrdinary singleton, with value ()
BitOrdinary finite bit, with values 0 and 1
Bits<n>Ordinary sequence of exactly n bits, retaining ordered positions
(A,B)One ordered product value, retaining its immediate arity and nesting
Q<A>One linear quantum owner with basis A
(Q<A>,Q<B>)Two linear owners, without any assumption of state separability

Rules:

  • An ordinary value may be copied or dropped.
  • A basis argument of Q must not contain a quantum owner.
  • An ordinary tuple may mix ordinary fields and quantum owners. Each field that contains a quantum owner retains its linear obligations.
  • No C<A> constructor exists.

Bit literals

A program writes a Bit literal as 0 / 1. The spelling is the same in ordinary computations and in basis computations.

Rules:

  • false / true migrate explicitly to 0 / 1 (parse). Every other Bit numeral is rejected (parse).
  • A numeral in a position that takes a static Nat denotes a natural. The distinction is one of stage and category, and it does not inspect quantum data.
  • No literal creates a quantum owner. Typing an expression against an expected type must not implicitly prepare or measure data.
  • Both routes type 0, 1, not, and and xor by one exact Bit judgment. Both routes evaluate the operands eagerly, from left to right. Both operands of and evaluate even when the left value is zero.
  • The checker does not coerce a quantum operand, a Bits<1> value, a static natural or a product to Bit.

Bits<n> registers

A Bits<n> register holds n bits in a fixed order. An ordinary Bits<n> value is one typed value with ordered classical elements. Bits<0> has one empty value. It is a copyable singleton basis distinct from Unit.

Rules:

  • empty_bits() constructs Bits<0>.
  • prepend_bit with static argument n takes Bit and Bits<n> and returns Bits<n+1>. The head comes before the tail.
  • A program may copy or ignore an ordinary register. A quantum owner Q<Bits<n>> retains the linear rules.
  • No profile treats two types of equal width as one type. No profile infers a missing static argument.
  • The retained source graph retains the exact Unit, Bit and Bits tags and the tuple trees. Flattening the classical transport ports creates no type coercion.
  • A closed size of zero retains the Bits tag. The ordinary empty value is copyable and emits no classical identity. Q<Bits<0>> retains a distinct linear owner and branch phi even with no wires.

Implementation note. Selected Raw retains an ordinary Bits<n> value as one typed source value with ordered classical elements. Source-step replay checks the ordered elements against the artifact that the native checker accepted. This bounded check is not an AST preservation theorem. Finite project also retains ordered classical elements and exact quantum register owners. Capacities gives the width limit of each profile.

Quantum owners

A program holds a quantum system through an owner. Q<A> is linear quantum ownership over the finite value space A. Typing keeps four things distinct: ordinary bindings, static bindings, linear owners and semantic effects.

Rules:

  • A program must move, return or explicitly consume every quantum owner according to an admitted rule (ownership).
  • An ordinary binding of a Q<A> value does not require a qlet spelling.
  • A move takes the linear ownership of a value away from every later use. Copying an ordinary value neither creates nor consumes a quantum owner.
  • A static binding must not be used as a runtime value.
  • The checker does not infer effects from ownership alone. An annotation must not downgrade the effect of its body.
  • Measurement explicitly consumes a supported Q<A> and produces ordinary data with Observe semantics.
  • An ordinary if consumes an ordinary Bit condition. It cannot read a Q<Bit>. Coherent control has its separate rule.
