Checked operations

A checked operation is the static constructor checked_op(implementation, Meaning). Use checked_op to request exact Meaning evidence for a static operation description, even when the receiving parameter does not name a Meaning. The constructor itself makes the request: it asks for a check that a source operation has a declared exact meaning.

A Meaning is a declaration meaning M: A -> B = ...;. It specifies the exact action of an operation from basis tree A to basis tree B.

A program writes checked_op inside the existing explicit operation arguments. It is not a monadic bind, a runtime function value or a constitutional certification.

The checked_op constructor

CheckedOperation ::= checked_op ( Identifier , Identifier )

The constructor takes two names. The first identifier names an existing operation. The second resolves to an existing finite Meaning declaration.

Rules:

  • Visibility, lexical shadowing, static premises and the checks of the basis trees apply to both identifiers.
  • Neither argument may be a runtime value, a constructed operation expression or an explicitly specialized provider expression.
  • An outer static constructor may contain a checked operation. Its own rules do not change.
  • For a general formal Op<A -> B, M>, the checker checks both ports against the declared domain and codomain of M. An endomorphic Meaning has one basis tree for its input and its output. It requires both ports to equal that single basis tree. The type model specifies how general pure arrows are typed and the limits on materializing them.
  • Attaching a Meaning name does not discharge the equality. Equal probabilities, equal bit width or equality up to global phase must not replace the check.
  • Capability requirements are separate. An abstract parameter acquires no inverse access and no controlled access from a Meaning name.

The checker accepts this fragment. It uses an endomorphic Meaning and the grammar of operation parameters:

use std::gate::z;

classical fn z_phase(b: Bit) -> (Bit, (Bit, Bit)) { (0, (0, b)) }
meaning ZMeaning: Bit = phase_by(z_phase);
unitary fn direct(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { z(q) }

unitary fn apply_z[const U: Op<Bit, ZMeaning>](q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit>
requires Applicable(U) { U(q) }

unitary fn client(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> {
    apply_z[checked_op(direct, ZMeaning)](q)
}

Implementation note. The common original-source judgment resolves the operation and the Meaning, checks their interface bases and records a pending Meaning-equality obligation. It can resolve an in-scope abstract operation formal and record the obligation for it. Finite materialization requires closed pure source declarations, so it rejects an abstract formal as the provider of this constructor. Attaching a Meaning in the common judgment creates no evidence that bypasses that refusal. Finite materialization retains the implementation and its source dependencies. It checks their phase-fixed meaning through the selected native checker before it produces executable evidence.

Implementation note. The parser reads each argument of checked_op, and each operand of a Meaning body, as a reference name. A reference name may be a qualified path. No conformance test covers a qualified name in these positions.

Owners and capabilities

A static description contains no live quantum owner.

Rules:

  • Applying an operation consumes and returns the specified owners.
  • A runtime local, a spent value or a captured owner must not be the provider of an operation.
  • Separate owners do not imply separable states.
  • A zero-width owner retains its phase and its ownership rules.

Meaning declarations

A Meaning declaration names a specification: the exact action of an operation from one basis tree to another. A finite Meaning declares meaning M: A -> B = ...;. The form meaning M: A = ...; is short for a Meaning whose input and output trees are equal. A Meaning has one of these bodies:

MeaningBody ::= permutation_by ( Identifier )
              | phase_by ( Identifier )
              | reference ( Identifier )
              | compose ( Identifier , Identifier )
              | tensor ( Identifier , Identifier )

Rules:

  • reference, compose and tensor are contextual identifiers in this position. They are not reserved words.
  • The operands of compose and tensor resolve to declared Meanings through the ordinary visibility rules. reference resolves its function as Reference programs describes.
  • A runtime value or the name of a classical function is not a Meaning operand.
  • A Meaning may refer to a Meaning that the module declares later. A dependency cycle is an error.
  • The checker checks every declared Meaning, including an unused one.

Composition

A compose body specifies one Meaning followed by another. For First: A -> B and Second: B -> C, compose(First, Second) has type A -> C. It applies First and then Second.

Rules:

  • The codomain of First and the domain of Second must be the same tree B. The checker makes no implicit conversion between trees of equal physical dimension.
  • In the endomorphic monomial case, where First and Second both have the basis tree A, meaning M: A = compose(First, Second); applies First and then Second. Write the actions as First|x> = zeta_8^a[x] |p[x]> and Second|y> = zeta_8^b[y] |q[y]>. The result sends x to q[p[x]] with phase (a[x] + b[p[x]]) mod 8.

Tensor

A tensor body specifies two Meanings side by side, one on each field of a pair. For Left: A -> B and Right: C -> D, tensor(Left, Right) has type (A,C) -> (B,D). It assigns the left operand to the low-order axes.

Rules:

  • In the endomorphic monomial case, Left has basis A and Right has basis C. The declaration meaning T: (A, C) = tensor(Left, Right); then requires that ordered pair.
  • The first field occupies the low-order axes. For dimensions dA and dC, column x + dA*y goes to p[x] + dA*q[y] with phase (a[x] + b[y]) mod 8.
  • Nested products and zero-width fields retain their type identity. In particular, a scalar phase on Unit is not discarded.

Equality of Meanings

A check against a Meaning is a check of exact equality. The rules below say what that equality observes. The checker accepts these declarations:

classical fn flip(b: Bit) -> Bit { not b }
classical fn z_phase(b: Bit) -> (Bit, (Bit, Bit)) { (0, (0, b)) }
meaning X: Bit = permutation_by(flip);
meaning Z: Bit = phase_by(z_phase);
meaning ZX: Bit = compose(Z, X);
meaning Ordered: (Bit, Bit) = tensor(Z, X);

Rules:

  • Equality retains every column, the exact phase and the axis order. It is not probability equality, and it is not equality up to global phase. For example, compose(X, Z) differs from ZX by a minus sign.
  • Either operand of compose or tensor may contain references or monomial targets. Equality observes the exact complex phase and the ordered basis trees. It also observes the scalar action on Q<Unit>, which has zero axes.
  • Forming a target does not prove a provider correct. checked_op and refined parameters require a fresh native comparison against the independently formed request. That comparison retains the original identities of the source, of the dependencies and of the provider.
  • Forming a Meaning creates no live owner and no inverse or control capability. The capability checks and the source-control checks govern those uses.

Implementation note. For monomial operands, compose and tensor normalize their targets within the six-bit finite bound and the work limits. A reference graph is retained even when its denotation is monomial, such as a reference to the identity or compose(H, H). The public monomial-only FiniteMeaning accessor rejects every graph that contains a reference.

Reference programs

A reference body uses a program as the specification. A program writes one when an ordinary function already states the action that it wants. For example, meaning H: Bit = reference(reference_h); names one closed ordinary function as the specification.

Rules:

  • For the equal-tree form meaning M: A = reference(f);, f must have the interface Q<A> -> Q<A>. The checked effect that callers of f see must be Unitary. In the example, the interface is Q<Bit> -> Q<Bit>.
  • For the rectangular form meaning M: A -> B = reference(f);, f must have the interface Q<A> -> Q<B>. The checked effect that callers of f see must be at most Isometry.
  • The argument must be a single resolved function identifier. Static arguments, constructed operations, classical or static functions and other Meaning names are not accepted.
  • Visibility checks apply. The dependency-cycle check covers all declarations, including cycles through apply_contract and checked_op.
  • A declared effect assertion must not replace independent checking of the complete body and its dependencies.
  • The public-effect rule applies. Outside the original module of the provider, it uses the checked public effect. Inside that module, it uses internal inference. Reference selection, specialization and cached evidence must not recover a sharper external eligibility from the body.

The checker accepts these declarations:

fn reference_h(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { h(q) }
meaning H: Bit = reference(reference_h);
meaning HH: Bit = compose(H, H);

Implementation note. A reference contributes its independently checked original Raw artifact and its dependencies. A fresh native equation compares the implementation with that request. For endomorphic functions, the emitted contract receipts retain both artifacts, their dependencies and the original source snapshot. Rectangular provider bodies and reference bodies receive separate native equations, and the Raw call intervals are rechecked against the requested matrix. A matching matrix, function name or source annotation cannot substitute another receipt. Unused targets, unused generic equality obligations and zero-repeat child requests are checked before emission.

Fixed Fourier specifications

The following closed reference functions specify the positive Fourier matrices on two and three qubits in the existing exact carrier. They are fixed examples. They are not a generic QFT implementation, and they add no Fourier constructor.

use std::gate::s;
use std::gate::t;

fn quarter(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { s(q) }
fn eighth(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit> { t(q) }
fn fourier2(q: Q<(Bit,Bit)>) -> Q<(Bit,Bit)> {
    let (a,b)=split(q);
    let b=h(b);
    let (a,b)=controlled(quarter)(a,b);
    let a=h(a);
    join(b,a)
}
fn fourier3(q: Q<((Bit,Bit),Bit)>) -> Q<((Bit,Bit),Bit)> {
    let (ab,c)=split(q);
    let (a,b)=split(ab);
    let c=h(c);
    let (b,c)=controlled(quarter)(b,c);
    let (a,c)=controlled(eighth)(a,c);
    let b=h(b);
    let (a,b)=controlled(quarter)(a,b);
    let a=h(a);
    join(join(c,b),a)
}
meaning F4: (Bit,Bit) = reference(fourier2);
meaning F8: ((Bit,Bit),Bit) = reference(fourier3);

With low-order axes first, the independent equation for the fixed dimensions N = 4 and N = 8 is

\[ F_N[y,x] = \frac{\exp(2\pi ixy/N)}{\sqrt{N}}. \]

The fixed reference regressions check every coefficient on both concrete adapters, including the output reversal and the exact phase. A consumer can use these targets in apply_contract or Op<A,M> under the same evidence rules.

Migration from bind_op

bind_op is the retired spelling of the constructor. To migrate a source, replace bind_op(implementation, Meaning) with the identical arguments to checked_op(implementation, Meaning).

Rules:

  • bind_op is reserved only for a located retirement error. It is never accepted as an alias, including in nested constructors.
  • The lexical boundary specifies reserved identifier collisions, comments, byte spans and the order of diagnostics.
  • Retained evidence includes exact source snapshots. A change of this spelling may therefore change a receipt or a QIRF source identity, even when the requested mathematical meaning and the ordered interface are unchanged.
  • Reconstruct the evidence for the migrated source and check it independently. Do not reuse stale receipts, and do not remove source bindings to force byte equality.

Status and limits

Limits:

LimitValue
Finite Meaning equationsThe six-bit bound of the exact carrier, with its arithmetic and work limits
Cells of a reference expression graph4,096
Depth of a reference expression graph64
Aggregate materialized artifact bytes of a reference expression graph100,000
  • The selected adapter also applies limits of its own: on call depth and dependency depth, on operations, on source snapshots and on aggregate providers. An expression within the limits above is not a promise that every concrete profile can materialize it.
  • Exhaustion or an unsupported equality is rejected without approximation.
  • The native acceptance profiles are unchanged.

Profiles:

  • The finite source route supports its closed observing entry.
  • The selected hierarchy route supports its pure input/output entry for these refined operations. A readout entry outside that profile is rejected. Meaning composition broadens no readout or instrument rule.
  • For general arrows and rectangular Meanings, the ordinary project adapter and the selected Raw adapter validate original pure bodies and their dependencies against two-port pure-leaf requests. Native checking reconstructs the matrix, checks V†V = I, and retains the exact phase and the ordered ports. Raw alpha-renaming and composition produce untrusted candidates that need fresh checking.
  • The hierarchy finite-leaf profile is square.
  • Observing contracts use the separately adopted function instrument overload, not a pure Meaning constructor.
  • Two things are outside this bounded profile: general symbolic equality, and arbitrary hierarchy requests that compare a matrix with a composite. An unsupported comparison is rejected.
  • A provider outside its concrete profile is rejected. It does not lose its Meaning request. Other static constructors retain their explicit projection restrictions.

The selected concrete projection retains the checked_op constructor and its original Meaning request. Within the profile of supported closed providers, it checks Meanings as follows:

  • ElaboratedProgram::check_operation_meanings checks the original binding requests and the annotated constructor descendants through the native finite gate, on their materialized Raw bodies. Only then can the checked collection produce a hierarchy proposal. That proposal needs fresh hierarchy acceptance.
  • Direct unchecked hierarchy lowering or Raw lowering is rejected while original Meaning obligations are open.
  • The checked collection can emit Raw for direct application, sequential composition, tensor composition, adjoints and controlled access. An independent source replay checks the instruction interval, the owner boundary and the ordered axes against each original finite request through a fresh native decision.
  • Unexecuted child requests and zero-repeat child requests are checked before emission.
  • For inverse access and controlled access, the independent source traversal retains the substep range and the axis boundary of each original subtree, including requests hidden inside called definitions. Inversion reverses that range and its boundary. Coherent control retains the inactive identity sector and the exact active-sector matrix.
  • Coordinate reconstruction follows the same surrounding controls. It preserves metadata-only axis changes and the Unit phase.
  • These finite equations use the six-bit bound, the shared work budget and the final whole-artifact acceptance. All finite equations and the sector replay consume the same caller budget.
  • Refined Raw source ctrl uses the exact sector gate as well as the Meaning gate.
  • Closed audit roots are re-elaborated, and all their original Meaning requests are checked in that expanded graph. Earlier leaf keys are not transplanted.
  • Every original control obligation requires a retained concrete call interval, including unused bodies and specializations. Unclosed generic intervals and erased intervals are rejected.
  • A body can contain source ctrl. Symbolic inverse transformation or symbolic control transformation of such a body is unsupported. The failure selects no other profile.
  • The complete emitted artifact requires fresh native validity and source replay before execution.

Proof status:

  • These checks are bounded implementation checks and artifact-attachment checks. They are not a proof that source elaboration preserves its intended meaning, or that a reference program is an adequate specification.
  • These checks do not establish general source-to-request preservation.
  • The adopted QS, PR, RS and EXACT interpretations, both scoped QLV1 guarantees and their open proof duties retain their recorded status. This chapter reports no guarantee and no source-preservation theorem.

History

  • The name checked_op is the ordinary naming decision recorded in #82. The rename changed no syntax-tree meaning, primitive, protocol, schema, checker or constitutional edition. The later bounded implementation retains the independent evidence gates.
  • General arrows and rectangular Meanings were resumed for 0.3.0-beta under #83.
  • The retired operations design packet proposed broader arrow and Meaning forms and constructed provider inputs. The naming decision does not adopt them.
  • Historical first sources and diagnostics are unchanged. They sit beside explicit derivatives for the renamed spelling.

Standard-library semantic namespaces

The standard library is the std qrate that an official Qleisli distribution bundles. It consists of ordinary checked .qli source. A semantic namespace is a top-level namespace of std, such as std::gate. Each semantic namespace admits a public member by one mathematical admission rule.

Use this chapter to find where a library function lives and what its contract is. The chapter is normative for edition 2026. It specifies the canonical distribution version, the naming and admission rules, the contract of every public definition, and the retired paths. It is subordinate to the authority hierarchy and the primitive boundary.

The chapter specifies intended contracts. A namespace, a source comment or a successful source check is not a proof of a mathematical implementation. When you meet a derived abstraction that you do not know, the inference and discovery boundary specifies how it leads to its contract and to ordinary source.

Canonical distribution version

A toolchain and its standard library are distributed as one pair. This section says which std belongs to a toolchain and how the loader checks the pair.

The product version of a toolchain is its complete version identifier, including every prerelease and build suffix. The canonical std of a toolchain is the std qrate whose version equals that product version. The compiler embeds the source and the manifest of that qrate. The embedded-manifest gate is the check that the loader applies to the embedded manifest.

Rules:

  • An official Qleisli distribution must bundle exactly one canonical std qrate. Qleisli 0.3.0-beta requires std 0.3.0-beta.
  • The equality covers every prerelease and build suffix. A range, a string that needs whitespace trimming, or a different suffix cannot satisfy it.
  • A manifest must write the canonical version string without the v prefix of a release tag.
  • A source program receives the embedded std without declaring a separate standard-library dependency.
  • To use an older or a newer canonical std, a user must select the corresponding Qleisli toolchain.
  • A user qrate keeps its own version. That version need not match Qleisli.
  • The embedded manifest must declare schema 2, edition "2026", the string [qrate].name = "std" and a string [qrate].version equal to the product version. The name and the version are the identity fields. The gate rejects an identity field that is missing, that is not a string or that does not match. It does so with the code project, before the loader loads the bundle.
  • The schema check and the edition check precede the identity check. Their diagnostics are those of any manifest.

The pairing couples std to the toolchain for distribution and for compatibility. It gives std no semantic privilege: std is ordinary checked source. The qrate and artifact Reference specifies the coupling between canonical std and the toolchain.

For the product version 0.3.0-beta, the embedded-manifest gate gives these results:

Embedded [qrate].versionResult
"0.3.0-beta"Accepted
"0.2.9" or "0.3.1"Rejected
"0.3.0"Rejected
"0.3.0-other"Rejected
"v0.3.0-beta"Rejected
"0.3.0-beta ", with a trailing spaceRejected
"0.3.0-beta+different"Rejected
A missing version, or the integer 17Rejected

A user manifest that carries any of these values is accepted, because a user qrate keeps its own version.

Implementation note. The private function check_bundled in src/frontend/project/edition.rs is the embedded-manifest gate. It compares the version with the compiler’s complete CARGO_PKG_VERSION. It parses the immutable embedded manifest once and caches only that packaging result across loads. A user manifest gets a fresh schema and edition check on every load. The gate caches no source, Meaning or native acceptance judgment.

Names follow mathematical meaning

A canonical name states the mathematical meaning of an operation. It tells a caller what the operation computes, not how an implementation computes it.

Rules:

  • The canonical name of a mathematical stdlib function must describe what the operation computes.
  • The name must not put the history, a benchmark, a decomposition or an algorithm of an implementation in place of that meaning.
  • When a caller needs a choice of algorithm, that choice belongs in an explicit parameter, policy or configuration layer. This rule specifies no policy syntax and no supported implementation.
  • A top-level mathematical namespace prefers a singular noun that names a semantic concept.
  • Every public operation has one canonical home, and that home has a semantic admission rule. routines, utils, helpers, misc or an equally empty collection is not a mathematical classification.
  • The layout of the source files does not determine membership.
  • A genuine parameterized mathematical family owns its canonical semantic API identity. A fixed-size name describes its own bounded contract. It cannot replace the identity of the family.
  • A reserved identity is not an available API. It is no evidence of specialization correspondence.

qft2 and qft3 are fixed-size names, and their contracts are supported fixed interfaces. Status and limits states that generic QFT is excluded.

Admission rules

Each namespace admits a public API by one rule. Read the table to decide where an API belongs, or to learn what the members of a namespace have in common.

NamespaceAn API belongs here if and only if …Ordinary source
std::basisIts defining contract is a total finite map on ordinary basis labels, with no quantum owner transition and no observation. Coherent use must satisfy the separate obligations of the enclosing construction.stdlib/src/basis.qli
std::transformIts defining contract is a mathematical basis transform with an explicit whole-input operator and ordered coordinates, such as a Hadamard or a Fourier transformation. A contract defined as a reflection about a subspace belongs in reflection. A measurement belongs in measurement.stdlib/src/transform.qli
std::reflectionIts defining contract is a phase-fixed reflection about a specified state or subspace, including the exact projector, the sign and the owner interface. Being unitary alone is not this classification.stdlib/src/reflection.qli
std::measurementIts defining mathematical operation is a complete measurement instrument with declared classical outcomes and residual quantum owners. This includes a destructive measurement and a measurement that retains data. An arbitrary observing routine is not enough.stdlib/src/measurement.qli
std::gateIt is an ordinary checked gate definition with an exact operator, a scalar phase and an ordered-owner contract. Gate membership confers no primitive authority and no verifier authority.stdlib/src/gate.qli
std::stateIts defining contract explicitly prepares a state, or replaces an owned state under a complete effect and reference contract. Pure preparation and observation-bearing reset are distinct.stdlib/src/state.qli
std::structureIt is an ordinary checked structural map that explicitly changes an owner partition or a representation order. Its exact input and output trees and its axis map are part of the contract. It is not a physical gate merely because it denotes a permutation.stdlib/src/structure.qli
std::arithmetic (reserved)Its public identity is a reusable parameterized arithmetic or number-theoretic operation whose contract is independent of one hard-coded circuit instance.None: the namespace has no bundled module and no public export.

Reserved arithmetic identities

The reserved namespace std::arithmetic holds two design identities. The design sets these names aside. Neither is an operation that a program can call.

Reserved identityMeaning
std::arithmetic::modexp<N>The reserved shape of modular exponentiation
std::arithmetic::primefact<N>The v1 semantic identity of prime factorization

Rules:

  • shor<N> is an algorithm name. It is not the canonical mathematical API of prime factorization.
  • A reserved identity is a design identity. It is not callable syntax, a commitment to a generic-parameter syntax, or a delivered operation.

Language primitives

Language primitives are bare typed identities of the language. They are not part of the standard library, and this section says how the two relate. The primitive boundary specifies all 13 retained identities, the 27-entry migration and the concrete profile limits.

Rules:

  • Name resolution selects a language primitive only after lexical bindings and after ordinary declarations and imports.
  • A language primitive is not a standard-library export, and the primitives are not a prelude.
  • std::quantum, std::observe, std::registers and std::classical are retired without aliases.
  • An ordinary module, including std::basis, has no primitive privilege.

Inventory

The standard library has 8 bundled ordinary modules. They expose 26 public definitions and 6 transparent prelude reexports, and they contain 5 private helpers.

The prelude and import quick reference lists the six reexported members, their lookup priority and the explicit opt-out.

Rules:

  • A contract identifier, such as B001 or R003, names a source contract. It is not a constitutional ledger entry and not a verification badge.

Interfaces and contracts

This section gives the contract of every public definition, one namespace at a time. Each table quotes the header of a declaration as its source file writes it. A header describes an interface. It is not a function type.

Rules:

  • A public quantum function has an explicit effect contract, which the checker checks under the order Unitary <= Isometry <= Observe. The checker checks the body of the function independently.
  • An external caller uses the public effect. Inference within the same module keeps its precision and any further external boundary.
  • Bundled source and user source follow the same effect rules.
  • A classical function has a total ordinary meaning. It may receive ordinary runtime values, including Bits that a program has already measured.
  • A classical function preserves the effects of its evaluated arguments. It cannot inspect a live quantum owner.
  • The truth table of a classical function grants no quantum preparation, no observation, no inverse or control access and no evidence of coherent injectivity. Coherent use keeps its separate checks.
  • Every quantum contract applies to an arbitrary permitted input, tensored with the identity on an external reference.
  • Separate owners may be entangled with each other or with a reference.
  • No measurement result authorizes an implicit discard, a clean release, or inverse or controlled access.

std::basis

PathDeclarationContract
std::basis::xor2pub classical fn xor2(x: Bit, y: Bit) -> BitB001: total XOR on the four pairs of input labels. The map is not injective on the product domain.
std::basis::and2pub classical fn and2(x: Bit, y: Bit) -> BitB002: total AND on the four pairs of input labels. The map is not injective on the product domain.

Each function takes two arguments, not one pair.

std::transform

PathDeclarationContract
std::transform::hadamard2pub unitary fn hadamard2(q: Q<(Bit, Bit)>) -> Q<(Bit, Bit)>R001: ordered H tensor H
std::transform::qft2pub unitary fn qft2(q: Q<(Bit, Bit)>) -> Q<(Bit, Bit)>F001: positive F4 with included reversal
std::transform::qft3pub unitary fn qft3(q: Q<((Bit, Bit), Bit)>) -> Q<((Bit, Bit), Bit)>F002: positive F8 with included reversal

F001 and F002 use F_d[y,x] = exp(2*pi*i*x*y/d)/sqrt(d) for d = 4, 8. For the two-bit input (a,b), x = a + 2*b. For ((a,b),c), x = a + 2*b + 4*c. The output coordinates follow the same convention and include the reversal of the circuit.

Rules:

  • The complete tuple tree, the ordered axes and the scalar phase are part of each contract. Equal bit width, agreement of probabilities or an inverse round trip cannot substitute for them.
  • R001 preserves the original order of its two owners and specifies exact Hadamard coefficients.

std::reflection

PathDeclarationContract
std::reflection::reflect_uniform2pub unitary fn reflect_uniform2(q: Q<(Bit, Bit)>) -> Q<(Bit, Bit)>R002: the phase-fixed reflection about the uniform two-bit state

R002 is 2|++><++| - I, with this exact sign. Its body uses the private total classical predicate nonzero2, which returns zero exactly on 00 and one elsewhere. The computed auxiliary of that predicate supplies the phase +1 on 00 and -1 elsewhere, before conjugation by R001.

Rules:

  • The protected computed scope requires two things of the temporary auxiliary: an exact return to zero, and separation. It requires them for all permitted inputs and references.
  • Moving the helper or naming the reflection does not supply that evidence.
  • The helper is private. std::reflection imports the ordinary public Hadamard transform.

std::measurement

PathDeclarationContract
std::measurement::measure_xpub observe fn measure_x(q: Q<Bit>) -> BitR003: destructive X measurement
std::measurement::measure_z2pub observe fn measure_z2(q: Q<(Bit, Bit)>) -> (Bit, Bit)R004: destructive ordered two-bit Z measurement
std::measurement::parity_zzpub observe fn parity_zz(a: Q<Bit>, b: Q<Bit>) -> ((Q<Bit>, Q<Bit>), Bit)R005: nondestructive Z-parity measurement of the data

Each contract describes every outcome with its unnormalized branch, without postselection:

  • R003 has the branch K_b = <b| H. It returns b for the X eigenvalue (-1)^b and consumes its target owner.
  • R004 has the branch K_(a,b) = <a,b| in the ordered coordinates of the register. It returns the left result and the right result in that order, and it consumes both owners.
  • R005 has the branch K_s = (I + (-1)^s Z_a Z_b)/2. It returns both data owners in their original order together with s, and it preserves coherence within each parity subspace. It measures and consumes its fresh-zero meter.

Rules:

  • R005 requires distinct owners. It does not require a product state.

std::gate

PathDeclarationContract
std::gate::idpub unitary fn id[const A: Basis](q: Q<A>) -> Q<A>Identity with coefficient +1. It keeps the full Basis tree and every zero-width owner. It emits no physical instruction and performs no implicit type conversion.
std::gate::xpub unitary fn x(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit>X, as H Z H
std::gate::zpub unitary fn z(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit>Z, the half-turn phase phase[1,1]
std::gate::spub unitary fn s(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit>S, the quarter-turn phase phase[1,2]
std::gate::sdgpub unitary fn sdg(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit>S†, as adjoint(s)
std::gate::tpub unitary fn t(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit>T, exactly diag(1, exp(i*pi/4)). The body controls the scalar phase on a fresh Q<Unit> owner and explicitly consumes that owner. It adds no physical wire.
std::gate::tdgpub unitary fn tdg(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit>T†, as adjoint(t)
std::gate::cnotpub unitary fn cnot(a: Q<Bit>, b: Q<Bit>) -> (Q<Bit>, Q<Bit>)Ordinary controlled X. The first owner is the control. The outputs keep their order, with phase +1.
std::gate::toffolipub unitary fn toffoli(a: Q<Bit>, b: Q<Bit>, c: Q<Bit>) -> ((Q<Bit>,Q<Bit>),Q<Bit>)Ordinary control of a packed CNOT. Both controls keep their basis labels. The target flips if and only if both controls are one, with phase +1 and no additional physical wire.
std::gate::controlled_phasepub unitary fn controlled_phase[const j: Nat, const k: Nat](a: Q<Bit>, b: Q<Bit>) -> (Q<Bit>, Q<Bit>)Ordinary control of phase[j,k]: exactly diag(1,1,1,exp(2*pi*i*j/2^k)) in control/target order. The concrete coefficient and profile conditions of the phase provider apply.
std::gate::swappub unitary fn swap(a: Q<Bit>, b: Q<Bit>) -> (Q<Bit>, Q<Bit>)Two-Bit SWAP with exact phase +1, as three ordinary CNOT calls that keep their controlled-X work. The output wires keep their original order. A target gate cost requires a checked realization.

Rules:

  • x, z, s, sdg and tdg each preserve the full exact phase and the original returned owner interface.

The exact phase of t

This section says how the body of t obtains its exact phase. The private scalar helper scalar_eighth has the exact meaning zeta_8 I_Unit. Coherent control of that helper gives diag(1,zeta_8) on the retained Bit. The zero-width target is a logical owner: the body introduces it with unit(()) and consumes it with finish.

Rules:

  • The absence of physical wires does not imply a zero synthesis cost or a zero gate cost.
  • A body that applies the scalar directly to Q<Bit> gives zeta_8 I_Bit. That body must fail an exact T request.
  • global_phase_eighth is the bare scalar primitive. phase_eighth is not an alias.

Implementation note. The body of t keeps a CircuitAction::Contract dependency. The terminal OpenQASM 3 exporter and the terminal QIR Base exporter expand the retained circuit of that dependency. They preserve the ordered axes, the control polarity and the adjoints before they lower to target gates.

std::state

PathDeclarationContract
std::state::init0pub isometry fn init0() -> Q<Bit>Exact zero-state preparation with coefficient +1. The function is nullary. It allocates one fresh physical wire and one owner.
std::state::resetpub observe fn reset(q: Q<Bit>) -> Q<Bit>An explicit discard, followed by init0

init0 prepares exactly |0>, tensored with the identity on every retained reference. Its body is the ordinary basis unit(()) as _ { 0 }, which uses the injective singleton rule.

reset has the channel rho_AR -> |0><0| tensor Tr_A(rho_AR). The fresh zero state is independent of the erased input.

Rules:

  • reset is Observe even on a zero input.

std::structure

PathDeclarationContract
std::structure::permute_axespub unitary fn permute_axes(q: Q<(Bit,Bit)>) -> Q<(Bit,Bit)>Structural two-axis map [1,0] with exact phase +1. The output wire order is reversed. The body emits no gate instruction.
std::structure::transpose_axespub unitary fn transpose_axes[const n: Nat, const i: Nat, const j: Nat](q: Q<Bits<n>>) -> Q<Bits<n>> requires i < j, j < nThe output-to-input axis map is the identity with the positions i and j exchanged. The phase is +1, and the body emits no gate instruction.
std::structure::emptypub unitary fn empty() -> Q<Bits<0>>Explicit singleton basis map from a fresh Unit owner to the exact Bits<0> tag, with coefficient +1 and no physical wire. The function is nullary.
std::structure::consume_emptypub unitary fn consume_empty(q: Q<Bits<0>>) -> UnitExplicit singleton map to Unit, followed by finish. It keeps the complete scalar and reference action. It performs no observation and no implicit coercion.

Rules:

  • A call of transpose_axes must satisfy i < j < n. The checker rejects a call that breaks this premise with the class size. Codes gives the code of that class on each route.
  • Each argument of a call is relative to the input order at that call.
  • A finite sequence of transpositions describes an arbitrary ordered permutation, under the usual specialization bounds.

The checker accepts this program:

use std::structure::transpose_axes;

pub unitary fn probe(q: Q<Bits<3>>) -> Q<Bits<3>> {
    transpose_axes[3,0,1](transpose_axes[3,1,2](q))
}

On Bits<3>, the program first exchanges positions 1 and 2, then positions 0 and 1. It gathers the original axes in the order [2,0,1]. The checker rejects the calls transpose_axes[3,1,1], transpose_axes[3,2,1] and transpose_axes[3,0,3] on the same input.

Physical swap and axis reordering

This section compares two functions that exchange two Bits. std::gate::swap and std::structure::permute_axes are ordinary checked .qli, as is every function of std::gate and std::structure. Under fixed input and output coordinates, both denote |a,b> -> |b,a> with phase +1. Their wire maps and their physical work differ.

Rules:

  • swap(excl a, excl b) returns authority to the updated original owners.
  • permute_axes(q) consumes its pair and returns it with the explicit axis map.
  • Neither operation is binding exchange.
  • Matrix equality alone grants an optimizer no permission to replace one routing implementation by the other.
  • Target routing and a quantitative resource claim each need their own checked correspondence and accounting. Zero source gate instructions are not a promise of zero physical routing cost.

Retired paths

A retired path is an earlier public path of the standard library that no module provides. The table says where the members of each retired path are.

Retired pathCanonical location
std::transforms::{qft2,qft3}std::transform::{qft2,qft3}
std::routines::hadamard2std::transform::hadamard2
std::routines::reflect_uniform2std::reflection::reflect_uniform2
std::routines::{measure_x,measure_z2,parity_zz}std::measurement::{measure_x,measure_z2,parity_zz}
std::gate::permute_axesstd::structure::permute_axes
std::arithmetic::{increment2,add2,mul2_mod15}Local arithmetic source in examples/order_finding/arithmetic.qli; no canonical std export

A grouped path in this table abbreviates one row for each member. The table defines no import syntax. Prelude, imports and qualified names gives the import forms.

Rules:

  • A program must name a supported declaration by its canonical location. A retired path has no compatibility alias, and the loader rejects an import of it.
  • All five former public members of routines have a namespace under Admission rules. The private nonzero2 is in std::reflection, with the reflection.
  • The three former arithmetic exports are the entire retired public arithmetic surface.
  • A contract identifier keeps its meaning when its definition moves.
  • The move changes no public result tree and no consume or return obligation.
  • Active imports, examples, corpus translations, tests and documentation must migrate together.
  • First authoring sources, earlier diagnostics, proofs, counterexamples and validation records keep their original paths and bytes. A historical record is not a compatibility API and not an executable migration target.

The loader accepts use std::transform::qft2;. It rejects use std::transforms::qft2;, use std::routines::hadamard2; and use std::arithmetic::add2;. It also rejects use std::gate::permute_axes;, and the message names std::structure::permute_axes and std::gate::swap.

The three retired arithmetic definitions are ordinary local source of the order-finding example.

increment2 / A001Q<(Bit,Bit)> -> the same tree; y -> (y+1) mod 4 with coefficient +1, first leaf weight 1 and overflow wrapping.
add2 / A002Q<((Bit,Bit),(Bit,Bit))> -> the same tree; (x,y) -> (x,(y+x) mod 4) with coefficient +1; both pairs little-endian and the addend retained.

  • These fixed teaching and test circuits have no input-range promise, no auxiliary and no measurement. They return every owner.
  • Their removal from std changes none of their bodies, contracts, evidence or license.

Checking

The standard library receives the checks of any source. Its place in the distribution exempts it from none of them.

Rules:

  • All eight modules, their private and unused declarations, and the source of the caller undergo the same mandatory common-source judgment.
  • Concrete lowering and fresh native acceptance are separate stages. The support for each stage is specific to a profile.
  • A path grants no sealed status, no body-derived effect, no independent exact Meaning, no provider capability and no acceptance exception.
  • Migrated source must be rechecked. A cached fact must not be rebound to other bytes.

Status and limits

Limits of the library:

  • Generic QFT is excluded from all of v0.3.0 and from the adopted development goal. The exclusion covers four things: its implementation, its public integration, the equivalence of the fixed and generic forms, and the completion of proofs that are specific to QFT. This chapter promises neither qft<N> nor a completion target.
  • The library contains no arithmetic implementation and no mechanism that selects an algorithm.
  • A single first-class permutation argument is unsupported.
  • On the bounded producer path of t, the exporters apply their target vocabulary and their workspace limits. They refuse an unsupported body.
  • A later structural refactor consumes these mathematical identities and the contracts that are complete. It may change layout, visibility and discovery. It must not redefine a meaning, restore the retired catch-all namespace or the retired arithmetic exports, or add a dependency on generic QFT.
  • The analysis tools QLT, QDB and QCP, and general growth of the standard library, have their own later scope.

Limits of the canonical version:

  • The embedded-manifest gate is implemented. It implements no resolver and no record API.
  • The binding of the resolved pair by qargo is unfinished. It requires the checks of qargo on the resolved environment and on the pairing of lock and build records.
  • Equal version strings alone cannot detect stale or substituted source content, establish an official artifact identity, or replace the source and evidence checks.
  • The duty to carry the authoritative edition identity through public and native artifacts is met in part. The native envelope carries the explicit edition through native acceptance. The ecosystem migration is not complete, and its CI is open.
  • Packaging identity is not a source-preservation proof. It discharges none of QS, PR, RS and EXACT.

Evidence:

  • Source checking, bounded complex and instrument comparisons, conformance of the checked IR, source preservation and specification review each have separate evidence and premises.
  • Tests: tests/project.rs checks the canonical paths and the rejection of every retired path. tests/editions.rs compares the bundled descriptor with stdlib/Qargo.toml and with every file of stdlib/src. The unit tests of src/frontend/project/edition.rs check the embedded-manifest gate. tests/axis_routing_boundary.rs checks the transposition example.
  • The source definitions and their exact requested checks are separate from source-to-target preservation and from quantitative PR and RS evidence.
  • The migrated source requires exact literal-output phase checks and clean-scratch checks. These include the narrow zero-input, one-output singleton table for preparation. Their coverage must be recorded with the final artifact. This chapter reports no execution of them.
  • Those checks supply no general export preservation theorem and no quantitative resource certificate.
  • This namespace contract completes no broader QS, PR, quantitative RS or EXACT proof obligation. It admits no constitutional guarantee.
  • Validation of the source migration is recorded separately. This chapter does not report a completed same-commit release gate.

Realization, specialization and resources

Checking an artifact and showing that a target implements its accepted meaning are separate tasks. A check does not settle how a target implements that meaning, how close an implementation comes, or what it costs. This chapter covers the claims that answer those three questions.

A realization is a claim that one emitted target artifact implements the accepted meaning of a program under a named target profile. A realization names a closed specialization. That is an instance of a definition in which every choice that determines its meaning and interface is fixed.

An engineering claim is an approximation claim. It states a finite bound, in a named metric, on the distance between an actual artifact and an exact ideal. It is neither acceptance nor a guarantee. A resource certificate is a checked quantitative bound on the resources of one emitted artifact.

This chapter specifies the boundary between the meaning of a program and a claimed target implementation. It applies the adopted PR-2026-01 and RS-2026-01 interpretations under the authority hierarchy.

The chapter fixes the request formats and the named profiles of the native engineering comparisons. Each of those profiles is closed and bounded, and it serves one comparison. None is the target capability schema. The chapter defines no such schema, no universal gate set and no synthesis algorithm, and it adds no source syntax. The target capability schema is future work that consumes the abstract obligations stated here.

Status and limits states the limits of the implementation and of the proofs. This chapter does not discharge the implementation and evidence obligations of the decisions that govern it.

Semantic validity and a target realization

Two questions are separate. One asks whether a program denotes a unitary operator. The other asks whether a particular target artifact implements that operator. This section keeps an answer to one from standing in for the other.

Semantic unitarity is a property of the exact denotation of a program. Physical Realizability is a forward correspondence obligation. Take an accepted closed instance p, the actual output artifact C and a profile T. A checked realization of C under T must implement the accepted meaning of p. It does so subject to its explicit premises about the interface, the encoding and the workspace.

Rules:

  • Semantic unitarity makes no promise about a target. It does not promise that the selected target can implement the operator, that synthesis can find an implementation, or that the logical wires of the source suffice.
  • When target synthesis fails, that failure must not reclassify a semantically unitary program as non-unitary.
  • Inverse access and controlled access have their own contracts. Neither follows from finding one realization.
  • A claim about a circuit that a search considered does not cover a different circuit that is emitted or executed afterwards.
  • Synthesis and search produce candidates, and they do so outside acceptance. An independently supplied candidate may qualify through the same checks. A complete synthesis algorithm for the entire semantic domain is not required.
  • A failure to find a candidate is not evidence of impossibility. An impossibility claim requires an obstruction whose hypotheses match the target.
  • A result on existence or on synthesis completeness for a whole domain is optional mathematics of a profile.

For example, Theorem 1 of Giles and Selinger establishes exact Clifford+T synthesis with at most one clean ancilla for 2^n × 2^n unitary matrices over Z[1/√2, i], under their specified gate and phase conventions. That result grants no arbitrary dirty workspace, and it does not verify the output of a particular compiler. See the original theorem.

Observing instruments on a target

This section states what a target artifact owes to a program that measures. The source instrument judgment defines the complete outcome maps of an Observe expression. Realization requires a separate judgment. That judgment is about the closed instance, the selected target profile and the actual emitted artifact.

For each ordinary input x and declared outcome c, let Φ[x,c] be the source map. Let Ψ[x,c] be the map of the emitted instrument after the declared projection of its records. The declared encoding channels are E_in for the input and E_out for the output. The exact obligation is

(Ψ[x,c] ⊗ id_R)((E_in ⊗ id_R)(ρ)) =
(E_out ⊗ id_R)((Φ[x,c] ⊗ id_R)(ρ)).

The equation holds for every finite external reference R and every joint input ρ at the complete source interface.

Rules:

  • The judgment fixes three things: the ordered quantum and classical interfaces, the logical encodings, and the projection of target records to source outcomes. It accounts for how every additional physical owner is initialized and how it is disposed of.
  • The projection assigns every target history to exactly one source outcome. This includes a history with records hidden from the source.
  • The unnormalized maps fix both the outcome probabilities and the residual quantum state on the declared retained owners.
  • The correspondence includes the consumed owners, the order of every owner that stays live and the action of every branch that contributes to a public outcome.
  • The evidence states how the profile realizes each required measurement basis, where measurements can occur, which owners stay live, and how reset or repreparation obtains its stated output.
  • For feed-forward, the evidence identifies the available classical outcome and the conditional operations. It also identifies any assumption about dynamic control, scheduling or latency that the branch needs in order to execute with the specified live owners.
  • Classical feed-forward selects a branch by a classical outcome. Coherent control acts on a live quantum selector and must preserve coherence between its sectors. Each needs its own realization evidence.
  • Destructive readout accounts for the consumed owner. A retaining instrument requires the declared output owners and their conditional quantum state.
  • An implementation that reads out and then prepares qualifies only if the full correspondence equation holds.
  • A profile that supports only terminal readout may refuse a target claim that requires mid-circuit measurement and conditional quantum action.
  • Target lowering fails for a profile that lacks a required target feature or the evidence for it. The source retains its instrument, type and effect.
  • An engineering approximation requires the explicit separate claim.

For example, a program can measure both data qubits in Z and report their parity. On an even Bell state, that has the same classical distribution as std::measurement::parity_zz. The two readouts lose the coherence between 00 and 11, whereas the retaining parity projector preserves it. Preparing replacements in the computational basis leaves that difference in the even outcome map.

This abstract obligation is an input to the future target capability schema. QCP or another backend may express the premises in its own profile vocabulary. Source semantics are defined independently of that vocabulary.

Closed specialization

A generic definition describes a family. A realization is a claim about one member of that family. A closed specialization identifies the member. It fixes every choice that determines the meaning and interface of the member:

  • the resolved definition, with the complete identities of its dependencies and of its sources;
  • the ordered static arguments, including natural sizes and basis types;
  • the selected providers, their types, their capability requirements and their Meaning bindings;
  • all relevant static constraints and finite evaluation results;
  • the declared constitutional edition and the applicable semantic profile.

For a target claim, the realization fixes four more things: the target and profile, the ordered layout and encoding, the workspace contract and any choices that depend on the target.

Rules:

  • An unresolved item must not be treated as a successful concrete certificate. This holds for an unresolved parameter, capability requirement, constraint or budget expression.
  • A spelling, a bit width or a function name is not a specialization identity. The exact type tree is part of that identity, including Unit factors and zero-width owners.
  • Generic checking must cover the admitted cases of the generic body under its declared premises. A favorable specialization must not excuse an invalid generic body or erase an obligation in an unselected branch.
  • A well-typed family need not fit one fixed target at every parameter value.
  • A family theorem may quantify over all admissible substitutions. Its statement must retain those premises. It must not describe one fixed finite circuit as implementing an unbounded family.
  • Three properties are separate: static totality, the computation of the resource bounds of an instance, and the feasibility of those bounds on a target.

The static language specifies static evaluation and the forming of closed instances. Diagnostics states when a failed export names the closed specialization.

Logical axes and physical placement

A program orders the axes of its owners through its types. A target holds those axes at physical locations. This section states how a realization relates the two orders.

The logical interface records the ordered axes of each owner by the exact source type trees. A physical layout assigns the live axes to target locations. For example, the ordered pair of logical axes can occupy the physical locations (17,4). The first axis stays the first logical axis.

Take a pure instance with semantic action U and actual target action C. A correspondence with encodings E_in and E_out has the form C ∘ E_in = E_out ∘ U.

Rules:

  • Nested products and Bits<n> retain their declared axis order and owner order. A zero-width owner retains its interface identity and contributes no physical location.
  • A target realization records the initial and the final placement, or their equivalent ordered encodings.
  • The encodings include the specified workspace and its boundary state where required. The equation extends to arbitrary joint inputs with an untouched reference.
  • An observing realization uses the outcome maps. It records the placement and the disposition of the owners that are live at each interface, including any retired locations where the profile supports them.
  • Routing may change the placement from (17,4) to (4,17) by an emitted physical SWAP, provided the evidence tracks each logical axis into its location after the SWAP. The SWAP contributes to the target cost.
  • A metadata relabeling changes the description of the layout and leaves the physical state in place. The encoding evidence must justify that relabeling.
  • A source-level axis permutation changes the logical action. It must be included in U with its specified order and phase.
  • An emitted implementation of a logical SWAP must realize that action under its declared encodings.
  • The placement evidence identifies each routing step. It accounts for the live locations that routing and synthesis workspace use.

The target model may expose this relation to QCP routing analysis. The future target capability schema consumes this abstract correspondence. The bounded routing check covers literal physical SWAP intervals and their stated placement premises.

Workspace and exact correspondence

Workspace appears at two levels. The author writes source clean and dirty workspace, and it is part of the program’s contract and of its owner accounting. Backend workspace is additional storage that an implementation uses to realize that meaning.

For a unitary instance with clean workspace, a representative equation is

(C ⊗ I_E)(encode_in ⊗ I_E)(|0>_W ⊗ ψ)
  = (encode_out ⊗ I_E)(|0>_W ⊗ (U ⊗ I_E)ψ)

Here ψ belongs to L_in ⊗ E, and U maps L_in to L_out. The isometric encodings map W ⊗ L_in and W ⊗ L_out to the respective physical interfaces. The reference E stays last and is untouched. Each side therefore uses the same explicit order of workspace, data and reference.

Rules:

  • Backend storage must not become an implicit source owner or a permission to discard a source value. The realization claim must state how that storage is initialized, how long it lives, how it is restored and what it costs physically.
  • The equality is exact, including scalar phase. W starts and finishes in the specified pure zero state.
  • A type width, an owner name or an example input does not prove this equation.
  • For other encodings, or for differing input and output interfaces, the realization must state its corresponding typed equation explicitly.
  • Dirty workspace requires the declared identity action on its unknown state and on all reference correlations. Returning its marginal state on a few inputs is insufficient.
  • An observing implementation requires the complete instrument correspondence. That correspondence is unnormalized and indexed by outcome, and it includes the declared assembly of the classical result. A normalized selected branch or matching measurement probabilities must not replace it.
  • Projective equality differs from exact operator equality. Dropping a global phase can change a coherently controlled operation. The exact contract does not quotient by that phase.
  • A different equality relation must identify its boundary and its compositional obligations explicitly. The exact contract of this chapter has no approximate acceptance and no error budget.

The exact clean and dirty requirements come from the adopted QS interpretation. Exact target-domain membership and Separate engineering approximation claims state the rules of the exact and the approximate profiles.

Controlled target realizations

A controlled operation raises three separate questions: what it means, whether source code has access to it, and whether a target implements it. This section covers the third.

The coherent Meaning of controlled(U) is the ordered direct sum I ⊕ U, with inactive sector zero and active sector one. Semantic unitarity establishes the operator property of U. The static Controllable(U) judgment separately governs source use under the operation type rules.

Rules:

  • Target lowering requires one thing more: a checked realization of the exact direct sum on the selected target.
  • For a transparent implementation, a structural derivation must check each original gate or named implementation with its control, dependencies, axis order and exact phase.
  • The implementation must act as the identity in the inactive sector and must implement the requested operation in the active sector.
  • Composition and powers may compose those exact sector equations when the interfaces and the control match. Provider calls and the controlled powers that QPE uses carry the same obligations.
  • A realization certificate binds four things: the original operation and Meaning, the actual emitted implementation, the target profile, and the ordered encodings of the control, the data and the workspace. It identifies where the implementation uses native controlled gates and where it needs additional synthesis steps.
  • Physical counts include workspace preparation, live width, restoration, generated inverse steps and routing when the implementation requires them.
  • An opaque provider requires explicit controlled evidence. That evidence is bound to the requested operator and the emitted artifact.
  • A scalar phase that multiplies only the active block changes its phase relative to the inactive block. Projective agreement or channel equality for the uncontrolled operation therefore must not supply the controlled equation.
  • An engineering approximation to a controlled operator must bound its error against the intended controlled Meaning itself. It retains the exactness distinction of Separate engineering approximation claims.

Isometries and initialized target interfaces

A semantic isometry V: A -> B satisfies V† V = I_A. The basis trees of A and B can differ, including in width. This section covers the target realization of an isometry, including the wires that the target initializes.

Suppose a target implements the isometry with a unitary dilation. Let E_in: A -> P_in and E_out: B -> P_out be the exact isometric encodings of the input and of the output. Let C: P_in -> P_out be the action of the actual target circuit. On every joint input ψ with external reference R, the realization must establish

(C ⊗ I_R)(E_in ⊗ I_R) ψ = (E_out ⊗ I_R)(V ⊗ I_R) ψ.

The mathematical adjoint reverses V on its image. On the full output space, V V† is the projector onto that image. For an exact unitary dilation, C† E_out V = E_in, including under an arbitrary external reference. An available checked reverse circuit therefore recovers the encoded input on that image.

Rules:

  • A realization of Op<A -> B>, or of its refinement Op<A -> B, M>, retains both exact ports and the requested Meaning.
  • Sequential composition matches the middle tree exactly. Tensor composition preserves the declared order of both ports.
  • The input encoding specifies any initialized backend wires and their ordered placement.
  • The output encoding identifies the retained logical output. It fixes the state of every backend wire that the claim returns clean. Other physical degrees of freedom require an explicit output contract.
  • Isometry typing introduces no implicit discard and no partial trace.
  • Source clean and dirty contracts bind source owners separately.
  • A target claim accounts for every physical wire that the dilation uses, including initialized backend workspace. It also accounts for the preparation, realization, cleanup and routing that the selected target model requires.
  • A theorem that a dilation exists supplies a candidate. The accepted artifact requires the displayed correspondence.
  • An application outside the established image needs its own contract.
  • The static Adjointable capability and the physical realization of a reverse operation require independent evidence under the operation type rules.

Exact target-domain membership

A target profile does not realize every exact Meaning. Membership in the exact domain of a profile is the premise that an exact realization on that profile needs. M ∈ ExactDomain(P) is an abstract judgment about the requested exact Meaning M and a specified target profile P.

Rules:

  • The evidence identifies the profile and its version, the literal gate vocabulary, the coefficient and parameter domain, the ordered interface and the phase convention. It also states which assumptions the profile admits about initialization, encoding, workspace and restoration. A same-wire profile and a clean-workspace profile can therefore have different exact domains.
  • Physical Realizability requires evidence of this premise for an accepted exact target realization.
  • A checked exact witness for the profile may establish membership and bind the actual emitted artifact to the same Meaning.
  • An existence theorem or a coefficient test may support this judgment within its own hypotheses. A necessary condition alone does not authorize a candidate.
  • A search failure or a capacity refusal leaves the claim unproved.
  • A target-domain refusal concerns the requested realization. The source retains its exact meaning and typing.
  • A failed exact request does not select the engineering path implicitly. An engineering approximation requires an explicit separate claim with the applicable metric, a closed budget and the correspondence to the actual artifact.
  • This judgment is independent of any eventual QCP implementation. The future target capability schema may use it.

For example, take a profile whose gates and computational-basis coordinates have coefficients in Q(ζ8). Every entry of the gate product lies in that field. Appending clean zero workspace and taking the corresponding returned coordinate selects entries of the same product. A controlled phase of one sixteenth of a turn has coefficient ζ16 at its active diagonal entry, which is outside Q(ζ8). The obstruction applies for any number of such clean axes.

A target with a declared native sixteenth-turn gate requires its own exact-domain evidence. The eighth-root execution profile reports an unsupported exact phase for such a request.

Separate engineering approximation claims

An artifact that only approximates the meaning of a program is not an exact realization. A tool can state how close the artifact comes, as an engineering claim. This section keeps that claim apart from every exact one.

The adopted EXACT-2026-01 interpretation governs this boundary. An approximation with an epsilon bound is an engineering claim about synthesis or export. It lies outside the constitutional semantic truth conditions of edition 2026.

Rules:

  • An engineering claim must not replace the exact source Meaning, semantic equality, or the obligations of phase and control, of owner and effect, and of clean and dirty restoration.
  • An approximation bound grants no purity, no inverse access, no controlled access and no exact release.
  • A checked engineering claim must identify all of the following: the exact ideal, the actual artifact, the interface, the target and profile, the metric, the finite bound, the input and reference domain, and the composition assumptions.
  • An instrument claim must retain the complete public outcomes and the residual outputs with arbitrary external references.
  • Four kinds of information are distinct: information about sampling, about algorithmic resolution, about synthesis and about the numerical runtime. An absent claim does not mean zero error.
  • Engineering receipts, and their API and CLI claim kinds, must stay mechanically distinct from exact correspondence evidence and from resource evidence.
  • Neither a small bound nor a reported epsilon = 0 bypasses the independent exact gates or automatically discharges constitutional PR or target RS.
  • An actual circuit may independently obtain ordinary acceptance for its own exact meaning. That acceptance does not identify its meaning with the source ideal.
  • Reusing engineering evidence through a Meaning or an operation interface must not weaken the exact promise of that interface.
  • Numerical, interval and approximate search methods may construct an exact artifact or proof. That result is eligible for the separate exact correspondence and resource checks. The spelling of a search parameter does not decide its claim kind.
  • Accounting exactly for the cost of an approximate artifact does not supply its missing exact correspondence to the source.
  • Neither engineering validation nor this section creates an interpretation, a guarantee admission or a broader discharge of QS, PR or RS.

The bounded engineering profiles below implement these contracts within their stated domains. They define no universal approximation metric. Each bounded literal OpenQASM resource profile uses its own closed engineering budget.

Common rules of the native comparisons

Five qleisli engineering commands check an engineering claim through the native checker, the Lean checker executable. This section gives the rules that the five commands share. Each command takes one positional file and these options:

OptionMeaning
--edition=2026Required. It selects the constitutional edition.
--against=REQUESTRequired. It names the UTF-8 JSON request.
--lean-kernel=PATHOptional. It selects the native checker. Without it, the command uses the checker that QLEISLI_KERNEL names.
--format=jsonOptional. The command writes the result envelope in place of text.

Rules:

  • Every engineering comparison requires --edition=2026. A command without it fails with the code edition.
  • A command with neither --lean-kernel nor QLEISLI_KERNEL fails with the code kernel. A missing, incompatible or failed checker fails the comparison. No comparison falls back to another checker.
  • A command line with a repeated option, an unlisted option or an extra positional argument fails with the code usage and exit status 2. Every other failure has exit status 1.
  • Each request and each QIRF artifact must hold at least 1 byte and at most 16 MiB (limit). The QLV3 envelope retains its 64 MiB limit.
  • A request must hold exactly the fields of its format, with the fixed values of its profile. An unknown or missing field, an unknown version or another profile value is refused (format).
  • Each comparison accepts execution scope only. It refuses inspection scope and caller scope.
  • A report names the selected checker path. The checker identity is unpinned under the provenance limitation. A hash identifies the reported bytes. It establishes neither the correctness of the native binary nor human authority.
  • Serialized CLI output is an inert report. It is never reusable native acceptance.

Native pure engineering comparison

qleisli engineering compare-pure ACTUAL --edition=2026 --against=REQUEST [--lean-kernel=PATH] [--format=json]

This command checks that one pure artifact lies within a stated distance of an ideal pure artifact.

ACTUAL is an original finite QIRF artifact. REQUEST holds the rest of the claim. It holds the original ideal artifact, as a separate text. It holds the matrix and the ordered ports of each artifact, specified independently. It holds the complete type trees of the common domain and codomain. And it holds a budget, which is a closed canonical nonnegative dyadic number.

The request has exactly these fields:

FieldValue
format, versionqleisli.engineering-pure-request, 1
claim_kindengineering
metricpure-euclidean-operator-norm-v1
checker_profilefrobenius-r8-pure-leaf-v1
target_profileqirf-r8-pure-v1, an IR profile rather than a hardware claim
compositionsingle-component-v1
error_categoryimplementation-distance
domain, codomainFull QIRF Basis objects, for example {"tag":"bit"}
actual, idealObjects with exactly input, output and matrix
epsilon{"numerator":"7","denominator_bits":3} means 7/8; use reduced signed decimal data, with zero encoded as "0" and exponent 0
expected_artifactOriginal UTF-8 ideal QIRF text, including its original byte spelling

Rules:

  • Ports and matrices use the native pure-leaf request encodings.
  • The exact finite-matrix carrier is R8. The profile adds no arbitrary-angle syntax and no coefficient extension.
  • The comparison refuses a malformed or open budget, a false body matrix, and insufficient arithmetic or work capacity.
  • Hidden observation, reset or discard must not acquire a pure label through this path, even when the requested budget is large.

The checker establishes:

  • Each original artifact passes its ordinary check and then a fresh exact PureLeaf check against its own independent matrix request. The checker checks both complete type trees and the ordered ports. It compares the matrices only after these checks.
  • A squared Frobenius witness, over canonical rectangular R8 matrices, meets the closed nonnegative dyadic budget. The witness is sufficient for the explicitly selected Euclidean operator norm.

The checker does not establish:

  • A successful conservative witness is an inequality, not a completeness claim. When a witness fails, the failure does not establish that no approximation or synthesis exists.
  • Neither check changes the exact equality gate.
  • The result does not establish source preservation, exact source correspondence, an instrument bound or a target-resource bound. The report states each of them as unestablished.
  • The report cannot be converted to AcceptedProgram, a Meaning, inverse or controlled access, cleanup evidence or resource evidence. This holds at epsilon 0 too.

The text report and the JSON report identify the engineering metric, the bound, the profiles and the composition. They also identify the digests of the original artifacts and of the request, and the selected checker path. They report three kinds of error separately as not-claimed: sampling, algorithmic resolution and numerical runtime. Those errors are not silently zero.

Implementation note. The Rust interchange::engineering_pure API constructs data-only requests. It returns a private, allocation-bound EngineeringPureReport after a fresh native check. Its serialized convenience entry independently decodes the same typed request. The native checker compares the typed context and both fresh graphs with the actual retained Rust execution description. A separate native engineering protocol binds both checks to the actual invocation and to both retained host graphs. The engineering response uses a distinct header and cannot enter an exact accepted-handle constructor.

Native ordered pure tensor comparison

qleisli engineering compare-pure-tensor ACTUAL --edition=2026 --against=REQUEST [--lean-kernel=PATH] [--format=json]

This command checks a bound for an artifact that is the ordered tensor of two components, where each component has its own budget.

This comparison combines exactly two ordered pure comparisons. It checks six original QIRF artifacts afresh: the actual and ideal parents, the actual and ideal left components, and the actual and ideal right components.

The request has exactly fourteen top-level fields:

FieldValue
format, versionqleisli.engineering-pure-tensor-request, 1
claim_kindengineering-pure-tensor-bound
metricpure-euclidean-operator-norm-v1
checker_profiletensor-additive-r8-pure-leaf-v1
target_profileqirf-r8-pure-v1
compositionordered-tensor-two-v1
error_categoryimplementation-distance
actual, idealParent leaf objects with exactly input, output, matrix
left, rightComponent objects described below, in that order
epsilonCanonical nonnegative dyadic, exactly the sum of the two component budgets
expected_artifactOriginal UTF-8 ideal parent QIRF text

Each component object has exactly domain, codomain, actual, ideal, epsilon, actual_artifact and expected_artifact.

Rules:

  • Types, leaf requests and budgets use the encodings of the pure comparison. Both artifact fields of a component hold the original UTF-8 QIRF text.
  • Each body retains its own dependency order, exact matrix request, ordered ports and full type trees.
  • Both parent interfaces must be the complete products of the component interfaces. Unit nodes are retained even when they occupy no physical wires. The checker derives the parent type trees from the ordered components. A width-only claim does not supply them.
  • The exact parent equations use the low-first coordinates left + left_dimension * right. Both parent matrices must equal the ordered tensors of their respective component matrices.
  • The comparison refuses missing or extra components, altered profiles, noncanonical or open budgets, a stale total budget, false body matrices, and arithmetic or work exhaustion. It refuses a false parent tensor equation (contract).
  • The limits of the pure comparison apply: the limit on each file, on the envelope, on a matrix and on work.

The checker establishes:

  • The checker adds the two closed component bounds exactly. It requires the sum to equal the explicitly requested total bound.
  • It does not repeat the sufficient Frobenius inequality on the whole parent. An additive component certificate may succeed when that whole-matrix witness is too loose.
  • All six body checks, the component inequalities, the parent equations and the bounded addition share one work counter.
  • The checked additive operator bound extends to every finite external reference, including entangled inputs. It does so under the freshly checked exact isometry premises.

The checker does not establish:

  • The result supplies no exact equality between the parents, no source preservation, no inverse or controlled access, no cleanup, no correspondence to an emitted target and no resource certificate. This holds at total epsilon zero too.
  • This comparison supplies only its stated additive bound for two components in one ordered tensor. It checks no recursive, sequential, controlled or instrument composition. Support of the native comparisons lists the composition that each comparison checks.

The text report and the JSON report state this engineering bound and its composition profile. They carry the same separate categories of unclaimed error as the pure comparison, and the same disclosures about preservation and resources.

Implementation note. In the dedicated QLV3 invocation, the native checker compares its freshly decoded typed request and all six graphs with the retained Rust QDV1 view. The order is parent-actual, parent-ideal, left-actual, left-ideal, right-actual, right-ideal. The private Rust report binds the immutable artifacts, the original request and the selected checker path. A changed component, matrix, budget or parent cannot reuse it.

Instrument engineering comparison

qleisli engineering compare-instrument ACTUAL --edition=2026 --against=REQUEST [--lean-kernel=PATH] [--format=json]

This command checks that an actual instrument lies within a stated distance of an ideal instrument.

The instrument comparison uses a complete adjoint Euclidean operator bound. Take the Kraus families of the actual and of the ideal instrument. The bound limits the difference between their adjoint actions on every joint observable family B, for every finite external reference R and classical input x:

norm(sum_y,h (K_actual[x,y,h] tensor I_R)^dagger B[y]
             (K_actual[x,y,h] tensor I_R)
   - sum_y,k (K_ideal[x,y,k] tensor I_R)^dagger B[y]
             (K_ideal[x,y,k] tensor I_R)) <= epsilon * norm(B)_infinity

The norms on operators are explicitly Euclidean operator norms. The family norm is the supremum over public outcomes. The two families may have different sets of hidden histories. The bound quantifies over joint observables, including correlations with the reference. It has no factor for the dimension of the reference, and it does not renormalize branches. The metric is not advertised as a diamond norm without a separate proof of norm duality.

The request has exactly fourteen fields:

FieldValue
format, versionqleisli.engineering-instrument-request, 1
claim_kindengineering-instrument-bound
metriccomplete-adjoint-euclidean-operator-norm-v1
checker_profilechoi-l1-r8-instrument-v1
target_profileqirf-r8-instrument-v1, an IR profile, not hardware
compositionsingle-component-v1
error_categoryimplementation-distance
actual_signature, expected_signatureThe complete requested signatures
identityThe original identity data
epsilonClosed dyadic data, for example {"numerator":"1","denominator_bits":2} for 1/4
majorantsThe witness described below
expected_artifactThe original ideal QIRF text

Rules:

  • The witness assigns a canonical nonnegative closed dyadic q to every complex CP-coefficient difference. The order is fixed: public outcome, output row, input column, other output row, other input column.
  • All actual and ideal public labels contribute. An absent label denotes zero. The witness length must be exact.
  • The comparison refuses malformed dimensions or coefficients, noncanonical or negative budgets, insufficient witnesses, and arithmetic or work exhaustion. It refuses an epsilon that the majorants exceed (contract).
  • Nothing that a producer supplies replaces reconstruction. This holds for outcome labels, matrices, probabilities and success flags.
  • The comparison refuses old outer frames and cross-kind replies.

The checker establishes:
