  • On both bodies, the checker reuses the ordinary steps: the root and dependency checks, the equality with the requested complete signature, the ordered result projection, the principal Observe checks, and the complete Kraus and Gram reconstruction.
  • The checker reconstructs each coefficient afresh from all matching hidden histories. Exact R8 arithmetic checks its squared magnitude against q*q. Exact summation checks sum(q) <= epsilon. Both q and epsilon have unsquared norm units.
  • The profile has one quantum input owner, empty classical inputs and the bounded dense reconstruction. The independent metric also defines general finite classical input families, for later composition work.

The checker does not establish:

  • The result leaves these unestablished: pure phase agreement, source preservation, inverse or controlled access, cleanup, resources and constitutional PR or RS. This holds at epsilon zero too. No instrument bound grants exact release.
  • Requested source and type trees are distinct from source-to-IR preservation.
  • The profile is single-component. It issues no composed certificate, and it checks no resource limit. A comparison of emitted target bytes requires the literal OpenQASM profile.
  • Sampling, algorithmic resolution and numerical runtime error are separate unclaimed categories. The pure comparison reports instrument bounds as unestablished.

Text and --format=json disclose the complete instrument bound, the digests of the actual inputs and the unpinned checker identity. For example:

qleisli engineering compare-instrument actual.qirf --edition=2026 --against=comparison.json --lean-kernel=PATH

Implementation note. The Rust request uses validated InstrumentSignature and InstrumentResult data. Its private EngineeringInstrumentReport retains both immutable artifacts, the original request and the selected checker path. The native QLV3 invocation compares both fresh graphs, the signatures, the identity and the complete budget and witness data with the Rust execution view. A preflight on the work that is left precedes the allocation of the Cartesian witness. The work counter bounds verification. It is separate from program resources and target resources.

Literal OpenQASM target comparison

qleisli engineering compare-openqasm3 TARGET --edition=2026 --against=REQUEST [--lean-kernel=PATH] [--format=json]

This command compares the bytes of an emitted OpenQASM program with an ideal instrument.

TARGET holds the actual emitted bytes. The closed profile accepts this literal ASCII structure, with zero to eight ordered gate lines between the reset and the measurement, and a final newline:

OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";
qubit[1] q;
bit[1] c;
reset q;
h q[0];
c[0] = measure q[0];

The ordered gate word constructs the actual instrument. The instrument consumes an explicit zero-width Q<Unit> owner, initializes one qubit, applies the word, and then consumes that qubit with a terminal Z measurement.

REQUEST has the fourteen field names of the instrument request. It encodes signatures, the identity and dyadic numbers in the same way. These fields have distinct fixed values:

FieldValue
format, versionqleisli.engineering-openqasm-request, 1
claim_kindengineering-target-instrument-bound
metriccomplete-adjoint-euclidean-operator-norm-v1
checker_profilecanonical-target-choi-l1-r8-v1
target_profileopenqasm3-canonical-one-qubit-terminal-r8-v1
compositionsingle-component-v1
error_categoryimplementation-distance

Rules:

  • Each gate line must be exactly h, x, y, z, s, sdg, t or tdg, followed by q[0];.
  • The target must hold at most 1,024 bytes and eight gates (limit).
  • The comparison refuses changed whitespace, headers, includes or operands, additional results, gates after the measurement and unsupported syntax.
  • The include line is a fixed token. Checking loads no external include file.
  • The full interface is exactly Unit -> Bit, with a classical result and the principal Observe effect. Both complete signatures of the request must equal this interface. Equal widths do not admit Bits<0>, products of Unit or other result trees.
  • expected_artifact retains the independently supplied original ideal QIRF, including all original dependencies. Neither a fixed H ideal nor an actual matrix that a producer supplies substitutes for it.
  • The standard gate interpretation is an explicit specification assumption. The adapter reuses the exact Raw and std meanings. It introduces no semantic primitive and no constitutional interpretation.
  • The comparison refuses an epsilon that the majorants exceed (contract).
  • A cross-kind checker is refused without fallback.

The checker establishes:

  • The unchanged exact instrument gates reconstruct both complete Kraus families and Gram equations. The checker then checks the closed epsilon and every Choi coefficient majorant.
  • The complete-adjoint bound covers every finite external reference and joint observable, without branch normalization.
  • Kernel-checked matrices and the original-body bridge preserve the sign of H, the literal Y phase, the S/SDG direction and the T/TDG direction before the terminal observation.

The checker does not establish:

  • This deliberately bounded profile is not a general OpenQASM parser, and it makes no claim of hardware conformance. It adopts no external reference specification and proves no general OpenQASM execution semantics.
  • This closed terminal experiment grants no open pure or controllable map.
  • The result leaves these unestablished, even at epsilon zero: source or export preservation, exact source correspondence, pure phase agreement, inverse or controlled access, exact cleanup and constitutional PR or RS.
  • Sampling, algorithmic resolution and numerical runtime errors are separately unclaimed.
  • Version 1 checks the instrument bound alone.

Text and JSON report the target-bound instrument inequality and the digests of the actual inputs.

Implementation note. The independent byte reader imports the Raw meaning data without acceptance definitions. The native mode is --engineering-openqasm-check. Its QLV3 body holds the literal target bytes. Its QDV1 comparison binds the typed request, the original byte array, the ordered word, the generated actual graph and the original ideal graph. Decoding is charged before traversal. It shares one work counter with the ideal reader, the exact instrument reconstruction and the metric check.

Implementation note. The private EngineeringOpenQasmReport retains the immutable target, ideal and request bytes, the full contract and the checker path. Its actual graph is data, without a Rust accepted-program constructor.

Literal OpenQASM engineering resource limits

Version 2 of the same request also puts limits on the gate counts of the target. It uses the claim kind engineering-target-instrument-resource-bound and adds one required field:

"resource_limits": {"model":"openqasm3-one-qubit-literal-gates-v1","gates":2,"t_gates":2}

gates bounds the emitted gate lines. t_gates bounds the subset t and tdg.

Rules:

  • Both limits must be closed integers from 0 through 8.
  • The required literal header, reset and terminal readout fix one reserved qubit, one reset and one measurement.
  • The model charges the literal one-qubit vocabulary. It excludes compiler work, synthesis search, hardware timing and composition across components.
  • The metric, the epsilon and the single-component contract stay required.
  • Changing the actual artifact, the original ideal or the request requires a fresh comparison.
  • A timed-out or rejected check emits no certificate.

The checker establishes:

  • The native checker checks the limits against the word that it decodes independently. The engineering instrument inequality uses that same word.
  • Text and JSON reports include the checked counts and limits, with the identities of the actual artifact, the original ideal and the request.

The checker does not establish:

  • The engineering receipt supplies no exact cleanup, no phase-sensitive coherent control and no constitutional PR or RS.

Implementation note. The typed execution view includes the model and the limits.

Literal OpenQASM gate comparison with resource limits

qleisli engineering compare-openqasm3-gate TARGET --edition=2026 --against=REQUEST [--lean-kernel=PATH] [--format=json]

This command compares an emitted gate definition with ideal pure artifacts and checks its literal gate counts against limits.

TARGET is a complete canonical OpenQASM 3.0 gate definition:

OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";
gate implementation a, b {
cx a, b;
}

For the general definition syntax, see the OpenQASM 3.0 specification.

Rules:

  • The header and the include line must have the literal spellings shown. The fixed include selects the standard gate meanings of the profile.
  • The declaration must be either gate implementation a { or gate implementation a, b {.
  • A body instruction starts at the first column, uses one space after the mnemonic and after a comma, and ends with a semicolon and LF. The closing brace occupies its own line with an LF. The body may be empty.
  • The admitted mnemonics are h, x, y, z, s, sdg, t, tdg, cx, cz and swap, with their exact ordered formal operands.
  • The checker reads at most 1,024 bytes and eight gate lines (limit).
  • The ports are Bit or the ordered pair (Bit, Bit). Formal a is the low coordinate and formal b is the high coordinate.

The request fields common to both compositions are:

FieldValue
format, versionqleisli.engineering-openqasm-gate-request, 1
claim_kindengineering-target-operator-resource-bound
metricpure-euclidean-operator-norm-v1
checker_profilecanonical-gate-frobenius-r8-v1
target_profileopenqasm3-canonical-ordered-gate-r8-v1
compositionordered-sequential-two-v1 or controlled-low-selector-v1
error_categoryimplementation-distance
epsilonClosed canonical nonnegative dyadic with numerator and denominator_bits
resource_limitsObject with model openqasm3-ordered-gate-literal-gates-v1 and integer gates and t_gates ceilings from 0 through 8

An ideal description has exactly expected_artifact and leaf. The former is the original UTF-8 QIRF text. The latter holds exactly input, output and matrix in the finite pure-leaf format. The encodings of canonical dyadic numbers and of finite coefficients match compare-pure.

Each composition adds its own fields:

  • ordered-sequential-two-v1 additionally requires split, first and second. split is the number of literal instructions in the first slice. first and second each have exactly ideal and epsilon. The two comparisons use the same full port tree. The checked dyadic sum of the component budgets must equal the requested total. The same decoded slices make up the whole word: the first slice, then the second.
  • controlled-low-selector-v1 additionally requires ideal over one Bit. The desired action on a, b is the identity on selector zero and exactly the ideal operator on selector one. The checker compares the entire literal two-wire matrix with that controlled operator. Scalar phase in the active sector enters the metric as a relative phase.

The checker establishes:

  • The checker verifies each original ideal independently against its exact port and matrix request.
  • The native checker reconstructs the literal actions over the exact R8 carrier. It uses the sufficient Frobenius comparison for the selected operator metric.
  • For the sequential composition, the additive bound applies to the composition for every finite external reference. For the controlled composition, the norm bound extends to arbitrary finite external references.
  • The checker checks the reported literal counts under the same request and the same work counter. The resource report counts formal wires, literal gate lines and the t/tdg subset.

The checker does not establish:

  • The engineering result covers only the named approximation and the literal resource bounds. Hardware scheduling and compiler or search work use separate measures.
  • Exact target correspondence, source capabilities and constitutional PR or RS require their own checks. This holds when a numerical search selected the circuit, and when the engineering epsilon is zero.

A change to the artifact, the profile, the metric, the budget, the split or the ideal requires a fresh check. A timeout or a refusal returns an error.

Implementation note. The execution view holds the original bytes, the decoded ordered instructions, the closed budgets and the fresh ideal graphs.

Quantitative resource claims

A realization says that an artifact implements a program. A resource claim says how much the artifact uses, for example its live width or its gate count. This section gives the rules for such claims.

Resource Safety is the third permanent obligation of edition 2026. The adopted resource interpretation applies to finite quantitative bounds on the actual accepted program and its claimed realization. A resource certificate states a checked bound for one emitted artifact. The subsections below describe the bounded checks of the canonical terminal OpenQASM profile.

Rules:

  • A resource certificate must identify all of the following: the actual closed instance, the emitted artifact, the target and profile, the resource measures, the input and scheduling premises, and the checked bounds over all admitted execution paths.
  • A change to the providers, the layout, the target, the workspace or the output bytes invalidates reuse, unless a checked correspondence establishes the changed claim.
  • A content hash establishes identity, not the bound.
  • The provider resource contract applies to each selected body and composition. An external, opaque or device-native implementation must meet the same admission requirements.
  • Gate count, depth and non-Clifford cost require declared target conventions. Literal IR T-word counts are not automatically physical or optimal T counts.
  • Five things are different claims: compiler memory, checker work limits, static termination, ownership safety and target resource bounds. In particular, the ownership-only predicate does not discharge quantitative RS.
  • A closed finite specialization can meet its stated obligations by checked accounting on its actual artifact. A family can use a symbolic bound such as Resource(P<n>) <= f(n) within edition 2026. Its proof must cover the claimed parameters and the actual compilation and resource binding.
  • Resource behavior outside current coverage can occur in a sized family, bounded runtime control, specialization, target synthesis or provider composition. The Guardian interprets the applicable obligation under the existing edition. The required proofs of the bound and of preservation must pass before the scope can claim constitutional conformance. Previously admitted guarantees continue to bind the current acceptance path.
  • A failure to meet a target budget rejects that target claim. It does not change the mathematical denotation of the program.
  • A quantitative claim about a behavior-preserving realization requires a separate resource certificate.

The QCP implementation and concrete target schemas have a separately scheduled scope. This chapter is not their implementation.

Physical live width

This measure counts the physical locations that an implementation keeps live.

Rules:

  • Physical live width includes logical data, explicit source workspace, backend synthesis workspace, and routing and target storage.
  • A count takes each actual physical location once. It accounts for the lifetime of the location and its permitted reuse.
  • Peak width is the maximum simultaneous live count. A sum of separate peaks is a conservative upper bound, not necessarily the realized peak.
  • Logical width alone does not bound the physical implementation width.

Exclusive access and generated work

This section says how a bound counts the wires of an exclusive access and the work that an implementation generates.

An indexed exclusive call partitions its parent for a time into the selected owners and the remainder owners. The caller resumes with the reassembled parent. The exit from this access keeps its wires live. Logical owner identity and exact clean return belong to Soundness. Count every active physical location for its whole live interval.

Include any generated preparation, inverse calls, uncomputation and physical routing in the bound for the implementation that uses them. A replacement bound must be checked on the actual replacement artifact against the applicable target budget and capacity. Structural splitting and joining rearrange the logical owner map. Physical SWAPs contribute to the target count.

Implementation note. The bounded indexed Raw proof RuntimeExclusiveResources.indexed_access_live_wires relates the actual access boundaries to the original owner map and counts each live wire once. routed_prefix_live_wires checks that accounting throughout each structural split/join route. The inner operation has its own resource obligations. The terminal placement check replays the emitted gate word and checks its actual width and costs, including caller spectators and checked scratch.

Routing segments

A routing check covers an interval of literal physical SWAPs. A fixed-occupancy SWAP segment records the ordered placement of all occupied locations. The record includes any scratch that is live during the segment, whether it belongs to the source, to synthesis or to routing.

Rules:

  • Each literal SWAP must name two distinct occupied locations that are connected in the declared profile.
  • A SWAP moves both locations in the placement and leaves every other location alone. It counts as one operation even when a later SWAP cancels it.
  • The final placement preserves the logical axis order and the exact joint coefficients with any reference.
  • The check of a segment does not establish that the interval is used for routing, or that its entry placement is correct. A complete certificate establishes both. It also checks the other target operations, allocation, release and reuse.

Implementation note. The native checker independently decodes the declared register width and the literal SWAP instructions from a designated byte interval of canonical OpenQASM output. It also checks the target capacity.

The canonical terminal profile

The canonical terminal profile reserves all declared physical locations and resets them before its first gate. It keeps the reservation through terminal measurement.

Rules:

  • The independent reader of the complete artifact counts from the output bytes. It counts reserved and reset wires, gates, literal SWAPs, T/TDG and measurements.
  • An exact finite workspace check may compare a designated gate interval with the independently checked original clean or dirty body. The comparison uses the declared ordered placement of data and scratch. The physical register must cover the checked Raw peak.
  • The checker can derive the ordered locations of the workspace from the checked original Raw frame and its complete injective physical placement.
  • A fresh scratch must occupy a location absent from that frame. For a fresh scratch wire, the checker can verify that nothing touches it between the initial reset and workspace entry, or after exact restoration.

Placement replay

Take a closed straight-line Raw prefix with zero preparations, structural owner operations and finite gates. For such a prefix, the checker derives the original frame by replay. It replays the original prefix and the decoded target gate word.

Rules:

  • Marked routing operations must match connected physical SWAPs in the emitted word. The checker matches an ordinary Raw SWAP as a gate, and that SWAP does not move the encoding.
  • The derived original frame must equal the checked workspace entry, including zero-width ports.
  • With one checked workspace interval and literal gates, the checker can carry the original exit owners through the target suffix. It uses the resulting placement to verify the emitted terminal measurements in classical output order.
  • All original quantum owners must be consumed by the end. Discarded owners and measurements outside the classical outputs do not add to the emitted readout.
  • The single-interval check requires an exclusive lifetime for fresh scratch.
  • Outside a workspace interval, the checker can compare a single original circuit event against a decomposed target word. It derives the ordered support from the original operands and controls. It compares the complete exact operators on that support, up to six axes.
  • The checker rejects gates on other wires and phase changes. Matrix checking spends the same cumulative work as the surrounding replay.
  • The replay can align a target word with several consecutive Raw circuit events and structural owner operations. It reads the actual owner transitions and checks the combined operator on the ordered support. Preparation, observation and source workspace boundaries require their own alignment.
  • A structural basis lift updates the physical placement only when its complete table is an axis permutation. It contributes zero gates. A routing SWAP must occupy a literal gate position.
  • For a Q<Bits<n>> data register, each original take_bit or put_bit index determines the ordered wire selection or insertion. The Raw repartition retains the other owners, including a distinct Q<Bits<0>> remainder. Repartition inside a workspace body is part of its independently evaluated exact operator.

Synthesis scratch

A gate decomposition may use allocated synthesis scratch. These rules say where that scratch sits and how the checker confirms that it returns to zero.

Rules:

  • The physical locations of the scratch must be declared and separate from all live owners.
  • The checker compares the full target word on the data and the scratch with the original operator, under the canonical zero embedding at both ends. The executable check keeps the same zero encoding at entry and exit.
  • The six-axis bound includes scratch.
  • A slice of several aligned events that uses synthesis scratch has the same zero-return check.
  • A complete trace may reserve locations for several disjoint synthesis slices. Original allocation, routing, source workspace and readout must not touch these locations. Every slice that uses them checks its own zero return.
  • An individual slice may instead use exclusive scratch. The checker verifies that the scratch is untouched everywhere else.

Reuse of clean scratch

A physical scratch location may be reused across ordered, disjoint, clean intervals.

Rules:

  • The checker requires an exact zero-return equation for each interval. An interval with zero gates also checks that equation, and no gate touches the location in it.
  • Every gate that touches the location must lie in one of those intervals. The location must be absent from terminal readout.
  • The literal multi-interval check derives every entry placement from the preceding original owners and target word. It reserves each designated scratch location across the complete trace. It keeps the location out of ordinary preparations, routing and terminal readout.
  • Each reuse interval must be bound to its own checked original workspace.
  • The written logical operation and the workspace body use the same admitted workspace source fragment. An independently checked controlled phase may therefore appear in the declared logical operation and in the body. Their exact restoration equation checks the complete action on the data and the scratch.

A successful native placement check has these properties:

  • Each reusable clean wire is in the counted reset register.
  • Every gate that touches that wire belongs to a checked restoration interval, with one operator step per decoded gate in the interval.
  • A routing action before a workspace or in the terminal suffix points to a literal SWAP on an allowed edge at a counted gate index.
  • The reported SWAP total includes the literal routing gates and any ordinary SWAP instructions in the target word.

Implementation note. The typed-source adapter reads workspace intervals from the original checked root and named calls. It binds each local interval to the identical Raw operations at its position in the root. It checks the selected and returned ports against the full caller frame and retains all untouched spectator ports. The exporter preserves the interval boundaries across exact rewrites. It proposes the corresponding gate positions and scratch locations. The native checker checks the proposal against the original source, including the clean and dirty intervals and the terminal result order.

The checked resource report

qleisli interop emit-qasm <source> --input=qli --resources

Use this command to see what an emitted program costs. The command gives the checked resource report for a closed typed program. The program has workspace scopes in its root or in a statically named call, or it has a protected computed scope.

Rules:

  • The JSON result contains the emitted text and the exact work spent in the placement check. It contains these counts: the reserved qubits, the reset wires, the gates, the literal SWAPs, the T/TDG operations and the measurements.
  • The native checker decodes the returned text, and the counts come from that decoding.
  • The placement check has one exact-work budget of 20,000,000. A check that exhausts it returns a limit rejection (limit) with no resource payload.
  • The report covers the supported canonical terminal profile and its declared physical register.
  • For --resources, the terminal emitter supplies the emitted register width as the capacity of the packet.

Implementation note. The internal packet binds the complete original QLV3 request and the literal target bytes. The native checker rechecks the original source, decodes the target and replays placement under the one budget.

Computed scopes

A with_computed interval holds forward steps, protected uses and inverse steps. A resource count covers all three.

Take a structural with_computed interval that the source check has accepted. The Raw resource read counts the full live frame plus one private scratch wire at peak. It counts one preparation, one clean release and both predicate passes. The literal circuit count includes every forward step, inverse step and protected use.

The terminal OpenQASM placement check can read this event in a closed original source root. This includes a pure interval before or after an explicit workspace.

Rules:

  • The check places the ordered source wires, followed by a private predicate wire. It reconstructs the whole forward, protected-use and inverse word from the Raw operation.
  • The decoded target word must agree on the complete support, including the predicate wire, with exact phase.
  • If the target decomposition uses additional scratch, the same synthesis check requires the scratch to start at zero and return to zero.
  • The predicate wire and the synthesis wires are reserved. Source allocation, routing and terminal readout do not use them.
  • Counts include the resets of those wires, the physical compute and inverse gates, and any additional synthesis gates.
  • This check uses the bounded terminal operator profile and its shared work budget.

For an admitted computed scope that uses a finite table, the exporter works from the retained table rows. It uses them to emit controlled XOR flips of the private auxiliary bits. It emits the protected operations on the ordered source, target and auxiliary coordinates. It then repeats the XOR flips to restore the auxiliary bits.

Rules:

  • For resource reporting, the source program must retain its original checked typed request.
  • The native checker builds the original table permutation and the protected word from the checked Raw event of that request. It compares them to the complete decoded target interval.
  • The same bounded operator profile covers these comparisons.

Implementation note. The Raw interval reader charges owner checks and issuance-history checks separately from literal circuit validation. Its circuit charge covers the full forward and inverse fields and the operand checks in each forward step and protected use. Both charges consume the same shared work budget. The source-bound compute and inverse comparisons consume exactly 16 * (1 + sum(2 * control_count + 7)), summing over the predicate clauses. This charge depends on the literal circuit fields.

Implementation note. The original runtime plan retains the predicate and the auxiliary action that the native checker computes for the exact source occurrence. Both the structural path and the finite-table path use those source results and check the actual literal action independently.

Phase words and target-dependent costs

One phase can cost a different number of gates on different targets. This section fixes the phase words of the eighth-root profile and states what their counts show.

In the eighth-root finite profile, let ω = exp(2πi/8). The one-axis phase with residue r is exactly diag(1,ω^r) on the declared axis. This includes an action on an input that is entangled with a reference.

Rules:

  • A supported source phase[j,d] has r = 8j / 2^d when this quotient is an integer. The primitive contract specifies the source and profile limits.
  • Adjoint changes the exponent to -r modulo eight. Repetition adds the residue on each action.
  • A scalar ω^r I differs from a one-axis phase. It can become a relative phase under coherent control.
  • The finite format represents the one-axis phase by a monomial with the chosen axis, the identity permutation [0,1] and the phase exponents [0,r]. The action of the historical word of r T gates is the same diagonal.
  • A decoder must keep decoding the gate and circuit constructors in their versioned profiles. The equivalent monomial representation requires no dedicated Phase constructor and no change to the established encoding of a T word.

For the canonical terminal OpenQASM vocabulary, the selected one-axis words and their literal t or tdg counts are

ResidueEmitted wordLiteral T/TDG
0empty0
1T1
2S0
3S, T1
4Z0
5S†, T†1
6S†0
7T†1

Rules:

  • These counts apply to the specified one-axis words. A coherent branch or control requires the complete ordered action on each sector with its original phase. For example, the terminal export uses two T instructions, one T† and two CX instructions for controlled S.
  • A negative control can introduce additional X gates.
  • A conjunction-based lowering includes its live scratch, preparation, computation and full reverse chain.
  • A model that decomposes CCX must include that decomposition. In the canonical terminal profile, CCX is a single literal gate. It is outside the t_gates counter, which counts exactly the emitted T and T† instructions.
  • Three things are separate claims: literal word counts of the source IR, optimized instruction counts of a target, and resource bounds.
  • A certificate binds the actual emitted word and the checked decomposition to its profile. It includes the required workspace and routing.
  • An exponent, an operation name or a normalized phase word supplies no bound for a different target and no optimal cost claim.

Small obstruction examples

A program can be semantically unitary and yet have no implementation on the same wires in a stated gate vocabulary. This section shows two small cases and the determinant argument behind them.

Embedding a k-qubit gate G into n wires, under a fixed ordered basis, gives determinant det(G)^(2^(n-k)). Determinants multiply under composition. Consequently the generator set of a target restricts the determinants that it reaches on the same wires.

Rules:

  • This restriction is a necessary condition. Sufficiency requires a separate theorem for that precise generator, phase and workspace profile.
  • For a basis-permutation vocabulary, signs multiply under composition. An even-only vocabulary therefore excludes odd permutations on the same wires.
  • The precomputed determinant classes of the generators, or the parity of an available permutation table, may reject a candidate before synthesis.
  • The obstructions use the stated generator vocabulary, controls and workspace premises.

The repository retains two exact small examples:

OperatorSemantic propertySame-wire obstruction for the stated profile
Positive-exponent three-qubit Fourier operator F8Unitary, with det(F8) = iThe embedded H/T/X and NCT generators considered by the regression have determinants only ±1 on three wires.
Four-bit c3x basis permutationA bijection with one transposition, hence determinant −1Those embedded generators have determinant +1 on four wires.

Both programs are semantically accepted. The regression tests/static_semantics.rs::review_same_wire_obstructions_do_not_reject_semantic_unitaries checks the original four-bit table, the complete exact F8 operator and the determinant calculation for the embedded generators. The original source is retained at tests/fixtures/review_v023/c3x.qli. The regression reads the corresponding current fixture at tests/fixtures/frontend_v030/coherent-basis/current/ordinary-type-cutover/current/review_v023/c3x.qli.

Diagnostics

A diagnostic for a failed realization claim or resource claim reports a restriction on the realization. Diagnostics and recovery gives the codes and the fields.

Rules:

  • The diagnostic must identify the closed instance, the requested profile and the failed premise.
  • It must distinguish a proved obstruction from unsupported synthesis and from exhausted checking capacity.
  • An unsupported target operation or a target-width error must not be presented as a failure of semantic unitarity.
  • The terminal exporter reports an unsupported operation (unsupported) and the capacity limit of the synthesis workspace (limit). It reports its own target refusal after source checking has completed.
  • In the export of a source project, a Raw operation that is emitted inside a closed generic body can fail. That failure identifies the specialization and points to the original expression.
  • Terminal export can identify the closed specialization and the original source expression when a rejected operation has a single retained origin. This includes steps from an explicit clean or dirty workspace body.
  • When a rewrite combines several expressions, the enclosing Raw operation can provide its own origin.
  • For a failed native workspace equation, the checker supplies the original Raw interval, and the host checks it against the retained workspace. The diagnostic can name the enclosing specialization, or a single specialization shared by all steps in the checked body.
  • Packet-wide errors and ambiguous bodies leave the specialization unspecified.
  • Imported artifacts have no original project diagnostics.
  • A location supplies no realization and no resource certificate.

Status and limits

The production inventory identifies the actual routes for native acceptance, proposal, execution and export. Ordinary native acceptance does not itself issue a target realization or a resource certificate. An engineering result is not acceptance and not a guarantee.

Limits

LimitValue
A request or a QIRF artifact of a native comparison16 MiB
The QLV3 envelope64 MiB
The literal target of either OpenQASM comparison1,024 bytes and 8 gate lines
gates and t_gates of a resource_limits object0 through 8
Exact operator comparison of the placement replay6 axes, including synthesis scratch
Exact-work budget of the placement check behind --resources20,000,000
Contract expansion of the terminal exporter1,000,000 steps
Allocated qubits of the terminal exporter12

Contract expansion shares the 1,000,000-step function limit across the whole export. That limit bounds the work of a producer. It is not a target-resource bound. Flat steps keep the flat input limit and the emitted-gate limit of the exporter.

Support of the native comparisons

CommandComparedcompositionResource limits
compare-pureTwo original pure QIRF artifactssingle-component-v1None
compare-pure-tensorTwo parents and their two ordered componentsordered-tensor-two-v1None
compare-instrumentTwo original instrument QIRF artifactssingle-component-v1None
compare-openqasm3Literal one-qubit terminal OpenQASM bytes and an original ideal instrumentsingle-component-v1Version 2 only: model openqasm3-one-qubit-literal-gates-v1
compare-openqasm3-gateA literal OpenQASM gate definition and original ideal pure artifactsordered-sequential-two-v1 or controlled-low-selector-v1Required: model openqasm3-ordered-gate-literal-gates-v1

Unsupported:

  • No native comparison checks a recursive composition.
  • No native comparison checks a composed instrument. Both instrument profiles are single-component.
  • A native comparison checks sequential and controlled composition only for a literal OpenQASM gate definition of at most two formal wires and eight gate lines.
  • The two resource models above are the only target-resource checks of an engineering claim. Each bounds the literal gate lines and the t/tdg subset of one bounded target. Neither discharges the constitutional quantitative RS obligation, which is pending.
  • The source compiler consumes no engineering claim. The language has no source epsilon annotation.
  • A request for another composition or another profile value is refused (format).

The terminal exporter

  • The terminal exporter in src/interop/export.rs performs bounded untrusted rewrites after program verification.
  • The exporter explicitly allocates and uncomputes conjunction scratch. It rejects output that exceeds its physical qubit capacity (limit).
  • For an accepted single-bit certified compute with an all-zero predicate, the exporter emits the physical body with the data axes followed by a separately reserved clean scratch wire. It reuses that wire after a complete verified zero return.
  • The terminal OpenQASM exporter can consume the original accepted handle of a closed typed source program. It emits a wire-level projection of a Unit result, or of a positive-width product of measured bits, in the verified SSA output order.
  • Nominal results, zero-width components of products and source parameters are outside this projection (unsupported). Typed QIRF transport is a separate obligation.
  • A nontrivial uncontrolled scalar has no realization in this gate vocabulary (unsupported).
  • External schema entries stay disabled until their binding gates are completed.
  • The OpenQASM 3 and QIR adapters are experimental test features. They are not suitable for real quantum hardware.

Implementation note. A borrowed cursor expands the actual retained function circuits, including nested controls, adjoints and ordered axis maps. The exporter then merges adjacent diagonal actions.

Code, tests, proof, preservation and specification review

Code:

  • The native comparisons, the placement replay and the resource report are bounded implementation checks. Each covers the profile that its section states.
  • General specialization certificates and general diagnostic coverage are open work.

Tests:

  • The regression named in Small obstruction examples covers the two obstruction examples.
  • A Rust and Lean regression binds the same emitted OpenQASM bytes to two original clean intervals. It checks their placement, exact restoration and readout.
  • The independent scripts/test_review_v024.py oracle checks emitted small QFT and control circuits, including complex phase, output axes and zero-return scratch. Such bounded numerical validation is distinct from a general transformation proof and from a resource certificate.

Proof, for the QPTL library:

  • controlled_mul proves the operator identity that composes the exact sector equations of a controlled composition.
  • controlled_pow proves the corresponding operator identity for powers.
  • controlled_phase_ne proves that a scalar phase on the active block alone changes the controlled operator. It holds for any nontrivial scalar on a nonzero operator.
  • dilation_recover_reference derives the recovery equation of an isometry, restricted to its image. It derives the equation from the exact forward square and the unitary implementation law.
  • extracted_sixteenth_ne proves the coefficient obstruction of Exact target-domain membership.
  • QPTL.FiniteMatrix.det_embedded proves the determinant formula of an embedded gate, for finite matrix bases and simultaneous reindexing of both interfaces.
  • QPTL.FiniteMatrix.exact_same_wire_obstruction covers a product of generators whose determinants lie in a set that is closed under multiplication and contains one. Such a product cannot equal a requested matrix with determinant outside that set. The premises retain the chosen target vocabulary, layout and exact phase.

Proof, for source workspace on the finite one-scratch checker:

  • WorkspaceTargetAction.clean_checked_separates uses the exact checked insertion and output coefficients with the fixed-scratch law of QPTL. The joint output density has support only in the zero-scratch block, for every input density on data and a reference.
  • WorkspaceTargetAction.dirty_checked_promotion binds every coefficient of the actual body to the logical operator promoted on the ordered data axes.
  • WorkspaceTargetAction.dirty_checked_reference applies that action to each joint reference column. It proves that every selected input coordinate retains the scratch bit of the output.
  • Qleisli.WorkspaceTargetAction.decoded_action connects the exact action of a decoded workspace slice to the literal Raw body on its full ordered data and scratch interface. The equality preserves the original phase for arbitrary reference columns.
  • native_clean_access_counted_once covers each reserved clean wire. It links native placement success to the literal reset of the wire and to one unique restoration interval for every emitted gate that touches it. It also places the interval inside the counted target gates and excludes the scratch wire from terminal readout.

Proof, for synthesis scratch:

  • WorkspaceTargetAction.synthesis_action connects the actual decoded gate word to the original local operator under the canonical zero encoding. It proves equality with full phase on every external reference column. The amplitude is zero whenever any synthesis scratch bit is nonzero. The checked placement replay recovers this evidence at the original Raw position and physical gate offset, for a single circuit event or an optimized span.
  • WorkspaceTargetAction.bound_synthesis_action connects the replay before a source workspace to that exact action.
  • WorkspaceTargetAction.native_suffix_synthesis_action connects the terminal suffix of the native decision to that exact action.
  • In both theorems, the equation uses the original circuit steps on the recovered support with their dependencies. Reindexing the checked local steps by the ordered layout of data and synthesis scratch recovers the same emitted instruction slice. The decoder establishes the arity and the distinct, in-range operands of each instruction.
  • The full physical register action on a fixed spectator slice therefore agrees with the checked local word, for arbitrary input amplitudes and external references. The literal gate interval and its synthesis scratch locations are within the reported gate and register counts.

Proof, for the resource report:

  • A Lean theorem proves that the decoded register width bounds the maximum Raw live width over the workspace occurrences that the replay visits. The bound includes caller spectators and temporary clean wires.
  • The native reply theorem binds the reported counts to the exact target bytes. It proves that the reserved width is within the requested target capacity.
  • Qleisli.TerminalPlacement.native_terminal_correspondence relates the same successful native decision to the selected original Raw root. Take the moment immediately before terminal measurement, after all decoded gates have run from reset. At that moment the entire physical complex column agrees with the corresponding pure Raw prefix under its ordered placement. The agreement includes phase and restored scratch.
  • By the same theorem, the final measurement distribution agrees for every public result word after summing the original hidden outcomes. The theorem also binds the resource counts of the reply and its workspace peak bound to that same checked packet.

Proof, for computed scopes:

  • Qleisli.RuntimeComputedResources.structural_counts binds the counts of a structural with_computed interval to the same original source-checked Raw occurrence. It retains caller spectators in the peak width.
  • QleisliKernel.Qirf.StructuralComputedRaw.read_work proves the debit of the executable Raw interval reader.
  • QleisliKernel.Qirf.StructuralComputedUse.read_circuit_work identifies the work state after the source-bound compute and inverse comparisons and before the check of the emitted auxiliary action.
  • The same literal XOR factorization proves the logical action for the independently checked Raw event, even for an arbitrary caller amplitude function. The source-bound theorem additionally identifies the predicate and the phase from the original body. The complete pure Raw event fold uses the local logical action without constructing a global matrix.
  • BoundSegment.structural_paid and FinishedTrace.suffix_structural_paid each recover the checked placement and the gate interval from the executable replay.
  • StructuralPlacement.literal_costs binds that interval, and the distinct data and scratch locations, to the decoded gate and reset counts.
  • ProtectedTablePlacement.literal_costs ties the decoded interval of a finite-table computed scope, and its distinct physical locations, to the reported gate and reset counts.

Proof, for engineering claims:

  • The proof of the pure comparison bounds the explicitly selected Euclidean operator norm, including arbitrary finite external references and literal scalar phase.
  • Proofs of pure composition establish additive error rules for sequential composition and for ordered tensor composition. The rules use the same Euclidean metric and the stated exact isometry premises, and they include arbitrary references.
  • The coherent-control corollary additionally requires equal domain and codomain and the independent access meanings.
  • These mathematical rules do not change the single-component profile, and they supply no compiler or lowering preservation.
  • Independent mathematical composition of instruments uses the actual Kraus families. Full Gram completeness implies adjoint contraction at every finite reference.
  • A literal pure operator gap delta and both pure Gram equations imply the one-way instrument bound 2*delta. No phase information is recovered.
  • Feed-forward composition retains the public (y,z) outcomes and the hidden (h,k) histories. Ordered tensor composition retains the declared left and right input, output, public and hidden products through explicit proved reference regrouping.
  • Both constructions have additive epsilon_1 + epsilon_2 bounds under their stated component bounds and Gram premises.
  • Separate completeness theorems require both original Gram equations. A bound alone does not establish them.
  • No compiler consumes these results. They give no proof that composition is preserved for original source or QIRF.

Preservation:

  • An engineering result does not establish source preservation or target preservation. A location in a diagnostic supplies no certificate.
  • The two admitted QLV1 guarantees cover original-root ownership and classical scope. They do not certify source lowering, target emission or quantitative bounds.
  • QS-2026-01, PR-2026-01, RS-2026-01 and EXACT-2026-01 are pending, as the initial guarantees record. No statement of this chapter discharges one of them, and this chapter admits no guarantee.

Specification review:

  • The standard gate interpretation of the literal OpenQASM profiles is an explicit specification assumption. This chapter records no specification review of its rules.

The changelog records the native comparisons and the resource limits of the literal OpenQASM comparison under 0.3.0-beta. Type foundation and common frontend

This chapter is the record of a retired design packet. The packet proposed one common frontend for both lowering profiles and the minimum explicit type surface of the 0.3.0 language. It was a nonnormative design analysis. It implemented no feature, issued no Guardian ruling and discharged no guarantee.

The Reference states the rules that were selected. Ordinary types, quantum owners and equality holds the type rules, and Operations, meanings and capabilities records the decisions on operations. A form that the packet proposed, and that no decision adopted, is not part of the language. Git history holds the full text of the packet.

History

The approved implementation order

The approved order was one source syntax tree, one module and name resolver, and one static elaboration with type and ownership checking, followed by separate finite and hierarchy lowerings. The release performs one 0.3.0 source cutover with a migration mapping, and it supports no second source dialect. The edition stays 2026: it identifies the constitutional regime, and release compatibility carries the syntax change.

Both lowering profiles use the mandatory common original-source judgment, as the type model states. The changelog records the removal of the separate frontend::sized module and of the sized command namespace.

Decision basis

IssuesRole in the packet
#22, #27, #43The adopted direction: ordinary finite types are unmarked, Q<T> is linear ownership, there is no C<T> universe, and Q<Unit> retains its owner and its scalar phase.
#84, #100The recorded boundary: definitional equality, canonical coherence and physical maps are distinct. Only unique static structure is inferred, never quantum meaning.
#44, #45, #46, #83, #89Basis kinds, operator interfaces, Meaning and capability judgments, and callable categories. Operations, meanings and capabilities records their decisions.
#32, #33, #35, #37, #196Surface normalization. An example in an Issue adopts no grammar by itself.
#197Later convenience work for 0.4.0: automatic coherence, richer patterns, omitted static arguments and a general policy for reuse across stages.
#63Bounded constant and static computation. The maintainer excluded it from all of v0.3.0, and the Issue is closed as not planned.

Selected rules

The target type contract selected the rules below as ordinary implementation choices under the approved plan. It records no human Guardian ruling.

Recommendations without a recorded decision

The packet recommended a mandatory final expression for a quantum block, an explicit () for an ordinary Unit result, and no return in quantum core source. It set this against #196 and #37. This record names no decision on those recommendations. One structured quantum result boundary states the rules of the language.

Preserved authoring experiment

The informed session at tests/fixtures/authoring_sessions/type-foundation-v030/session.json preserves complete first sources, source hashes, command arguments and JSON diagnostics. It is an informed design study. It is neither a blind model benchmark nor an adoption of its generic syntax. The recorded tool version is 0.3.0-alpha, and all four observations used qleisli check --format=json with an explicit local native checker path.

The original failures stay preserved, and the repair is a separate attempt. The successful Unit check exercises no controlled scalar phase. It proves no source preservation and establishes no generic typing.

Constitutional impact recorded by the packet

ObligationRecorded impact
QSShared judgments must preserve linear owners, exact trees, ordered axes, phase, classical scope, effects and independently requested meanings. A lowering correspondence cannot be inferred from the validity of its output. The scoped QLV1 guarantees keep their exact predicate and artifact boundary.
PRA common source frontend grants no target realization and no correctness of an exported artifact. Target synthesis and its workspace are separate.
RSThe parser, type and specialization work and storage are bounded before construction. These engineering limits are not the quantitative Resource Safety theorem.

The packet implemented no constitutional interpretation. An ordinary design choice within the adopted QS, PR and RS obligations is a maintainer decision. A claim of formal discharge, or a change to the interpreted boundary, needs the established human adequacy and admission process.

Operations, meanings and capabilities

This chapter is the record of a retired design packet. The packet proposed how operation descriptions, Meanings and capability requirements would work in the 0.3.0 language, together with the type foundation. It was a nonnormative candidate for an ordinary implementation decision. It ratified no text, recorded no Guardian judgment, admitted no guarantee and changed no adopted interpretation.

The Reference states the rules that the decisions below adopted. A form that the packet proposed, and that no decision adopted, is not part of the language. Git history holds the full text of the packet.

V1 algorithm goals

Six algorithm families guide the design of Qleisli 1.0.0. The names below identify proposed standard-library APIs. The shared goal is to express the algorithms in ordinary checked Qleisli where possible and to verify and count operations from the program’s structure as instances grow.

Prime factorization

std::arithmetic::prime_factorize<N> targets integers greater than one that fit in N bits. A successful result represents the prime factors with their multiplicities. A Shor-style realization uses reversible modular exponentiation and phase estimation to find the period of powers of a chosen coprime base. Classical postprocessing derives and verifies candidate factors.

The design calls for typed results, ordinary control flow for retries and failure, and resource accounting across attempts. Reversible arithmetic subroutines must compose while returning clean workspace to zero. Design issue #318

Phase estimation

std::spectral::phase_estimate<P> targets a P-bit classical estimate of the phase θ modulo 1 of a unitary on a supplied eigenstate. Acting on that state, the unitary multiplies it by exp(2πiθ). For a supported phase of the form k / 2^P, the ideal estimate encodes k with probability one. Other supported phases have a specified output distribution.

The standard realization uses checked access to controlled powers of the unitary and a reusable inverse quantum Fourier transform. Design issue #319

Marked search

std::search::find_marked<N> targets the search for an N-bit value that satisfies a supplied predicate. A Grover-style realization starts from a uniform superposition and uses phase reflections to increase the probability of measuring a marked value. Classical verification checks the measured candidate against the predicate before returning it as a witness.

The iteration schedule depends on what the realization knows about the number of marked values. An unsuccessful attempt reports the lack of a verified witness from that attempt. Establishing that the marked set is empty requires its own evidence. Design issue #320

Markov-chain quantization

std::markov::quantize targets a discrete-time quantum walk from a classical Markov chain. For each state x, the transition probability P(x,y) determines the amplitude √P(x,y) of the successor state y in a coherent encoding of the transition row. A Szegedy-style construction composes two reflections built from the transition isometry to produce a walk unitary that can be used by phase estimation or search.

The v1 target covers instances whose required amplitudes fit the exact coefficient ring generated by roots of unity of power-of-two order and by 1/2. Broader coefficient domains and continuous-time walks are v1+ goals. Design issue #321

Quantum singular value transformation

std::spectral::qsvt targets a transformation of the singular values of an operator supplied as a block encoding, where a designated block of a unitary represents the operator after scaling. The circuit combines uses of that unitary with phase operations. Its designated output block encodes the transformation determined by the supplied phase sequence.

The v1 target takes exact phase data from the supported coefficient ring, including dyadic phases such as exp(iπ/8). The contract describes the transformation induced by that sequence. Deriving a sequence from a desired polynomial is a separate synthesis task. Design issue #322

Amplitude estimation

std::spectral::amplitude_estimate targets the probability of a designated success outcome for a coherently prepared state. For a state ψ and a projector Π onto the success subspace, the quantity to estimate is ‖Πψ‖². The result has a defined decoding rule and a precision and confidence guarantee.

The chosen circuit has its own exact output distribution. The precision and confidence describe the statistical error of the decoded estimate. The resource contract counts calls to preparation and success-marking operations, along with repetitions and measurements. Design issue #323

Subsequent authority and edition

The authority hierarchy orders further work: Constitution; binding Guardian interpretations and discharged guarantee ledger; current formal obligations and checked evidence; Language Reference; then implementation, conformance tests and examples.

The human Guardian determines what must be proved and whether a formalization adequately expresses the obligation. Authority and constitutional obligations

This chapter is normative for authority, change review and the distinction between specification, acceptance and proof. It is subordinate to the ratified CONSTITUTION.md. It does not supply a binding mathematical interpretation of QS, PR or RS.

The top-level architecture principle explains how policy becomes a formal obligation, the Constitution preserves its guarantees, and the compiler executes the authorized rules. The qrate and external-artifact boundary applies that hierarchy to program identity, package configuration, generation and canonical std distribution without granting those artifacts semantic authority.

Edition 2026 was ratified effective 2026-10-04 (Asia/Tokyo). The repository record governance/ratification-2026.json identifies the exact adopted text and the affirmative human decision. The same decision adopted the preserved governance candidate and appointed Masahiko G. Yamada as the initial sole human holder of the Constitution Guardian Office. GOVERNANCE.md records that separate role. The ratification record and process explain these acts and their scope.

Normative authority hierarchy

The order of authority is:

LayerAuthority and responsibility
1. ConstitutionCONSTITUTION.md establishes the permanent QS, PR and RS obligations, institutional authority, continuity and amendment rules.
2. Binding interpretations and guarantee ledgerHuman Guardian interpretations apply the Constitution to defined cases. Discharged ledger guarantees form the protected minimum for their recorded scopes and premises.
3. Formal obligations and checked proofs or evidenceCurrent formalizations must express the applicable requirements and connect their discharge to actual production acceptance and accepted artifacts.
4. Language ReferenceThe Reference specifies admitted language behavior consistently with the higher requirements and the stated verified boundary.
5. Implementation and conformance evidenceImplementations, tests and examples must conform to the applicable specification. Informative guides explain it without creating new rules.

This order cannot make a failed proof true. The Constitution Guardian Office determines what must be proved and whether a proposed formalization adequately addresses the constitutional case. Lean or the designated independent proof checker establishes mathematical derivability under the recorded assumptions. Neither decision substitutes for the other.

Maintainers choose ordinary designs and implementations within that boundary. The Office has no general veto over those choices. A constitutional suspension requires a written constitutional ground and the review or remedy needed to resolve it, as specified in GOVERNANCE.md.

Only natural humans may exercise the Office’s authority. AI, automated tools and proof assistants may assist with drafting, analysis and verification. They cannot issue, approve or automatically adopt a binding interpretation or act as a human holder’s proxy. Affirmative human adoption must be substantive; silence, general implementation permission and passing checks are insufficient.

Interpretation, obligation and discharge

A proposed interpretation is material for human review. Its presence in an issue, document or Lean declaration does not make it binding.

A binding interpretation is an affirmative ruling of the authorized human Guardian for an identified case or scope. Its record must identify the applicable constitutional obligations, required proposition or evidence, relationship to existing guarantees, and reasons the ruling remains within the Constitution. It establishes an obligation; it does not prove that obligation.

A pending obligation is binding but lacks its recorded formal discharge. It cannot be ignored because it is absent from the discharged ledger. A correction or supersession requires a reasoned human ruling and must not evade an applicable obligation or weaken an existing protected guarantee.

A discharged guarantee requires the checked proof or evidence and an explicit ledger record binding the interpreted property, scope, premises, semantic definitions, proof boundary and actual accepted artifacts. An ordinary helper lemma is not promoted into the ledger merely because Lean proves it. The ledger records only human-admitted guarantees concerning QS, PR or RS, not every theorem proved during development. Helper and transport proofs stay in their proof sources and validation records; where they preserve an existing admission, they support its current evidence without creating a new entry. One proof may discharge several obligations when the correspondence is explicit and mechanically justified.

Later releases must preserve every applicable ledger guarantee against their current production acceptance and artifacts. Refactoring definitions or replacing implementations requires justified semantic transport where their representations differ. Retaining an old proof about an old checker, or proving an implication between two already closed propositions, does not establish that connection.

Current adoption and proof status

The appointed Guardian explicitly adopted QS-2026-01, PR-2026-01 and RS-2026-01 in a separate human act on 2026-10-04. The event is recorded in governance/interpretations/initial-2026-adoption.json, bound to the exact reviewed text preserved in initial-2026-reviewed.txt in that directory.

The scoped-guarantee record identifies those meanings and evidence. These two entries do not discharge all of QS or any PR/quantitative RS obligation.

The initial QS, PR and RS interpretations state their scopes, required properties and premises. Their adoption does not constitute formal discharge. Existing theorems, tests, audits and engineering decisions have not been automatically promoted into constitutional guarantees; their recorded scope and outstanding obligations remain in force.

Before v1.0.0, release claims must disclose their applicable interpretations, actual proof coverage, provisional formalizations and outstanding obligations. A capability with incomplete required coverage must not be described as fully constitutionally certified for that scope. Already discharged guarantees remain binding throughout this period. From v1.0.0, a claim of full constitutional conformance requires all applicable obligations over the current admitted scope and preservation of the accumulated ledger.

Constitutional text and record-identity checks establish only the properties they actually check. They do not authenticate human identity independently, prove QS, PR or RS, or implement all ledger-continuity and production-coverage requirements of Issue #141.

Production acceptance and the trust boundary

The adopted architectural policy in repository TRUSTBOUNDARY.md remains in force. Reference meanings require human specification review independently of the checker and producer. Library placement, authorship, compiler output and successful tests confer no semantic acceptance authority.

The single-verifier decision #276 places production acceptance in the Mathlib-free native Lean checker. Fresh decisions bind private accepted handles to immutable artifact/request bytes. Rust performs parsing, diagnostics, transport, proposal generation, simulation and packaging outside semantic acceptance. Missing, incompatible or failed native checking must not fall back to Rust acceptance.

That implementation boundary is distinct from the Lean proof kernel and from proof of the complete production pipeline. An accepted IR artifact alone does not establish preservation of its source, execution result or exported target. Claims must identify the actual accepted representation, requested contract where present, emitted artifact and relevant checker/profile identity, together with their preservation links and remaining assumptions. Native compilation, decoding and runtime correspondence do not become proved merely because the checker is implemented in Lean. Full supported-profile Soundness remains a separate proof milestone; ratification does not complete it.

An epsilon-bound approximation cannot replace an applicable exact QS, PR or quantitative RS obligation. Exact phase, coherent control, all-input clean return and dirty restoration retain their stated contracts. An approximate artifact may carry checked engineering claims, but those claims do not make it the source’s exact constitutional realization. Exact equality in a separately permitted quotient is distinct from approximation; this supplement admits no quotient or waiver of an existing phase contract.

Numerical and interval computation may construct evidence for a final exact proposition checked at the designated independent boundary. Floating-point observations and an error certificate alone are insufficient. An independently checked exact admitted artifact remains eligible for a checked resource bound even if its construction used an internal parameter named epsilon. A cost bound for an approximate implementation does not supply missing exact source correspondence. Target assumptions remain explicit; this is not a claim of noiseless physical hardware.

Neither is implemented by this ruling.
