Primitive boundary and admission

A language primitive is an operation that the language itself supplies. A program calls it by a bare spelling, such as h or measure_z. Edition 2026 has 13 language primitives. Each one has a typed identity that fixes its typing rule and its effect. A language primitive grants no native acceptance and no general inverse or control capability.

This chapter specifies the source primitive boundary of edition 2026. It covers how the checker looks up a bare spelling, the contract of each primitive and the migration of the 27 retired qualified names. It also covers the ordinary library and the roles of each production path. Its last subject is primitive admission: the reviewed decision to add semantic authority.

Three documents rank above this chapter: the authority hierarchy, TRUSTBOUNDARY.md and STDLIB.md. The inventory of this chapter is a technical classification. It is neither a human adoption of a minimal generating set nor a constitutional interpretation or guarantee. A program reaches an operation through a bare spelling or through an ordinary definition. This form of source access changes neither the meaning of the Raw constructors nor the native acceptance authority.

The project route and the selected-entry route both use the common checker. When a program breaks a rule, the common checker gives the diagnostic a class, such as name. A rule in this chapter names that class. Codes gives the code that each route reports for a class.

The inference and discovery boundary shows where to find a primitive’s contract or inspect a derived definition.

A concrete adapter lowers a checked program to a concrete proposal under fixed capacities. This chapter names two of them. The finite adapter lowers a program to finite Raw IR. The selected adapter prepares a selected entry concretely for the ordinary Raw gate or a dedicated hierarchy gate. The capacities and the supported forms of an adapter are its concrete profile. Status and limits gives both profiles.

Meaning, spelling and implementation

An operation has a meaning, a spelling in source and an implementation. This section keeps them apart. The project separates four categories of meaning. Each category has its own authority and its own obligation.

CategoryAuthority and obligation
Semantic primitive, or irreducible semantic ruleA rule at the independent semantic and checking boundary: an existing operation, instrument, ownership transition or effect rule. Three things about it require review: its intended meaning, its premises and the acceptance that the checker implements. Moving the rule into a backend or a package does not remove these duties.
Language primitiveOne typed PrimitiveId. A program can use its bare spelling only where lexical resolution leaves that spelling unbound and the resolution of ordinary declarations and imports does too. The identity fixes the typing rule and the effect. It grants no native acceptance and no general inverse or control capability.
Derived library definitionOrdinary .qli source that you can inspect. The checker checks it like user source, and its contract is reviewed separately. Its home under std:: grants no privilege.
Backend implementation intrinsicAn implementation of an existing meaning. The target output, the phase, the axes, the workspace and the resources keep their separate preservation and realization obligations. An internal operation tag is not an additional source primitive.

Rules:

  • Only native Lean checking issues a production accepted handle. Parsing, Rust catalogs, lowering, simulation and exporter output issue none.
  • An intended mathematical specification must stay independent of acceptance. It requires specification review.
  • None of these is primitive admission, proof of irreducibility or source preservation: a technical inventory, a refreshed source hash, a successful test.

Bare lookup and ordinary shadowing

A program calls a primitive by writing its name alone. A local binding or a declaration of the program can have the same name, and it then takes the place of the primitive. This section gives the order in which the checker decides what a name refers to.

A bare spelling is an unqualified callable name. An ordinary declaration is a declaration in .qli source, which receives the same checks as user source. The checker looks in four places, in this order, and resolves a bare spelling to the first one that applies:

  1. A lexical binding, whether runtime or static. The checker finds a binding here even when the binding is moved or has the wrong callable category.
  2. An ordinary declaration of the same module, or an ordinary public declaration that the module imports explicitly. The ordinary visibility and collision rules apply.
  3. One of the six original public declarations that the derived prelude supplies, unless the module opts out.
  4. The language primitive with that spelling.

Rules:

  • Resolution is lexical. The checker does not select among overloads by the types of the arguments.
  • A lexical binding determines the use. When that binding has an ownership or category error, the error is final. Lookup never retries a declaration or a primitive of the same name.
  • An ordinary declaration determines the use even when its spelling matches a primitive. Its signature, public effect, access requirements and body obligations apply.
  • A spelling resolves to a primitive only when steps 1 to 3 leave it unbound. A name that no step binds is an error (name).
  • Once lookup has selected a callee, a failed check never selects another callee or another authority. This holds for a failed type, arity, effect, capability, concrete-profile or native check.
  • Parameters, let bindings, fold binders, static providers and restricted classical or basis expressions keep their category and scope rules.
  • A primitive is not an import, a prelude declaration, a reserved identifier or a hidden alias. A program calls h(q) or global_phase_eighth(q) without a use.
  • An ordinary function may have the name h. It receives ordinary source checking, and its name grants no Hadamard meaning. A moved local h shadows both that function and the primitive.
  • The prelude must not reexport a bare primitive spelling (name).
  • A program reaches the ordinary gates and the state and structure definitions through ordinary declarations, imports or qualified references. Six common derived definitions are also in the prelude.
  • The bare name phase_eighth is not an alias of global_phase_eighth. It is an unresolved name (name).
  • A retired qualified path is never a lookup path. Retired qualified names gives its rules.

The checker accepts this program. The ordinary declaration empty_bits determines the use, so the basis body yields the label 1 and not the empty label:

classical fn empty_bits() -> Bit { 1 }
pub isometry fn f(q: Q<Unit>) -> Q<Bit> { basis q as () { empty_bits() } }

The checker rejects this program (type). The local x determines the use, and the checker does not retry the x of the prelude:

observe fn main() -> Bit { let x = 0; measure_z(x(init0())) }

The checker accepts this program. A module that opts out of the prelude keeps the bare primitives measure_z, h and unit:

#![no_implicit_prelude]
observe fn main() -> Bit { measure_z(h(basis unit(()) as _ { 0 })) }

The checker rejects this program (name). After the opt-out, no step binds init0:

#![no_implicit_prelude]
observe fn main() -> Bit { measure_z(init0()) }

tests/frontend_types.rs, tests/selected_coherent_basis.rs and tests/shared_resolution/prelude.rs check these sources.

Implementation note. src/frontend/resolve/locals.rs resolves a lexical binding before any global name. Resolution::lookup in src/frontend/resolve.rs applies steps 2 to 4, and PrimitiveId::lookup_unbound supplies step 4.

Primitive inventory

The table lists the 13 language primitives. Use it to see what a primitive takes and what it returns; each spelling links to the section with its rules. Static arguments stand in square brackets after the spelling, as in phase[1,2]. A and B stand for complete supported Basis trees, not for bit counts. The effect is the principal effect of a call.

SpellingIdentityStatic argumentsRuntime argumentsSignatureEffectTyping
hHNone1Q<Bit> -> Q<Bit>UnitaryFixed
phasePhase[j,k]1Q<Bit> -> Q<Bit>UnitaryFixed
global_phase_eighthGlobalPhaseEighthNone1Q<A> -> Q<A>UnitaryInferred from the argument
unitUnitNone1Unit -> Q<Unit>UnitaryFixed
finishFinishNone1Q<Unit> -> UnitUnitaryFixed
splitSplitNone1Q<(A,B)> -> (Q<A>,Q<B>)UnitaryInferred from the argument
joinJoinNone2(Q<A>,Q<B>) -> Q<(A,B)>UnitaryInferred from the arguments
measure_zMeasureZNone1Q<Bit> -> BitObserveFixed
discardDiscardNone1Q<A> -> UnitObserveInferred from the argument
take_bitTakeBit[n,k]1Q<Bits<n>> -> (Q<Bit>,Q<Bits<n-1>>)UnitaryFixed, with k<n
put_bitPutBit[n,k]2(Q<Bit>,Q<Bits<n-1>>) -> Q<Bits<n>>UnitaryFixed, with k<n
empty_bitsEmptyBitsNone0() -> Bits<0>UnitaryFixed
prepend_bitPrependBit[n]2(Bit,Bits<n>) -> Bits<n+1>UnitaryFixed

The last column says how the checker types a call. A primitive with fixed typing has the signature that the table gives for its static arguments. A primitive with inferred typing takes its result type from the type of its arguments.

Rules:

  • A call must supply the static arguments that the table lists (static-arity) and the number of runtime arguments that it lists (arity).
  • The runtime argument list and the tuple shape of the result are separate. join(a,b) takes two arguments, and unit(()) takes one.
  • Each quantum argument evaluates once, in source order. The call consumes its owner. The primitive returns or eliminates that owner explicitly.
  • Every quantum equation of this section extends to an arbitrary retained reference, on which it acts as the identity.
  • Distinct owners may be entangled. A zero-axis owner is linear.
  • A concrete adapter may refuse an identity that it does not support (unsupported). The refusal does not restore qualified lookup, and it does not replace the source judgment.

tests/review_v021.rs checks each of these declarations as an accepted project of its own:

unitary fn f(q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{h(q)}
unitary fn f(q:Q<Bit>)->Q<Bit>{phase[1,2](q)}
unitary fn f(q:Q<(Bit,Unit)>)->Q<(Bit,Unit)>{global_phase_eighth(q)}
unitary fn f(v:Unit)->Q<Unit>{unit(v)}
unitary fn f(q:Q<Unit>)->Unit{finish(q)}
unitary fn f(q:Q<(Bit,Unit)>)->(Q<Bit>,Q<Unit>){split(q)}
unitary fn f(a:Q<Bit>,b:Q<Unit>)->Q<(Bit,Unit)>{join(a,b)}
observe fn f(q:Q<Bit>)->Bit{measure_z(q)}
observe fn f(q:Q<(Bit,Unit)>)->Unit{discard(q)}
unitary fn f(q:Q<Bits<1>>)->(Q<Bit>,Q<Bits<0>>){take_bit[1,0](q)}
unitary fn f(a:Q<Bit>,z:Q<Bits<0>>)->Q<Bits<1>>{put_bit[1,0](a,z)}
unitary fn f()->Bits<0>{empty_bits()}
unitary fn f(b:Bit,z:Bits<0>)->Bits<1>{prepend_bit[0](b,z)}

Implementation note. src/frontend/primitive.rs::PrimitiveId and its ALL list hold the 13 identities. src/frontend/check/primitive.rs types them for the common checker. The finite and selected adapters consume the same identity. They do not classify a name by its string. Internal tags of the adapters, such as X, Cnot, Init0 and Empty, are transport and emitter vocabulary and have no language identity.

h

h applies the Hadamard gate to one Bit owner: H|b>=(|0>+(-1)^b|1>)/sqrt(2). The result is on the same axis.

Rules:

  • The argument must have type Q<Bit> (type).
  • h keeps, as a primitive rule, the action that mixes amplitudes. A deterministic basis map alone cannot express that superposition.

phase

phase[j,k] applies diag(1,exp(2*pi*i*j/2^k)) to one Bit owner. The static arguments j and k are exact dyadic arguments.

Rules:

  • The argument must have type Q<Bit> (type).
  • The static arguments must pass the coefficient and profile checks of the concrete adapter. Status and limits gives them.
  • phase is a relative phase on a Bit. It is distinct from a scalar.

global_phase_eighth

Let ζ = exp(i*pi/4). global_phase_eighth multiplies the state of one owner by the scalar ζ. Its action is ζ I_A.

Rules:

  • The argument must be one quantum owner of type Q<A> (type). The basis A may be Unit, Bits<0> or a complete packaged tree.
  • global_phase_eighth keeps an explicit scalar phase that has no physical wire.

The checker rejects each of these declarations (type). An ordinary Bit is not a quantum owner, and a tuple of two owners is not one owner:

pub unitary fn f(b: Bit) -> Bit { global_phase_eighth(b) }
pub unitary fn f(q: Q<Unit>,r: Q<Bit>) -> (Q<Unit>,Q<Bit>) { global_phase_eighth((q,r)) }

tests/quantum_unit_source.rs checks these sources.

unit and finish

These two primitives begin and end an owner of type Q<Unit>, which has no axis. unit introduces a fresh zero-axis owner with coefficient +1. finish consumes a zero-axis owner with coefficient +1.

Rules:

  • The argument of unit must have the ordinary type Unit (type). The call unit(()) is unary: its one argument is the value ().
  • The introduction of an owner is an explicit semantic transition. It is not the classical value (), and it is not an implicit preparation.
  • The argument of finish must have type Q<Unit> (type). finish consumes exactly that owner and keeps all preceding scalar work.
  • finish performs no observation. It infers no clean state for another basis.

split and join

These two primitives take a product owner apart and put one together. split partitions one product owner into two owners. join combines two owners into one ordered product owner. Both have coefficient +1.

Rules:

  • The argument of split must have type Q<(A,B)>, a product of two fields (type).
  • split keeps the complete child trees and the left and right axes. It does not flatten implicitly, and it does not promise that the two owners are separable.
  • Each argument of join must be a quantum owner (type). The two owners must be distinct: a second use of one owner is an error (ownership).
  • join(a,b) is a call with two arguments. It is not a call with one tuple argument, and it is not a physical SWAP.

The checker rejects this declaration (ownership). join receives the owner q twice:

pub unitary fn f(q:Q<Unit>)->Q<(Unit,Unit)>{join(q,q)}

tests/quantum_tuple_unitors.rs checks this source.

measure_z

measure_z measures one Bit owner and returns the result as an ordinary Bit. It is the complete destructive Z instrument with the Kraus operators K_b=<b|. It includes every unnormalized reference branch.

Rules:

  • The argument must have type Q<Bit> (type).
  • measure_z consumes the logical owner.
  • A pure label cannot represent the observation. A function that calls measure_z under a unitary or isometry label is an error (effect).

The checker rejects this declaration (effect):

unitary fn f(q:Q<Bit>)->Bit{measure_z(q)}

tests/body_effects.rs checks this source.

discard

A program calls discard to give up an owner explicitly. discard takes the explicit partial trace of one complete subsystem. It keeps the marginal of the reference and every erasure history.

Rules:

  • The argument must be one quantum owner of type Q<A> (type).
  • discard is not a clean release, not a proof of a zero state and not an implicit destruction at scope exit.

take_bit and put_bit

A program uses these two primitives to take one Bit owner out of a register and to put one in. take_bit[n,k] extracts coordinate k of a Bits<n> register and keeps the order of the other coordinates. put_bit[n,k] inserts its first argument at coordinate k and keeps the other coordinates. Both have phase +1. They are the explicit routing and typing rules of an atomic register.

Rules:

  • The static arguments must satisfy k<n (size).
  • The argument of take_bit must have type Q<Bits<n>> (type). A zero-width remainder, as for take_bit[1,0], is an owner.
  • The arguments of put_bit must be two distinct owners of types Q<Bit> and Q<Bits<n-1>> (type).
  • put_bit is not a physical SWAP and not a coercion by width alone.

empty_bits and prepend_bit

These two primitives build ordinary labels. Neither one touches a quantum owner. empty_bits() returns the exact ordinary empty label of type Bits<0>. The label is copyable and has no owner. prepend_bit[n] builds an ordinary label with the head before the tail. It has no quantum action.

Rules:

  • empty_bits takes no runtime argument. The call empty_bits(()) is an error (arity).
  • In a restricted basis or classical expression, only the resolved identity EmptyBits receives the constructor rule. An ordinary function of the same name does not gain it.
  • The arguments of prepend_bit[n] must have the ordinary types Bit and Bits<n> (type).
  • prepend_bit keeps the type rule of a sized label. It is not a preparation and not a measurement.

Effects and types

The effect and the types of a primitive call follow these rules.

Rules:

  • Unitary classifies the quantum action at fixed ordinary inputs. It does not make ordinary copying or dropping a reversible classical computation.
  • Bit, Bits<1>, Unit, Bits<0>, nested and flat tuple trees, and products of separate owners are distinct types.
  • Effect inference checks a body independently of its public annotation. External callers, specialization and provider selection use the public effect.
  • A Unitary or Isometry label must not conceal observation, reset or discard (effect).
  • Unitarity alone grants neither inverse nor control access.

Derivation and removal

A later change can derive a primitive rule in ordinary source, or remove it. These rules constrain such a change.

Rules:

  • A further derivation or a removal of a primitive rule must first express the whole recorded interface in ordinary checked source.
  • It must also provide the applicable independent correspondence. The correspondence covers phase, type, reference, owner and effect, cleanup and resources.
  • A gate identity that holds only up to phase, or a match of widths, is insufficient.
  • The admission process applies to an addition of authority.

Retired qualified names

A retired name is one of the 27 qualified entries of the four retired compiler namespaces std::quantum, std::observe, std::registers and std::classical. The table accounts for every one of them. For each retired name it gives the source access to write instead, and the derivation or the semantic rule that the language retains.

Retired nameSource accessDerivation or retained semantic rule
std::quantum::hbare hThe Hadamard action and its exact amplitude rule.
std::quantum::phasebare phaseThe exact dyadic relative-phase rule.
std::quantum::phase_eighthbare global_phase_eighthThe full scalar ζ I, named explicitly to distinguish it from T.
std::quantum::unitbare unitExplicit introduction of a zero-axis Unit owner.
std::quantum::finishbare finishExplicit elimination of a Unit owner, with the phase retained.
std::quantum::splitbare splitExplicit ordered binary partition of an owner.
std::quantum::joinbare joinExplicit ordered combination of owners.
std::quantum::init0ordinary std::state::init0basis unit(()) as _ { 0 }: the injective singleton-to-Bit rule with table [0] and coefficient +1. It is an isometry with one fresh physical wire.
std::quantum::xordinary std::gate::xh(z(h(q))), the exact X including coefficient +1.
std::quantum::zordinary std::gate::zphase[1,1], the exact diag(1,-1).
std::quantum::tordinary std::gate::tCoherent control of global_phase_eighth on an explicit Unit owner, then finish. The result is the exact diag(1,ζ), with no auxiliary physical wire.
std::quantum::sordinary std::gate::sphase[1,2], the exact diag(1,i). Readability does not require a power of T.
std::quantum::sdgordinary std::gate::sdgadjoint(s), the exact diag(1,-i).
std::quantum::tdgordinary std::gate::tdgadjoint(t), the exact diag(1,ζ^-1).
std::quantum::idordinary std::gate::id[type(A)]It returns the same owner with coefficient +1. The explicit Basis argument preserves the complete tree.
std::quantum::cnotordinary std::gate::cnotOrdinary coherent control of X, with the control first and the target second. Both owners return in order.
std::quantum::toffoliordinary std::gate::toffoliOrdinary control of the packed CNOT. Three distinct owners and the original nested result tree.
std::quantum::controlled_phaseordinary std::gate::controlled_phase[j,k]Ordinary control of the phase provider, in the exact order of control and target, under the same coefficient and profile premises.
std::observe::measure_zbare measure_zThe complete destructive measurement rule.
std::observe::discardbare discardThe explicit subsystem erasure rule.
std::observe::resetordinary std::state::resetdiscard(q); init0(), with the effect Observe. It returns a fresh zero owner. The erased input is not cleanly uncomputed.
std::registers::take_bitbare take_bitThe typed extraction rule of an atomic register.
std::registers::put_bitbare put_bitThe typed insertion rule of an atomic register.
std::registers::emptyordinary std::structure::emptybasis unit(()) as _ { empty_bits() }: the explicit singleton representation from Unit to Bits<0>, with phase +1 and one zero-axis owner.
std::registers::consume_emptyordinary std::structure::consume_emptyfinish(basis q as _ { () }): the exact singleton representation from Bits<0> to Unit, followed by explicit elimination of the owner.
std::classical::empty_bitsbare empty_bitsThe ordinary constructor of the empty label.
std::classical::prepend_bitbare prepend_bitThe ordinary sized constructor of head and tail.

Rules:

  • A retired name is not a callable alias. The four retired namespaces have no callable entry and no compatibility alias. The table preserves the migration and nothing else.
  • An import of a retired name is an error, and its diagnostic carries migration guidance. The project route reports the code project, and the selected-entry route reports name.
  • A qualified call of a retired name is an error with the same guidance. The project route reports unknown_name, and the selected-entry route reports name.
  • Migration guidance is never a lookup path.
  • A derived replacement has its ordinary public interface and the static arguments that it declares. Replacing an import is not a fallback to the same name.
  • The channel of std::state::reset is rho_AR -> |0><0|_A tensor Tr_A(rho_AR), with a fresh output owner. This formula includes arbitrary reference correlations.
  • The conversions between Unit and Bits<0> in the table are explicit source maps. They are never a definitional type equality or an inserted coercion.
  • A scalar phase accumulated before such a conversion stays in the composition.
  • A pure structural elimination does not invoke discard.

The checker rejects this declaration (name). The guidance names the bare primitive empty_bits:

pub unitary fn f(q:Q<Unit>)->Q<Bits<0>>{basis q as () {std::classical::empty_bits()}}

The checker rejects this program. The derived id requires its static argument, as in id[type(Bit)], and the selected-entry route reports static:

observe fn main() -> Bit { measure_z(id(init0())) }

tests/frontend_types.rs and tests/shared_resolution/prelude.rs check these sources. tests/common_authoring_diagnostics.rs checks the codes of both routes for a retired name.

Implementation note. retired_name_hint in src/frontend/primitive.rs holds the guidance for the 27 names. The resolver in src/frontend/resolve.rs rejects such an import or qualified call before it looks up the module.

Source retention and resources

These rules state what a call retains from its source and what a resource claim requires.

Rules:

  • An ordinary call retains five things: its original definition, its caller instance, its static arguments, its public effect and its complete source and dependency identity.
  • A checked Meaning override retains the exact original Raw witness, the checked leaf, the matrix, both ports and the reference receipts. An endpoint of the same width or a digest alone is not source correspondence.
  • An original zero-repeat child keeps its checking obligations. A dormant repeat-zero witness is not an equation between an arbitrary hierarchy and a finite implementation.
  • The ordinary preparation std::state::init0 uses the Raw LiftBasis 0-to-1 table [0]. A finite target export must inspect that table and the mapping of the fresh wire and owner. It must not replace an arbitrary rectangular map by an initialization.
  • A structural singleton map retains its complete Unit or Bits<0> tree and its original root. It retains them under composition, repeat, control and adjoint, wherever the concrete profile supports them. Explicit cleanup and the rejected observation, phase and width cases are part of that profile.
  • Source recognition alone enables none of these emitters.
  • Semantic ownership, clean and dirty scratch, and target workspace are separate.
  • The Unit owner in the definition of std::gate::t has zero physical wires. It does not promise that the target T cost is zero.
  • The three ordinary CNOT calls of std::gate::swap differ from the structural output routing of permute_axes, even when a fixed-coordinate matrix agrees.
  • None of these is quantitative Resource Safety: a count of representation sharing, a count of logical instructions, a budget of checker work.
  • Every target or resource claim needs its own artifact, model, units and evidence.
  • Exact cleanup must hold for every permitted input and reference. Approximation never excuses dirty scratch.

Core forms and independent meaning

This section lists the Raw constructors and says where the meaning of the core forms comes from. A Raw constructor is one variant of the public Rust type RawOp in src/ir.rs. RawOp has 22 constructors.

FamilyConstructors
Preparation and fixed gatesInit0, Gate, Cnot, Toffoli
Explicit ownership packagingPackUnit, UnpackUnit, Split, Join
Finite action and basis isometryApplyUnitary, LiftBasis
Coherent selectionQuantumIf
Checked computed/cleanup scopesCertifiedCompute, ComputeUseUncompute, StructuralCompute
ObservationMeasureZ, Reset, Discard
Classical values and branchingClassicalConst, ClassicalNot, ClassicalXor, ClassicalAnd, ClassicalBranch

Rules:

  • A Raw constructor is untrusted data. It is not an accepted handle, and the 22 constructors are not 22 library functions.
  • The table is not the entire semantic vocabulary. SingleGate, CircuitAction, protected operations and hierarchy constructors have their own explicit inventories and obligations.
  • An added Raw constructor must pass admission. Calling it an implementation detail does not bypass admission.
  • A source alias does not imply a Raw constructor.
  • RawOp has no free-standing Release0. Clean removal is part of the explicitly checked scope.
  • A reference definition requires human specification review.
  • Lean proves stated relationships to the reference definitions. It does not decide that a chosen formula is the intended gate, instrument or resource model.

The meaning of the core forms comes from these layers:

LayerSource and scope
Data and interfacessrc/ir.rs; lean-kernel/QleisliKernel/Semantics/{Raw,Observation,Finite}.lean. These expose the original operations, ports, finite actions and effects. Data construction is untrusted.
Pure reference meaninglean/Qleisli/Semantics/Finite.lean supplies literal gate amplitudes, controlled and monomial actions, and encoded equations. Semantics/Raw.lean retains the original events, the ordered axes, the full complex composition and the meanings of clean scopes. These references do not define meaning as successful checking.
Instrument reference meaninglean/Qleisli/Semantics/RawInstrument.lean retains all erasure outcomes, classical values, hidden histories and unnormalized operators. Reset is erasure followed by fresh-zero preparation. The reference does not select only a successful sampled branch.
Hierarchy operator specificationlean/Qleisli/HierarchicalOperators.lean specifies positive dyadic phase, ordered wiring, control and composition. A complete theorem that leads from production hierarchy acceptance to an operator is separate from this specification.
Executable acceptancelean-kernel/QleisliKernel/Raw/{Structure,Pure,Observation}.lean, the finite and QIRF checks and the dedicated hierarchy checks validate the IR fields, the owners and effects, and the enabled evidence. The source catalog is not their authority.
Production composition and proof limitsProtocol.Validity, Protocol.NativeContract and their bridges Qleisli.NativeValidity and Qleisli.NativeContract keep their precise artifact and request scopes. Dedicated hierarchy components have separate bridges. The production boundary records their exact coverage.

Ordinary library and module resolution

The library that comes with the compiler is ordinary source. This section lists its modules and gives the rules by which the imports of a program resolve.

The bundled library is the set of eight ordinary source modules that the compiler embeds under std::. It has 26 public definitions, six transparent prelude reexports and five private helpers. The helpers serve reflection, scalar phase, parameterized phase, packed CNOT and fixed Bit identity.

Module and sourcePublic definitionsContract provenance
std::basis, stdlib/src/basis.qlixor2, and2Total finite ordinary maps of basis labels. Neither is injective over its two-input domain. A coherent enclosing construction must meet its own obligations.
std::transform, stdlib/src/transform.qlihadamard2, qft2, qft3Ordered H tensor H. Positive finite Fourier phase, with the first leaf least significant and the output reversal included. No auxiliary and no promise about the input state. The Fourier interfaces have fixed width.
std::reflection, stdlib/src/reflection.qlireflect_uniform2Phase-fixed reflection about the uniform state, with exact cleanup of the computed auxiliary. The private nonzero2 is a normal basis helper. Hadamard comes from ordinary transform source.
std::gate, stdlib/src/gate.qliid, t, s, sdg, tdg, z, x, controlled_phase, cnot, toffoli, swapOrdinary phase-fixed gates. T controls a scalar phase on a zero-width Unit owner. The phase, Pauli and controlled gates derive through ordinary providers. The Bit SWAP uses three CNOTs. No library definition grants primitive authority or a target-cost guarantee.
std::state, stdlib/src/state.qliinit0, resetinit0 is the ordinary explicit singleton-to-Bit preparation. reset is an observing discard followed by a preparation. The original owner, the phase and the complete reference instrument are retained.
std::structure, stdlib/src/structure.qlipermute_axes, transpose_axes, empty, consume_emptyThe structural two-axis map [1,0] and statically indexed register transpositions, with exact phase +1 and no physical gate instructions. The explicit introduction and the explicit elimination of a zero-width Bits owner use singleton basis maps.
std::measurement, stdlib/src/measurement.qlimeasure_x, measure_z2, parity_zzComplete destructive X and Z instruments and a nondestructive data-parity measurement, with their original owner and result trees and their reference behavior.
std::prelude, stdlib/src/prelude.qliReexports id, x, z, t, cnot, init0The original ordinary declarations. The reexports add no body, primitive, effect or evidence authority.

reflect_uniform2 is the reflection 2|s><s| - I, where |s> is the uniform state of two Bits. The semantic namespace Reference gives the admission rule, the exact public interfaces and the migration mapping of every mathematical module.

A loader collects the source modules of a program. The finite loader loads a project from its source root. The selected loader loads modules that are supplied to it explicitly.

Rules:

  • A bundled module receives the common checks: the declaration, type, owner, access, dependency and effect checks. It has no compiler-import exception.
  • Concrete materialization and native checking occur under the scope of the consumer. Selected source checking alone does not natively certify every bundled specialization.
  • A local module must not have the name std or a name that begins with std::. Both loaders reserve those names for the bundled library.
  • ModuleOrigin::Bundled gives no ambient source replacement and no checking exemption.
  • An unknown path is an error.
  • The resolver registers complete interfaces. It resolves an explicit import with the ordinary visibility and collision rules.
  • A cycle that consists of imports alone is allowed.
  • A self-import is an error. It collides with the declaration of the same module (name).
  • A mutual dependency through a body, a provider, a Basis or a Meaning is an error (cycle). Only a checked decreasing runtime self-call is permitted.
  • Lookup finds a private declaration in its own module. An import from another module and a host entry require a public declaration.
  • An import spelling supplies no runtime initialization and no evidence.
  • The prelude contract admits transparent public reexports. It admits no as, glob or relative import.
  • Resolution, original source identity, concrete materialization and independent acceptance are separate duties.
  • std::routines and std::transforms are retired without aliases.
  • The three fixed arithmetic definitions A001–A003 are ordinary local source in examples/order_finding/arithmetic.qli. They preserve amplitude +1, modular overflow, the addend and the full-space value-15 extension. They have no canonical std export.
  • std::arithmetic is reserved for parameterized arithmetic and number theory. A reserved family name promises no callable API.
  • The English source contracts and STDLIB.md state intended meanings and conventions. Their presence alone does not prove that the implementation conforms.
  • Until version 0.5.0, an algorithm addition ordinarily belongs in the approved corpus, not in an expansion of stdlib. This chapter adopts no library algorithm.

The project route reports every import that fails to resolve with the code project. The selected-entry route reports the class that the rule names.

Implementation note. src/frontend/source.rs::BundledRegistry embeds the eight sources and their fixed manifest. Both loaders retain the complete original sources, their provenance and their original ASTs. Each loader checks the bundled bytes under its own byte policy before it parses or copies them.

Required generic-contract bindings

A generic rule must bind all of the following data. It binds them independently of QFT, QPE or any other algorithm name. The list is a contract for the planned migration to generic rules. It enables no serialized schema and claims no generic completeness.

  1. Original implementation. Retain the original artifact bytes, the complete operation bodies, the selected root, and the checked dependency graph and its order. Bind the called providers, the shared nodes, and the zero-count or otherwise unused obligations that the profile requires. A stale index, an equal name, a matching digest without correspondence, or a native-valid replacement is insufficient.
  2. Complete interfaces. Retain separate domain and codomain type trees, classical result trees, ordered quantum ports, owner identities, wire coordinates, and explicit input and output encodings. Unit, Bit, atomic Bits and product trees are distinct even at equal width. State and check the encoding dimensions, the isometry premises and the entry and exit compatibility. Composition matches the complete intermediate contract, not only its bit count.
  3. Actual semantic action. Check the actual gates, the exact coefficients and phase, the axis order, the controls, the ownership and effect transitions, and the permitted branches. For an instrument, retain every unnormalized hidden history and the ordered public projection. State the premises on arbitrary inputs and references. Distinct owners are not evidence of separability.
  4. Independent expected meaning. Fix the requested meaning before the search for candidates, whether it is a library, operator or instrument meaning. Retain its original definition, its request bytes, its source and specification identity, and its dependencies. The match of a recognizer cannot define it, and neither can a probability table derived from the implementation. Review the intended mathematical meaning separately from the proof of conformance.
  5. Capabilities and workspace. Bind forward, adjoint and control access separately from semantic unitarity. Bind them together with the owners, the effects, the clean and dirty workspace, and the exact restoration premises. A body that observes, resets or discards cannot obtain a pure label by hiding those operations. A resource claim must additionally bind its target, cost model, workspace and artifact.
  6. Actual checking execution. Identify the protocol, schema, profile and checker compatibility separately from the edition and the product version. Retain the original byte decoding, the requested root, the derived obligations and continuous checking states. Where the execution representation that the host retains crosses the Lean boundary, compare the complete representation independently. A serialized success flag or an old receipt cannot replace a fresh decision.
  7. Consumed or emitted artifact. Bind a checked conclusion to the immutable object that execution or emission consumes. A claim about source, runtime or targets requires its own preservation link. Accepting both endpoints independently does not prove a correspondence between them.
  8. Declared domain and failure. State every finite, coefficient and phase limit, every depth and work limit, and every interface limit. A generalization of the phase domain requires its own specification, proof and profile migration. Reject unsupported forms, changed contracts and exhausted budgets without an authority fallback.

Rules:

  • The generic checker may establish a reusable composition or contract rule.
  • A mathematical result that is specific to an algorithm belongs to the library, specification and proof modules that instantiate those rules. The Fourier sum and the QPE distribution are such results.
  • Adding an algorithm must not require granting its name a trusted semantic rule.
  • An intended definition must stay independent of acceptance.
  • QleisliKernel.Qft, Qpe, the hierarchy Fourier and QPE checks, and their lean/Qleisli bridge proofs are implemented, specialized components. The role assignment does not move or delete them.
  • The supported checks, the exact finite contracts, the VM-22–VM-29 authority gates and the existing proof coverage must stay until reviewed replacements cover them.

Admission and replacement process

This section gives the steps of primitive admission. The adopted interpretations require an explicit review before any addition of semantic authority. The decision is recorded in an Issue, and this chapter keeps no second backlog. The account of a proposal must contain all of the following:

  1. Identify the addition. Specify whether it changes semantic rules, exposes an existing rule under a source name, derives checked source, or implements an existing meaning as an intrinsic. List the affected source and Core forms, checker predicates, reference definitions and production paths.
  2. Justify irreducibility. Explain why each of these is insufficient: ordinary checked source, bounded elaboration, a verified transformation, a capability or evidence object, a qrate definition, and target lowering. Performance, popularity, backend availability and implementation difficulty alone do not qualify.
  3. State the independent contract. Give the exact whole-input map or the complete instrument. Give the type and tuple tree, the encodings, the finite domain, the phase, the ordered axes, the owners, the effects, the capabilities and the failure behavior. Include arbitrary permitted inputs and references. A gate name or a probability table is not the contract. State the premises, and do not assume separability.
  4. State workspace and realization obligations. Distinguish semantic data, clean and dirty scratch, and backend workspace. Require exact permitted cleanup and reference restoration. State the target and gate assumptions and the realization correspondence that PR requires. The contract implies no unspecified target schema, no projective quotient and no approximate cleanup.
  5. Analyze QS, PR and RS. Identify the existing binding interpretations and ledger scopes, the changed dependencies and assumptions, and the acceptance and artifact bindings as implemented. State the quantitative measures and the preservation obligations under RS. Ownership checks and checker work budgets do not substitute for them.
  6. Provide production evidence. Check the actual executable definitions, the transport and decoding, and the interface and request binding. Add bounded independent positive and negative cases, as applicable, for phase, axis order, references, wrong effects, duplicate or dropped owners, workspace and stale identities. Build and audit the changed proofs, and retain the explicit source, runtime and target gaps.
  7. Record the decision and migration. Follow the authority hierarchy for specification review, for any constitutional interpretation beyond the adopted ones, and for guarantee admission. An ordinary alias or an implementation choice that the existing interpretations cover does not require a separate Guardian ruling for each edit. Update the reviewed inventories, the compatibility mapping and the applicable proofs before enabling the changed boundary. A manifest edit does not grant approval.

Rules:

  • Project axioms, unsafe or partial executable definitions, and runtime overrides are forbidden.
  • A reviewed physical or semantic assumption must be explicit in the contract. It is not permission to declare a Lean project axiom, and it is not permission to accept an unchecked assertion of a producer.
  • A replacement of an implementation, or the exposure of an equivalent derived definition, must retain the old intended meaning and the applicable guarantees through explicit correspondence.
  • A semantic change must not hide under an unchanged name.
  • Release compatibility and migration are recorded separately from the constitutional edition. Not every primitive edit changes the constitutional regime.
  • A needed constitutional amendment follows the edition procedure of the Constitution.
  • Historical artifacts and records are retained. They must not be rewritten to match the replacement.

Example: a proposal seals qft2 solely because a backend executes it faster. The proposal fails the irreducibility justification, because the ordinary checked std::transform::qft2 expresses its phase-fixed finite contract. An optimization or a target intrinsic can instead propose a realization of that same meaning and supply the required independent checks.

This example assesses the stated rationale. It does not claim that a historical proposal was formally rejected, and it does not claim that the optimization is verified.

Edition-aware deprecation and replacement

These rules govern the deprecation and the replacement of a primitive within an edition and across editions.

Rules:

  • A proposal must distinguish two things: retiring a spelling or an implementation, and changing the meaning of the primitive.
  • It must record the exact source and Core forms before and after the change, the semantic contracts, the profile and API mapping, the release compatibility, and the proof and guarantee dependencies.
  • An equivalent derived replacement needs checked correspondence for the full recorded domain, including phase, references, owners and effects, and workspace. A few matching examples are insufficient.
  • Each historical primitive set must stay recoverable from its exact Git revision and its reviewed inventories, with its original edition, its profile and its applicable meaning.
  • Old manifests and adoption records must not be rewritten to describe a replacement.
  • A later edition may deprecate source access under its explicit migration policy. It must not erase or weaken an accumulated guarantee for its historical scope.
  • Within edition 2026, the evolution of an implementation preserves the old intended meaning. An incompatible source removal requires the ordinary breaking-release process, even when it preserves the safety implication.
  • A changed constitutional regime follows the amendment procedure of the Constitution.
  • Neither an edition increment nor another primitive name waives non-weakening.

Guardrails

These checks detect when the source and the inventories of this chapter drift apart.

CheckWhat it fixes or rejects
scripts/check_verification_inventory.pyFreezes the source identities, including the common and concrete catalogs, and the public constructor families of the Raw, finite and hierarchy forms with their fields. Pins the typed source identity and the concrete adapter sources. Discovers unlisted production checking sources and added checking files.
The typed inventory guard of that scriptFixes the PrimitiveId members, their ALL order, the canonical bare spellings and the unbound-only lookup body.
The mutation suite of that scriptRejects an added Raw constructor even when its source digest is refreshed. Its calibration separately exercises typed source growth and an unhandled selected adapter.

Rules:

  • Refreshing the metadata of these checks is not primitive admission and not proof.
  • An added source identity cannot pass by a refreshed file digest or by an inserted row of an internal selected emitter.
  • The mutation calibration is a drift and coverage check. It is not a judgment of irreducibility or admission.
  • A change must be reviewed together with the source, the catalog and constructor inventory, and the affected acceptance and proof contracts. Updated hashes cannot supply human specification review or a constitutional judgment.
  • These checks and the guarantee-continuity machinery keep their stated scopes. They do not mechanically judge specification intent or irreducibility, they do not authenticate a human ruling, and they do not complete every gate of the admission review.

  • the source-signature checks of tests/review_v021.rs;
  • tests/sized_source.rs::primitive_signatures_agree_through_symbolic_and_concrete_preparation and concrete_phase_and_repeat_limits_check_zero_and_unused_providers;
  • tests/project.rs::std_prefix_and_invalid_module_names_cannot_shadow_bundled_modules, the refusal checks of the retired foundation paths, semantic_stdlib_modules_are_bundled_source_with_private_helpers and import_only_cycles_load_but_call_cycles_and_name_collisions_reject;
  • tests/semantic_contracts.rs::primitive_evidence_preserves_exact_phase, unit_has_scalar_phase_and_a_distinct_owned_type and tensor_proofs_keep_low_order_axes_and_allow_a_correlated_reference.

Status and limits

The common checker types all 13 identities. Each concrete profile has its own capacities, and the table gives them. A code in the table is the code that the adapter reports.

FormFinite adapterSelected adapter
phase[j,k]k<=8 (unsupported) and j<2^k (contract). The Raw R8 phase lowering also requires an integral eighth-root exponent (unsupported).k<=8 and j<2^k (limit), with the symbolic-word profile of dyadic hierarchy preparation.

  • The finite adapter rejects an unsupported phase coefficient. It never rounds.
  • The selected adapter refuses instrument initialization after observation (unsupported).
  • The sufficient checks of the selected phase profile are not a complete semantic normal form.
  • The symbolic phase-word model has modulus 256. Its exact sufficient checks are not a complete semantic normal form or a general phase-domain theorem.
  • The common checker rejects a join whose product basis has more than 4096 type nodes or more than 64 levels (limit).
  • Aggregate type, width, depth, work and native limits also apply.
  • A refusal of an adapter never retries through a retired route.
  • The selected loader reserves all eight bundled module slots and counts their bytes toward its aggregate limit. The finite loader has separate bounded and explicit legacy byte policies and local limits on filesystem discovery.
  • Generic QFT completion and the correspondence between fixed and generic forms are outside all of v0.3.0 and the current goal. The role assignment adds no generic QFT to the 0.3.0 scope and claims no completed independent library decomposition.
  • The consolidation of the specialized Fourier and QPE components, a generic prototype and the migration of the compatibility paths are planned work. The common frontend of 0.3.0 and its specified namespace migration are separate from that work.

The project separates code, tests, proof, preservation and specification review:

KindStatus
CodeThe common checker types the 13 identities. The finite adapter lowers all 13, and the selected adapter lowers every one except discard. Acceptance is solely by the native Lean checker in lean-kernel/.
TestsThe regression sources of Guardrails exercise the inventory. Listing a regression in this chapter does not report a test run. A successful test is not admission.
ProofAn ordinary accepted root has the two admitted scoped guarantees QS-QLV1-OWNERSHIP-2026-01 and QS-QLV1-SCOPE-2026-01, for ownership and classical scope. They are protected. The general QS, PR, quantitative RS and EXACT duties are binding and pending. An optional finite request or leaf contract establishes an additional result only within its premises. PathSum.compile_sound proves the correspondence of individual path states. Alone it proves none of these: the complete complex sum, a Fourier or QPE specification, source preservation, completeness, control or observation integration. No theorem establishes the complete analytic operator composition of a hierarchy. The inventory is not a mathematical proof of global minimality: retaining a rule records the semantic interface that the implementation needs. The audit does not prove that no alternative algebraic derivation of global_phase_eighth exists.
PreservationThe contracts of the inventory are intended contracts. They do not claim completed general preservation proofs. The bounded engineering source checks of Source retention and resources claim no general source-preservation theorem. This chapter asserts no general source or runtime, CPTP, clean-release, target-realization or quantitative resource theorem.
Specification reviewA reference definition and any added sealed semantics require human specification review. No hash, guardrail or test supplies that review. No human has adopted the inventory as a minimal generating set.

The authority hierarchy records the adoption and the proof status of the constitutional obligations.

Implementation note. src/frontend/compile/lower/ enforces the bounds of the finite adapter, and src/frontend/specialize/elaborate.rs enforces the bounds of the selected adapter.

History

  • Release 0.3.0-beta is the release that this chapter describes.
  • #369 and #167 made the cutover from the qualified compiler namespaces to bare primitives and ordinary library definitions. The cutover changed source access and ordinary definitions. It did not change the meaning of the Raw constructors or the native acceptance authority.
  • #131 is the 0.3.0 architectural contract that assigns the five roles to each path.
  • #273 tracks the migration to generic rules: the consolidation of the specialized components, a generic prototype and the later migration of the compatibility paths. The required generic-contract bindings are the contract for that migration.
  • #154 defines the gates of the primitive admission review. The guardrails do not complete every gate of that Issue.

Initial scoped QS guarantees

Status: admitted by the human Guardian on 2026-10-04 (Asia/Tokyo). Masahiko G. Yamada affirmed the adequacy of both formalizations and approved their registration as proved scoped guarantees. The separate event is governance/guarantees/initial-2026-admission.json; its SHA-256 is 9f20661fd98ec56c58286b70f4e9d9f49c76570313b5ddc90ae4685d4e251dd2. The QS interpretation, that human judgment and the checked proofs have separate roles. A checked helper lemma does not promote itself.

The exact reviewed proposal is preserved at repository file governance/proposals/initial-guarantees.json. It contains the exact two guarantee definitions, declarations, source identity, proof-evidence references, assumptions and requested decision, with SHA-256 bf9eb89d9ebadd41f16f40c5896b824b0e04fe1655264e102fb179948fa06c02. Its historical candidate status remains unchanged. This chapter explains that record and the subsequent admission; it is not a second normative definition. The included JSON at the end is rendered directly from the frozen record.

The two admitted components

Scoped guaranteeActual theoremIndependent property
QS-QLV1-OWNERSHIP-2026-01QleisliKernel.Protocol.Validity.check_ownershipSafeQleisliKernel.Semantics.Ownership.OwnershipSafe
QS-QLV1-SCOPE-2026-01Qleisli.NativeValidity.check_scopeSafeQleisliKernel.Semantics.ClassicalScope.ScopeSafe

Both start from success of the actual QleisliKernel.Protocol.Validity.check bytes definition. They quantify every packet, request-presence result and initial/remaining natural-number work budget satisfying that premise. Each produces an Acceptance witness that retains the packet split, original body/request bytes, actual decoded artifact and order, decoded optional request, intermediate work values and successful inspection. The guaranteed program is the root selected from that artifact. Neither theorem needs an optional finite request to be present.

At admission the ordinary native wrapper invoked that definition through QleisliKernel.Cli.runValidity with contract = false and work budget 10,000,000. The v0.3.0-beta wrapper uses 20,000,000 under #461. The mathematical premise quantifies the initial work and requires Lean execution success. The contract-mode branch and hierarchy modes have different entry points and are outside these two admitted scopes.

Ownership safety accounts for the actual root’s quantum ports and output owners, including zero-width owners, exclusive live wires, complete live frames, fresh identities, both branch arms and complete quantum phis. It uses independent Inputs, Run and Returned judgments over the original operation lists. This is a structural ownership property. It does not derive source tuple or basis equality from matching bit widths.

Classical scope safety accounts for the root’s classical inputs, fresh definitions, visible uses, both lexical branch arms, simultaneous phi operands and returned identities. Its independent Inserts, Run and Visible judgments resolve phi inputs before introducing destinations. They do not assert computed values or probabilities.

The terminology change to OwnershipSafe under Issue #287 preserved the predicate and proof content. It created no new acceptance rule, assumption or guarantee. Exact clean-workspace discharge remains a distinct QS duty; quantitative Resource Safety remains an RS duty.

What the evidence establishes

tests/fixtures/constitution_v030/initial-guarantees/Review.lean exposes the actual elaborated theorem types, the declarative predicates and their axiom information. The proposal binds its captured output and the validation record, including the reviewed source identity and recorded build/audit/replay checks. The standard axiom basis is propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound; no project axiom was added.

The source hash identifies the reviewed implementation and proof definitions. It does not determine whether those predicates adequately express the intended two QS components. The separate human admission records that judgment. A locally observed native binary identity also does not prove native compiler or runtime correspondence and is not a portable release attestation.

The theorems include the actual Lean decoder computations in their acceptance witnesses. Correspondence with an independently specified external wire format, native IO/runtime, selected executable provenance, Rust decoding and re-materialization remain separate. The statements concern the Lean-decoded root; they do not by themselves establish source preservation or the meaning of an execution result or exported artifact.

These two components also do not establish ordinary-root quantum CPTP/effect soundness, clean/dirty workspace semantics, full source type or tuple-shape preservation, a requested algorithm’s meaning, hierarchy coverage, PR or quantitative RS. Those exclusions bound the admission; they do not waive the broader duties in the adopted interpretations.

Human decision and later continuity

The Guardian reviewed whether each independent property and its exact actual-checker formalization adequately expresses its stated narrow QS component and supports its admission with the checked proof evidence. The affirmative reply was: “2件とも提示された範囲・前提で妥当と認め、保証登録を承認する”. The original proposal retains proposed and human_adoption: null as the exact historical text submitted for review. The later event and live ledger record the affirmative decision through the authority process.

Admission of both components leaves QS-2026-01, PR-2026-01 and RS-2026-01 pending as broader obligations. It does not certify every production path or authorize a release. Later releases must connect each admitted component to their current actual acceptance and artifacts, preserving its meaning and premises with justified semantic transport when necessary. Retaining today’s old theorem or source hash is insufficient. The historical reviewed source and registry are retained beside the first validation record; governance/guarantees/current-evidence.json separately binds current proof evidence and acceptance sources. An unrelated source change can update that binding after checking without rewriting the protected meaning or human act.

The current checker protects the elaborated independent semantic dependency closure and every field of the actual Acceptance witness. Its fixed extractor compares exact definition bodies, types, constructors and recursor rules with a baseline rebuilt from the approved historical source archive. The proof lane also retains the original theorem and Acceptance/Artifact reviews. This matters because an unchanged theorem’s outer type can hide a weakened witness field. The retained enforcement counterexample at tests/fixtures/constitution_v030/witness-weakening/ compiled after replacing the original-packet binding with True; the live Lean comparison rejects that change even when mutable source identities are refreshed. It is a regression in evidence enforcement, not a counterexample to the admitted theorems.

This first identity transport permits formatting and theorem proof-body changes that preserve the exact elaborated closure. The actual current checker’s body may change within the protected dependency closure; its type and successful input-byte/original-root theorem types remain fixed and checked. Binder and universe names, module origins, definition proof subterms and semantic representations remain conservatively protected. Representation-changing transport is still unimplemented. The historical/current extraction and compiled weakening, decoder and proof-refactor examples are preserved in tests/fixtures/constitution_v030/initial-guarantees-continuity/.

Default checks validate recorded identities only. --verify-lean executes the fixed extractor in the built/audited current environment and fixes the current evidence record for the whole run, rejecting concurrent source/evidence replacement. A recorded hash or implication about an obsolete checker cannot substitute for that check. The original admission, two scoped guarantees and three broader pending duties are unchanged.

The live ledger uses schema v5, retaining the schema-v4 separation of admitted identities from current evidence. Each admitted entry has a canonical identity that binds its constitutional edition, interpreted obligation, human admission and exact reviewed proposal entry. That identity excludes mutable current source/proof evidence. Separate bindings must cover every registered guarantee exactly once through fixed verifier profiles; one QLV1 profile currently covers both admitted entries. Neither a new JSON approval nor a successful unregistered helper proof creates an admission. Historical v3 bytes are archived, and trusted-base checks reject removal or substitution of any earlier identity. The complete ledger and selected evidence remain fixed throughout live replay. The v4 identity migration kept the same two guarantees and three pending broader duties. The subsequent EXACT-2026-01 adoption adds a pending supplement across QS, PR and RS in v5; it creates no fourth jurisdiction or discharged guarantee. Release readiness and full constitutional conformance remain separate.

Project name and pronunciation

This is the canonical project-identity wording for Qleisli. Other introductions and naming guidance should link here or reproduce this meaning without changing it.

Qleisli is pronounced exactly like Kleisli. The name expresses a Kleisli-style lift of the classical software ecosystem into a quantum ecosystem. The spelling is Q + Kleisli. The initial Q denotes quantum: it changes the semantic world indicated by the spelling, not the pronunciation.

Metaphor and formal semantics

“Kleisli-style lift” is the name’s origin and a design metaphor. It does not require every language construct, compiler layer or theorem to be formalized as a literal Kleisli category or as one particular monad. Any formal categorical semantics is a separate technical claim that must be specified and justified independently under the authority hierarchy. The name itself changes no language acceptance rule or proof obligation.

The Q changes the world, not the pronunciation.

History

  • This wording follows the decision in Issue #234 for Qleisli 0.3.0.

Copyright 2026 Qleisli Project Contributors. SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0.

Documentation build environment

Contributors should begin with the architecture principle and authority hierarchy. Major language/tooling designs must record how they preserve that architecture before implementation.

Qleisli Programming Language is the book’s starting point. book.toml configures its source, metadata and HTML output; src/SUMMARY.md defines the chapter order.

Pinned mdBook

The authoritative tool pin is MDBOOK_VERSION: '0.5.4' in the check-docs job of the CI workflow. CI downloads the corresponding official Linux binary, verifies its pinned SHA-256 and checks mdbook --version before building. The HTML is retained as a CI artifact for review.

For a local source installation, run:

cargo install mdbook --locked --version 0.5.4
test "$(mdbook --version)" = "mdbook v0.5.4"
mdbook build docs
python3 scripts/check_book.py

Run the commands from the repository root and open target/mdbook/index.html. mdbook serve docs provides a local preview. These generated files are already ignored under target/; the Markdown sources are under docs/src/. Missing chapters fail the build instead of being created automatically. scripts/check_book.py reads the rendered book and the sources, as Checked rules describes.

The source installation uses mdBook’s own Rust requirements. A matching official binary is an alternative; neither choice changes Qleisli’s Rust MSRV or dependencies. The upstream Rust Book documents the same exact-version, locked source-installation pattern.

When updating mdBook, review its release notes, update the CI version and official binary checksum together, update the local commands here, then inspect the rendered book. This tool pin is separate from product-version maintenance.

Publishing the book

Pull requests build the book and check its links. After a push to main, CI packages the checked target/mdbook/ directory, mirrors its contents to the gh-pages branch and deploys the same archive to the published book. The repository uses GitHub Actions as its Pages publishing source. The github-pages environment allows deployments from main. The HTML renderer’s site-url is /Qleisli/ so the 404 page can load its styles and navigation even when a reader follows a broken nested URL.

Source authority and tool responsibilities

mdBook renders the specification; it does not participate in the specification.

Normative authority belongs to adopted source documents and decisions. A CONSTITUTION.md or Language Reference must state its adopted status and scope; neither is established by adding it to the book. Tutorial chapters are descriptive, and draft notation must stay identified as a draft.

mdBook is an external documentation CLI. It is not a Qargo dependency, part of the Qleisli toolchain, or something for qleisliup to manage. Its configuration controls presentation and book assembly, not language acceptance, qrate resolution or API introspection.

Qleisli-aware API documentation belongs to qlidoc. The current implementation offers qleisli doc for source documentation; this setup does not introduce a standalone qlidoc command. API extraction and semantic checks stay with the Qleisli ecosystem. mdBook may render their resulting documentation as content.

No external mdBook plugins are enabled. If a preprocessor or renderer such as KaTeX or a link checker is added, pin its version and installation alongside mdBook in the documentation CI, record the local setup here, and review their compatibility together. Such tools belong to this documentation environment. Use qli fences for Qleisli examples; mdBook’s Rust playground is disabled, and an HTML build does not execute or verify Qleisli programs.

The v1 algorithm goals describe planned capabilities and link to their design issues. Specification chapters derive from adopted decisions, the code and its proofs. Book links to repository material outside its chapters use repository URLs so they also work in the rendered HTML.

Style guide

The Language Reference follows the shape of The Rust Reference: each chapter states the rules of one subject, and a reader can skip how the compiler implements them. These rules apply to a chapter when a change writes or rewrites it. A chapter that predates them keeps its wording until its rewrite. Diagnostics and recovery is written by these rules, and Coherent basis maps shows the layout of a chapter on one construct.

Four chapters render adopted constitutional records and are exempt. They keep the wording that their records bind: ratification, authority hierarchy, initial interpretations and initial guarantees.

Voice

  • Use the present tense and the active voice. Write “the checker rejects the call”, not “the call will be rejected”.
  • Put one idea in each sentence. Split a sentence longer than about 30 words, and keep each paragraph to one topic.
  • Do not write “now”, “new”, “currently”, “still” or “remains” for the state of the implementation. The book describes the language as it is. Git and the changelog record how it changed.
  • Use “actual”, “exact” and “complete” only where the word carries a technical meaning, as in “an exact phase”.

Plain wording

A reader who has finished the lessons should be able to follow a Reference section on first reading. Prelude, imports and qualified names shows the wording.

  • Open a section by saying what its construct is for and when a program uses it. Then give the rules. Where a section begins with its syntax, this description follows the syntax, as Rules and their placement lays out.
  • Give each sentence a subject that acts: the checker, the program, the caller. Write “the checker reports that failure”, not “failure reporting occurs”.
  • Take a stack of nouns apart. Write “the effect that callers of the target see”, not “the caller-visible target effect”.
  • When a rule covers a list of cases, state the rule first and name the cases in a second sentence.
  • Give the reason for a rule only where the chapter or a linked rule states that reason. Do not invent one.
  • Plain wording changes no rule. Keep the force of every “must”, “must not” and “may”, and keep every diagnostic code, limit and identifier.

Terms

  • Define a term before you use it. Set the term in bold where the text defines it, and nowhere else.
  • Use one word for one concept.
  • Write “capability” for Applicable, Adjointable and Controllable, and “capability requirement” for an entry of a requires clause that names one. Write “access” for what a capability permits, as in “inverse access”, and for the excl and ctrl markers of a call.

Rules and their placement

  • Begin a chapter with a paragraph that defines its subject.
  • Lay out a section on a construct in this order: its syntax, a description, its rules as a bulleted list under the label “Rules:”, then examples.
  • Write a rule with “must”, “must not” or “may”, and name the diagnostic code of a program that breaks it.
  • Keep every rule in one place. Other chapters link to that section instead of restating the rule.
  • Put implementation detail in a quoted block that begins with Implementation note. Such a note names the component that does the work. It adds no rule, so a reader can skip it.
  • State a limit as a number.

What stays out of the body

  • Dated update notes, release names, and Issue or pull request numbers belong in a final section “History”. The body states the result of a decision.
  • State the limits of the implementation and the proof status once, in a section “Status and limits” near the end of the chapter. Keep the separation of code, tests, proof, preservation and specification review there.

Examples

  • Label a block qli for Qleisli source, text for grammar and output, and sh for commands.
  • Take an example from a source that a test checks, and say whether the checker accepts or rejects it.
  • In a lesson, ask readers to predict an observable result before they run the program. Change one expression at a time so they can explain the difference. When teaching from a rejected program, show the diagnostic alongside the expression that caused it and let readers try the repair.
  • When a later lesson reuses a project, name the file to edit and say whether a listing replaces the file or just one expression. Give readers an observable result to check before they make the next edit.

Checked rules

scripts/check_book.py enforces the rules below on the chapters that SUMMARY.md lists. The other rules of this guide need a reviewer. Passing the check is not a review of what a chapter says.

RuleChapters
No word of the form <T> outside a code span, because it renders as an HTML tagEvery chapter
Every code fence is closedEvery chapter
A code span in a table row writes a pipe as |, because a bare pipe ends the cellEvery chapter
No “now”, “new”, “newly”, “currently”, “still”, “remain”, “remains”, “remained” or “remaining” in proseChecked chapters
An Issue or pull request reference stands only in a section “History”Checked chapters
A paragraph has at most 120 words. A list item and a quoted block each count as one paragraph; a table row is not counted.Checked chapters
A code fence has the label qli, text, sh, toml or jsonChecked chapters

The word rule reads prose only. It skips code, link targets and words in double quotation marks, which mention a word rather than use it.

A checked chapter is a chapter in neither of two lists in the script:

  • EXEMPT names the four constitutional chapters that keep the wording of their records and the v1 goals chapter that links each goal to its design issue.
  • PENDING names the chapters that predate this guide. Remove a chapter from the list in the change that rewrites it. The check fails on a pending chapter that keeps the rules, and on a list entry that SUMMARY.md does not name.

A chapter that joins SUMMARY.md is therefore checked from its first change. python3 scripts/test_check_book.py runs the checker’s own tests.

Maintaining the book

The chapters of the book live directly in docs/src/. They are the only maintained copies. Edit the chapter files directly. The book builds with mdBook’s default preprocessors, without include wrappers or custom build steps.

The architecture chapters display SVGs rendered from the Mermaid sources in docs/src/architecture/diagrams/. If a diagram changes, regenerate its SVG with Mermaid CLI 12.2.0 from the repository root. The book build copies the rendered files.

for name in system compiler verifier rust-crates; do
  diagram="docs/src/architecture/diagrams/$name"
  mmdc --no-font-embed --svgId "qleisli-$name" \
    --input "$diagram.mmd" --output "$diagram.svg"
done

The lessons teach with executable programs. The architecture chapters follow the lessons in SUMMARY.md and refer to the projects and reports that the lessons produce, so keep the two parts in step. The roadmap identifies planned features explicitly. Repository root documents are linked where needed, not embedded. Links between chapters are relative; links to code, fixtures and build configuration use their repository URLs. No external plugin is required.
